articles.title: Quantifying the Impact of Postoperative Complications Using PROMIS-Global Physical Health Scores in Orthopaedic Trauma Patients.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study aimed to (1) correlate orthopaedic trauma postoperative complications and PROMIS-GPH scores and (2) quantify the impact of complications on reduction of scores.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: Multicenter of 3 institutions.

abstract.label: PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA
abstract.text: Included were all orthopaedic trauma patients with operative injuries from 2018 to 2024 who completed at least 1 postoperative PROMIS-Global Physical Health (PROMIS-GPH) survey at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, or 1 year.

abstract.label: OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS
abstract.text: Primary study outcome was the development of major or minor complications. Major complications were defined as any fracture-related reoperation within 1 year or fracture-related readmission within 90 days. Minor complications were defined as symptomatic hardware removal within 1 year or 90-day readmission or emergency department visit. Average PROMIS-GPH scores at each timepoint was compared between patients with major or minor complications and no complications.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 3475 orthopaedic trauma patients with operative injuries who completed at least 1 postoperative PROMIS-GPH survey were included. Female patients were 62.1% of the cohort. Average age of the entire cohort was 58.4 (range 18-103). The most common fracture subtypes were ankle injuries (21.9%) and hip injuries (21.8%). Of all patients, 9.2% had major complications and 13.6% minor complications. Of patients with no complications, 29.3% were in the lowest PROMIS-GPH quartile at some timepoint compared with 36.1% with minor complications and 43.6% with major complications (P < 0.0001). Being in the lowest quartile of PROMIS-GPH scores was a significant predictor of major complications (aOR 1.5, 95% confidence interval: 1.2-2.0, P = 0.002). At all timepoints, patients with no complications had significantly higher scores than patients with major or minor complications, by at least an average 1.5 points.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Significant associations between postoperative major or minor complications and poor PROMIS-GPH scores existed in orthopaedic trauma patients presenting for operative management.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Study. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Acute Suffering, Act of Togetherness and On-Scene Space: A Concept Synthesis for Caring in Prehospital Emergency Care.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Prehospital emergency care attends to patients experiencing acute suffering; a sudden and profound disruption affecting the person's life, body and existential well-being in the context of illness, injury or crisis. In this unpredictable and vulnerable setting, a central question emerges: how can caring needs be effectively met?

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: The aim of this paper is to develop a concept synthesis grounded in a caring science paradigm within the prehospital context, clarifying the nature of caring.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: A concept synthesis based on a caring science theoretical framework was conducted using a combined deductive-inductive approach, integrating theory, clinical experience and relevant literature through an abductive and iterative process.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The synthesis introduces three interrelated concepts: acute Suffering (S), act of Togetherness (T) and On-scene space (O), situated within Prehospital emergency care (P). These concepts collectively shape the STOP synthesis. STOP positions caring as the core of prehospital emergency care, emphasizing a holistic perspective that extends beyond a purely biological understanding. It provides a structured framework for understanding and practicing the complexity of caring in this setting.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Using the STOP-sign metaphor, the STOP synthesis highlights the importance of pausing in prehospital emergency care to recognize the patient as a multidimensional human being experiencing acute suffering. By integrating the concepts of acute Suffering, act of Togetherness and On-scene space within the prehospital context, the synthesis promotes a shift beyond a solely biomedical perspective toward a caring science understanding of suffering and care. The synthesis may support prehospital professionals, particularly nurses, in integrating caring and medical knowledge in clinical practice and provides a theoretical basis for future research, education and a holistic prehospital emergency care.

articles.title: Prospective Observational Study Assessing Patient Characteristics, Management and Early Outcomes of Major Trauma Patients With Prehospital Shock. A preliminary report of the Sydney COAST study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Despite advances in trauma resuscitation, significant gaps remain in understanding how early physiological and biochemical derangements influence clinical outcomes. The Sydney 'Clinical Outcomes following Acute Shock in Trauma' (COAST) registry was developed by clinicians containing both prehospital and in-hospital data, allowing for the identification of risk factors that influence early mortality for major trauma patients with shock. This study reports the formation of the registry and the patient cohort enrolled over its first 12 months.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A multi-centre, prospective registry of shocked adult trauma patients treated by prehospital medical teams and transported directly to a Sydney-based major trauma centre. Shock was defined as either (1) systolic blood pressure less than 100 mmHg, (2) shock index greater than one, (3) blood transfusion or (4) administration of inotropes. Descriptive statistics were used to report outcomes including injuries, pathology, transfusions, immediate intervention, mortality and length of stay.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Two hundred fifty seven patients were enrolled. The predominant shock criteria for inclusion was hypotension (90% of cases), whilst 53% received prehospital blood transfusion. Interventional haemorrhage control was required in 31% of cases, whilst 74% received in-hospital transfusion. Injury severity was high (median injury severity score of 27). Four-hour mortality was 4.7% (9% at 24-h and 21% at 30-days).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Consistent with recent observational studies, the Sydney COAST registry captured a cohort of critically ill trauma patients, not all of whom may have had haemorrhage. This will serve as an important dataset, allowing clinicians to better understand factors driving traumatic shock whilst exploring avenues for improving care in these cases.

articles.title: SIT, CARE, DO: A Point-of-Care Time-Out for Clinicians Using Artificial Intelligence Tools.

abstract.text: There is no shortage of principles surrounding the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical care, but these principles are poorly operationalised for use at the point of care. SIT, CARE, DO maps Australian and international guidance from five jurisdictions onto a nine-item time-out, framed as self-challenge questions before, during and after AI use. It is intended to help clinicians discharge their share of the distributed responsibility for safe integration of AI into clinical care.

articles.title: Supply of Fibrinogen Concentrate Across Queensland Health.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To describe fibrinogen concentrate (FC) supply across Queensland Health.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Statewide FC supply from January 2016 to September 2026 was analysed by service type, geography, major trauma designation, viscoelastic haemostatic assay (VHA) availability and temporal trends.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 24,717 g FC supplied, 97.0% was distributed to 54 hospitals, 2.0% to retrieval services and 1.0% to ambulance services. Of hospital supply, 25.4% reached regional and 6.1% remote/very remote hospitals; 66.2% was supplied to major trauma services and 92.9% to VHA-capable hospitals. Population-adjusted FC supply increased from 8.19 to 59.2 g per 100,000 population between 2016 and 2025.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: FC supply has increased substantially across Queensland, extending to regional, remote and prehospital services. This highlights the value of statewide patient-level utilisation data for haemovigilance.

articles.title: Educational Quality and Information Reliability of E-FAST Training Videos: A Multi-Rater Assessment Using an Overall Understandability and Actionability Composite.
articles.journal_full: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (E-FAST) requires adequate operator training. We evaluated the educational quality, information reliability, and overall composite understandability and actionability of E-FAST training videos on YouTube.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 74 videos identified using three predefined search terms. Two emergency physicians, one radiology specialist, and one radiology resident independently assessed videos using the Global Quality Scale (GQS), JAMA Benchmark Criteria, DISCERN, and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Audiovisual Materials (PEMAT-A/V). The study-specific PEMAT-A/V composite equally weighted understandability and actionability; rounded reviewer-level scores were averaged without further rounding. Adequacy was defined as ≥ 70%. Spearman correlations, logistic regression, and threshold-based and continuous-outcome sensitivity analyses were performed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Median GQS and DISCERN scores were 3.50 and 59.75, respectively. Overall, 33 videos (44.6%) met the composite PEMAT-A/V adequacy threshold. Institutional videos had higher GQS, DISCERN, and composite PEMAT-A/V scores than individual videos, whereas the JAMA difference was not significant. PEMAT-A/V scores correlated positively with GQS (r = 0.669), DISCERN (r = 0.542), and JAMA (r = 0.353). In the primary adjusted model, GQS (OR = 12.95, 95% CI: 1.80-93.31) and institutional uploader status (OR = 4.52, 95% CI: 1.14-18.18) were associated with adequate classification. The positive GQS association persisted in sensitivity analyses, whereas associations for uploader type and other scales varied across outcome definitions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: More than half of the videos did not meet the study-specific composite PEMAT-A/V adequacy threshold despite generally favourable quality and reliability ratings. GQS showed the most consistent adjusted association with the composite outcome. These ratings should not be interpreted as evidence of improved learning or clinical performance.

articles.title: Medication Safety Risks Associated With Inappropriate Use of Non-Crushable Tablets in Enterally Fed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Hospitalized patients receiving enteral feeding are at high risk of medication administration errors. In clinical practice, non-crushable oral tablets may be inappropriately prescribed, potentially resulting in adverse outcomes. This study examined the association between inappropriate use of non-crushable oral tablets during hospitalization and early post-discharge emergency department (ED) visits among patients receiving enteral feeding.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a nationwide population-based cohort study using a national health insurance claims database in 2020, including 173,476 hospitalized patients receiving enteral feeding. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the association between inappropriate use of non-crushable tablets and the hazard of the first ED visit during the 3-day post-discharge follow-up period.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 173,476 patients, 40.2% were exposed to inappropriate medication use. Exposure was associated with a significantly higher hazard of a first ED visit during the 3-day post-discharge follow-up period (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.954; 95% confidence interval, 1.721-2.217). The association varied significantly across age groups and inpatient departments, with the largest adjusted hazard ratios observed among patients aged <65 years and those treated in hematology and oncology, infectious diseases, and neurosurgery. Selected comorbidities, including hypertension, cerebrovascular accident, and dementia, were also associated with a higher hazard of an early ED visit.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Orders for non-crushable tablets among hospitalized patients receiving enteral feeding were common and were associated with a substantially higher hazard of an early post-discharge ED visit. The association varied across age groups and inpatient departments, although these subgroup findings should be interpreted cautiously. These findings highlight an important medication safety concern during transitions of care and support further evaluation of system-level strategies, including prescribing safeguards, clinical decision support, and multidisciplinary medication review, to improve the quality and safety of medication management.

articles.title: Pooled Prevalence of Infectious Diseases Among First Responders in the Prehospital Setting: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis by Occupation.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2, τ2, and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%-5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonization. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%-25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%-12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

articles.title: Safety and Clinical Impact of Emergency Department Closed Reduction for Gartland Type III Supracondylar Humerus Fractures.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pediatric type 3 supracondylar humerus fractures (SCHFs) are typically immobilized in situ before definitive operative fixation because of concern for neurovascular injury during closed reduction. This study assesses the safety and clinical outcomes of emergency department (ED) closed reduction versus in situ splinting for type 3 SCHFs before definitive fixation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective review was conducted of all pediatric extension-type 3 SCHFs that underwent closed reduction versus no reduction by orthopaedic surgery residents in the ED at a single Level 1 trauma center over a 5-year period. Data included pre- and postreduction neurovascular examinations, multiple radiographic parameters, durations of time between injury, consult, and reduction to the operating room (OR), total operative time, and OR fluoroscopy duration.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 112 patients, 54 underwent closed reduction (CR) while 58 were not reduced (NR). Nine (20%) patients in the CR group and 9 (18%) patients in the NR group had abnormal neurological exams on presentation. Four (8%) patients in the CR group and 2 (4%) patients in the NR group had abnormal vascular exams. All 4 patients who underwent closed reduction had improved vascular exams from Doppler-able to palpable radial pulses (P=0.12). No vascular injuries occurred with closed reduction. Importantly, 6 patients in the NR group with initial normal exams developed abnormal neurological deficits while awaiting surgical fixation (P=0.03). The CR group demonstrated significantly improved radiographic parameters postreduction, including AP and lateral displacement, anterior humeral line displacement, lateral Baumann angle, and hourglass angle. The time from consult or reduction to OR was significantly less for the NR group compared with the CR group (9.83 vs. 13.45 h; P<0.01). The time from injury to the OR was also significantly less in the NR group (21.0 vs. 17.0 h; P=0.02). The CR group trended towards shorter operative times (33 vs. 40 min; P=0.15).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Closed reduction of pediatric type 3 SCHFs in the ED by orthopaedic surgery residents is safe and can improve both neurovascular deficits and radiographic fracture alignment. As most pediatric extremity fractures undergo closed reduction in the ED, type 3 SCHFs should not be considered an exception.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level III-retrospective comparative study.

articles.title: The unexpected orange hue in a patient with spondyloarthritis receiving biologic therapy.
Dental Coverage, Fluoridation, and Emergency Department Use: Implications of Recent Policy Changes.
articles.journal_full: Inquiry : a journal of medical care organization, provision and financing

abstract.text: Emergency departments in the United States are increasingly being used as a last resort for dental problems that could often be prevented or treated in routine dental care settings. Non-traumatic dental conditions, including dental caries, abscesses, pulpal and periapical disease, and periodontal disease, lead to millions of ED visits and billions of dollars in treatment costs. These visits rarely provide definitive dental treatment, and the burden is higher among Medicaid, Medicare, and uninsured patients. This policy insights discusses how three recent policy developments may worsen this problem: Medicaid cuts under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, state-level rollbacks of community water fluoridation, and the CMS rule excluding routine adult dental services from Marketplace Essential Health Benefits. Although these policies are different, they share a common pathway of weakening access to prevention and routine dental care. We argue that reducing preventable dental ED visits will require protecting Medicaid adult dental benefits, restoring flexibility to include adult dental benefits in Marketplace plans, preserving fluoridation, and building stronger ED-to-dental referral systems.

articles.title: Determinants of parental decisions to attend pediatric emergency departments for non-urgent conditions: a cross-sectional study.

abstract.text: Non-urgent visits to Pediatric Emergency Departments (PED) contribute to overcrowding and delay urgent care. This study aimed to explore the extent and characteristics of the phenomenon of non-urgent visits in the PED, and to identify parents' and children's predisposing factors associated with visiting the PED for non-urgent conditions. In this cross-sectional study, 313 parents of children who arrived at the PED in a general hospital completed a questionnaire. The visits were categorized as urgent or non-urgent according to the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale. A high proportion (56%) of visits were non-urgent. Prior consultation with a family physician was identified as a significant protective factor. Non-urgent visits were more common among parents of younger children and parents with fewer children. Previous contact with a family doctor or pediatrician predicted a visit to the PED. Encouraging parents to consult a physician before visiting the PED and providing them with accessible information about primary health services can help reduce non-urgent visits. Incorporating information on identifying urgent and non-urgent situations into parent education immediately after birth or during meetings with a pregnancy and childbirth nurse are recommended.

articles.title: Arthroscopic Stabilization Reduces Recurrence but May Delay Return to Sport After First-Time Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocation in Elite Male Athletes: A Systematic Review.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To evaluate arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management for first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation in adult athletes, with a focus on recurrent instability, return-to-play rates, and time to return to play.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Five databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Studies comparing arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management in adult athletes (≥18 years) with first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation were included. The primary outcome was recurrent instability. Secondary outcomes included return-to-play rates and time to return to play. A narrative synthesis was performed given the nonrandomized and heterogeneous nature of included studies. Evidence certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Five studies (232 participants: 111 operative, 121 nonoperative) were included. Recurrent instability rates ranged from 3% to 14% in the operative group and 24% to 80% in the nonoperative group. Return-to-play rates were high for both approaches (operative: 93%-100%; nonoperative: 97%-100%). Nonoperative management was associated with earlier return to sport (2.3-5.7 weeks vs 18.7-39.3 weeks for operative management in studies reporting this outcome). All studies involved elite athletes, with female athletes substantially under-represented.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Arthroscopic stabilization was consistently associated with lower rates of recurrent instability than nonoperative management after first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation but required a longer time to return to play. Nonoperative management enabled an earlier return to play but was associated with higher recurrence. The evidence is limited primarily to male military, collegiate, and professional athletes, restricting generalizability to female, recreational, and broader adult athletic populations.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

articles.title: When It All Falls On the Physicians: A Qualitative Study of Physician Workforce Changes Post-Dobbs in Four States With Abortion Bans.
articles.journal_full: Women's health issues : official publication of the Jacobs Institute of Women's Health

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: We aimed to explore how abortion bans in four highly restrictive states affected physician workforce dynamics among physicians of diverse specialties after the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization decision.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The Medical Integrity Initiative conducted in-depth interviews with physicians in Alabama, Idaho, Oklahoma, and Tennessee, states with strict abortion bans and severe legal penalties for physicians. Participants included specialists in emergency medicine, maternal-fetal medicine, medical genetics, obstetrics, oncology, and reproductive endocrinology and infertility. We used stratified and snowball sampling and conducted interviews via Zoom from July to October 2024. Grounded theory methodology informed the inductive approach to data analysis. We began with open (descriptive) coding and followed it with axial (interpretive) analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirty-two physicians across all specialties reported new challenges following the Dobbs decision. We identified the following overarching themes: 1) heightened liability concerns, 2) shifting burden of care onto academic hospitals, 3) added advocacy responsibilities, 4) emotional strain and ethical dilemma of leaving the state, and 5) increased challenges regarding workforce size and workload. Challenges that participants described included colleagues' exodus, difficulty recruiting providers and trainees, and labor and delivery unit closures. Many reported that they considered leaving their state. Participants expressed a desire for their institutions to support evidence-based clinical practice.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Physicians experienced changes in workforce composition and responsibilities following the Dobbs decision. Collective action and robust occupational, legal, and mental health support from their institutions and medical societies might enable physicians to safely stay and sustainably advocate in states with abortion bans.

articles.title: Comparison of subarachnoid block using hyperbaric levobupivacaine plus fentanyl versus hyperbaric bupivacaine plus fentanyl in elective lower limb orthopaedic procedures: A randomized controlled study.
articles.journal_full: Revista espanola de anestesiologia y reanimacion

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Racemic bupivacaine is the reference agent for subarachnoid block, but its cardiotoxic potential has prompted interest in its S-enantiomer, levobupivacaine. We compared intrathecal hyperbaric levobupivacaine plus fentanyl with hyperbaric bupivacaine plus fentanyl in lower limb orthopaedic surgery.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Eighty patients with American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status I or II, aged 18-60 years, undergoing elective lower limb orthopaedic surgery were randomly allocated to 12.5 mg of 0.5% hyperbaric levobupivacaine with 25 µg fentanyl (Group A) or 12.5 mg of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine with 25 µg fentanyl (Group B). The primary outcome was duration of analgesia; secondary outcomes were block characteristics, haemodynamic variables, and complications.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Seventy-nine patients were analysed (Group A = 40, Group B = 39). Duration of analgesia was comparable (192.3 ± 40.0 vs. 181.6 ± 40.6 min; mean difference 10.7 min, 95% CI-7.4 to 28.7; p = 0.243). Group A had slower onset of complete motor block and longer time to peak sensory level (p < 0.05), but faster motor recovery (76.4 ± 14.1 vs. 119.0 ± 14.8 min; p < 0.001). Postoperative pain scores and rescue analgesic requirements were lower in Group A, and complications occurred only in Group B (p = 0.005). Haemodynamic profiles were comparable.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Hyperbaric levobupivacaine with fentanyl has a slower onset, a comparable duration of analgesia, and faster motor recovery than hyperbaric bupivacaine with fentanyl, and is an effective alternative for lower limb orthopaedic surgery.

articles.title: Multidisciplinary Learning Profiles in Surgical Services: A VARK and Experiential Learning Theory Analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Surgical services engage multidisciplinary residents from various specialties; however, the educational delivery frequently adopts a "one-size-fits-all" model. This reliance on passive, aural-visual instruction may not adequately address residents' diverse cognitive preferences, leading to a misalignment between instructional design and residents' specific needs.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To identify Visual, Aural, Read/Write, and Kinesthetic (VARK) learning preferences among surgical and nonsurgical residents who rotate through surgery services and examine associations with specialty, gender, and postgraduate year (PGY).

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: This is a single-institution, retrospective, cross-sectional study that assessed VARK learning style profiles in general surgery, emergency medicine (EM), obstetrics and gynecology (OB-GYN), and orthopedics residents through the lens of Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory, using descriptive statistics and Chi-square analyses.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: St. Luke's University Health Network, at the level I and level II academic trauma centers located in Bethlehem and Easton, Pennsylvania.

abstract.label: PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: A total of 123 residents in general surgery, EM, OB-GYN, and orthopedics who rotated through Trauma and Surgical Critical Care from 2023 to 2025.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: This study included 78 male and 45 female residents. Multimodal was the most common preference (N = 60; 48.8%), followed by Kinesthetic (N = 40; 32.5%). OB-GYN uniquely favored Aural as a secondary preference, while EM and Orthopedics demonstrated the strongest Kinesthetic profiles. Gender was statistically significantly associated with VARK preferences (p = 0.037). Females predominantly preferred Multimodal (28; 62.2%) compared to males (28; 41%). In contrast, males showed higher Kinesthetic preferences (27; 34.6%) than females (13; 28.9%). Learning profiles remained stable across PGY levels.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: These findings indicate that a uniform instructional approach is suboptimal. Educators should move away from passive observation to active, multimodal engagement, incorporating kinesthetic and specialty-aligned strategies to better support the diverse educational needs of residents in high-acuity surgical services.

articles.title: Respiratory Infections at Mass Gatherings: A Travel-Medicine Review with Hajj and Umrah as a Longitudinal Case Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Mass gatherings combine international mobility with dense, repeated contact and can amplify respiratory infections across travel corridors. Hajj, Umrah and Kumbh Mela, offer a uniquely recurrent case study, while other religious or sporting mega-events, and music or cultural festivals provide contrasting exposure systems.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A focused narrative review was conducted of peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews, and authoritative public-health guidance. Searches and project evidence synthesis prioritized publications from January 2021 to August 2026, with selected foundational sources. We examined respiratory symptoms, laboratory detections, clinical disease, vaccination, antimicrobial use and resistance, surveillance, environmental modifiers, and pre-, during-, and post-travel practice. No meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias scoring was undertaken.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Respiratory risk is determined less by attendance alone than by contact intensity, duration, ventilation, vocalization, shared accommodation, traveler susceptibility, and pathogen circulation. Recent Hajj evidence confirms a substantial burden of respiratory symptoms and clinical consultations, but estimates vary because denominators range from volunteers and tested samples to healthcare encounters. Rhinovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and bacterial pneumonia remain important. There is continued abuse of antibiotics for predominantly viral syndromes and acquisition of resistant organisms link individual care to global antimicrobial resistance. Syndromic, laboratory, event-based, genomic, and wastewater surveillance are complementary, not interchangeable. Heat, dust, air quality, fatigue, and differential access to protective infrastructure modify respiratory symptoms, severity, and care seeking. Comparative events share mechanisms but not directly transferable rates.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Travel-medicine practice should treat mass gatherings as longitudinal exposure systems spanning preparation, transport, the event, and return. Layered vaccination, risk-based masking, ventilation and crowd-flow measures, prompt diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, and explicit travel histories, can reduce respiratory morbidity while preserving denominator discipline and access to protective infrastructure.

articles.title: Integrating Social Determinants of Health Into Emergency Medicine Clerkships: A Qualitative Study of Student Reflections.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Social determinants of health (SDH) significantly influence emergency department (ED) care and patient outcomes, yet experiential learning opportunities in SDH remain inconsistently integrated into clinical education. Prior work has been effective but resource intensive. We sought to explore an adapted SDH-focused clinical experience that built on prior curricula and pre-clerkship SDH instruction while minimizing additional non-clinical resources.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We implemented a semi-structured SDH-focused experience within a required emergency medicine (EM) clerkship which sought to integrate prior knowledge from a pre-clerkship SDH curriculum. In the ED, students partnered with care managers or social workers to identify patients affected by SDH, conducted patient interviews, and completed written reflections. De-identified reflections from one academic year (2023-2024) were analyzed using an inductive thematic analysis approach. Two investigators independently coded an initial subset, developed a shared codebook, and applied iterative constant comparison to generate themes with investigator triangulation to enhance trustworthiness.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Students described intersecting barriers to care, including language discordance, financial insecurity, and immigration-related challenges. Reflections also linked these barriers to direct clinical consequences such as delays in care, limited follow-up access, and patients leaving against medical advice. Students described how communication barriers and limited interpreter availability impacted care delivery and safety. Reflections also described structural inequities and the role of interdisciplinary teams in mitigating these challenges. Two additional themes, chronic illness and aging and health systems science, were interpreted as cross-cutting factors that modified how SDH were experienced rather than as determinants themselves.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: A semi-structured, experiential SDH curriculum embedded within the ED clerkship elicited reflections in which students identified and interpreted real-world barriers to care. These findings describe how students applied SDH concepts in the ED rather than demonstrating change attributable to the activity. This approach offers a feasible model for embedding SDH learning within existing clinical workflows.

articles.title: Wake-Up Call for the Right Ventricle: Rethinking Pulmonary Embolism Diagnostics in Critical Care.
articles.journal_full: Australasian journal of ultrasound in medicine

articles.title: Association of a Fever Clinic Package With Waiting Time Among Walk-in Emergency Department Patients Ineligible for Fever-Clinic Streaming.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: Seasonal surges of patients with fever may delay emergency department (ED) care. This study examined whether a multicomponent fever clinic package was associated with waiting time among walk-in ED patients ineligible for fever-clinic streaming.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This single-center retrospective before-and-after study compared year-end/new year periods in 2024-2025 and 2025-2026. The primary outcome was time from registration to first physician documentation, used as a proxy for initial physician assessment. Gamma generalized linear models were adjusted for patient characteristics, physician staffing, preceding-hour demand, study day, and arrival time. A calendar-day cluster-robust analysis and an interaction analysis between study period and arrival mode were also performed. Post-assessment throughput was exploratory.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 2056 ED visits, 793 walk-in visits ineligible for fever-clinic streaming had evaluable waiting time. Median waiting time decreased from 54 to 26 min (p < 0.001). The period with the fever clinic package was associated with shorter waiting times (adjusted mean ratio 0.57, 95% confidence interval 0.46-0.70; p < 0.001), and calendar-day cluster-robust inference was consistent with this association. The association differed by arrival mode (p for interaction < 0.001), with model-estimated waiting time decreasing among walk-in visits but not among ambulance arrivals. No consistent adjusted difference was observed in post-assessment throughput.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The period with the fever clinic package was associated with shorter waiting times among walk-in ED patients ineligible for fever-clinic streaming, without a consistent adjusted difference in post-assessment throughput. Residual between-period confounding and inseparable package components preclude causal attribution; studies with contemporaneous comparators are warranted.

articles.title: Clinical Profiles Among Adolescents Referred for Suspected Clinical High Risk for Psychosis: an Exploratory Retrospective Study.

abstract.text: IntroductionThe Clinical High Risk of psychosis (CHRp) concept is widely used to identify adolescents at risk of psychotic disorder. However, current tools lack specificity regarding actual transition, as they struggle to distinguish developmental vulnerabilities from true prodromal psychotic states.MethodsThis retrospective monocentric study included 26 French adolescents aged 11-18 referred between 2021 and 2023 to a specialized CHRp consultation. The multidisciplinary evaluation, involving involving child and adolescent and adult psychiatry professionals, combined the CAARMS, developmental and attachment-based interviews, and final synthesis considering differential diagnoses.ResultsNine adolescents were classified as CHRp, and 5 of them transitioned to psychosis. CHRp adolescents were significantly younger and more often referred through emergency department. An exploratory multidimensional analysis identified two clinical profiles: a psychosis-spectrum profile and a broader psychological and environmental vulnerability profile characterized by attachment-related difficulties, child welfare placement, and self-harm behaviors, without transition to psychosis.ConclusionA diagnostic approach grounded in developmental and environmental specificities may enhance the predictive specificity of CHRp status in adolescents. Differentiating psychotic vulnerability from alternative psychopathological trajectories-particularly attachment-related and intrafamilial relational difficulties-may appear crucial for tailoring early interventions. It may help identify a more homogeneous and genuinely at-risk population.

articles.title: Mitigating Failure Modes in Next-Generation Batteries via High-Entropy Materials: A Cross-System Review.

abstract.text: The demand for advanced energy storage drives the exploration of novel battery materials. High-entropy materials (HEMs), multicomponent alloys, oxides, and related compounds with high configurational entropy, stabilize structures and create synergistic "cocktail" effects that mitigate dendrite growth, volume expansion, and side reactions. This review critically examines how the structural heterogeneity of HEMs influences electrochemical performance across battery components. We first discuss anodes, where HEMs suppress volume change and improve cycling stability, and then cathodes, including disordered rock-salt and layered HEMs for Li-, Na-, and K-ion systems. For electrolytes, we distinguish multi-component liquid formulations from high-entropy solid electrolytes (garnets, argyrodites, NASICONs and halides), which widen electrochemical windows and enable low-temperature operation. In Li-S and metal-air batteries, HEM catalysts benefit from multi-site adsorption and bifunctional activity; we compare them semi-quantitatively with low-entropy Li-S catalysts and distinguish the requirements of Li-O2 and CO2/H2O-containing Li-air operation. A cross-system analysis then maps shared failure modes to entropy-driven strategies across monovalent, multivalent, and catalytic systems. Finally, we discuss the characterization challenges that limit mechanistic understanding and outline future directions, including AI-guided materials design.

articles.title: The global research landscape of emergency medical services in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major cause of death, and emergency medical services (EMS) are central to recognition, resuscitation, transport, and linkage to post-arrest care. Although previous bibliometric studies have mapped the broader cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation literature, the intersection of EMS and OHCA warrants focused characterization.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We performed a retrospective bibliometric analysis of records indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 1972 through June 2026. The search combined OHCA terms with terms for EMS, paramedics, and emergency medical technicians. Annual output, research categories, journals, authors, and countries were described. VOSviewer version 1.6.20 was used for author co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and cited-reference co-citation analyses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The search identified 3,005 records. Annual output increased markedly after 2010, peaked at 244 publications in 2021, and remained above 200 publications per year from 2022 to 2025; 130 records were indexed for the partial 2026 year. Emergency Medicine (1,745; 58.1%) and Critical Care Medicine (1,014; 33.7%) were the most frequently assigned Web of Science categories. Resuscitation published 694 records (23.1%). The United States had the greatest country-level output (1,022; 34.0%), followed by Japan (375; 12.5%) and Canada (281; 9.4%). The most prolific author was Shin SD (98 publications). Co-authorship mapping showed registry-centered regional communities, while keyword analysis yielded ten interpreted domains spanning epidemiology, resuscitation interventions, dispatch, registries, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, equity, and technology-related topics. Co-citation analysis identified four major intellectual communities.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: EMS-focused OHCA publications indexed in Web of Science show sustained output and international collaboration associated with established registries. Limited visibility of low- and middle-income settings within this database warrants further investigation. Equity, implementation, and digital and resuscitative technologies are potential areas for further research; the pooled network analysis does not establish their temporal growth.

articles.title: Early clinical experience with vericiguat after acute decompensated heart failure in elderly patients with HFrEF: a prospective observational study.

abstract.text: Vericiguat has demonstrated clinical benefit in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), particularly in those at high risk of recurrent heart failure events. However, evidence regarding its early use in elderly patients following hospitalization for acute decompensated HF (ADHF) remains limited. In this prospective single-center case series, 143 consecutive patients aged > 70 years hospitalized for ADHF with HFrEF were enrolled and vericiguat was administrated. Clinical evaluations, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), six-minute walk test (6MWT), Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ), and laboratory parameters were assessed at baseline and after 4 weeks. After 4 weeks of treatment with vericiguat, 44.8% of patients were in NYHA class II and 55.2% in NYHA class III, no patients were in NYHA class IV (p < 0.001); LVEF improved from 34 ± 4.7% to 46.8 ± 7.5% (p < 0.0001); exercise capacity increased significantly (p < 0.001), while a significant decrease in MLHF-Q, NT-proBNP levels and hsCRP was observed (p < 0.001). No symptomatic hypotension, syncope or relevant deterioration in renal function or electrolytes occurred during the observation period. In this single-arm cohort of older patients with HFrEF recently stabilized after ADHF, initiation of vericiguat was feasible and coincided with substantial short-term changes in functional status, LVEF, and circulating biomarkers, without major safety signals during 4 weeks of observation. Given the absence of a control group, these changes cannot be attributed to vericiguat and may reflect, at least in part, recovery from the acute event, decongestion, optimization of background therapy, learning effects, and regression to the mean. These findings should therefore be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in controlled studies.

articles.title: Acute Care Utilization and Cost Outcomes of Home-Based Palliative Care for Persons Living with Dementia in the United States: A Systematic Review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Given the shift toward value-based payment models, which reward high-quality and cost-effective care, an increasing number of palliative care programs are being integrated across care settings in health systems and organizations in the United States to reduce patient use of more costly services such as hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits. Home-based palliative care (HBPalC) is one community-based palliative care delivery model that may help delay facility and nursing home placement and reduce hospital use and costs.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This review synthesized evidence on hospital utilization and cost outcomes associated with HBPalC among people living with dementia (PLWD) in the United States.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: PubMed, Embase, and Cumulated Index in Nursing and Allied Health Literature were searched from inception through October 2025. All U.S.-based studies were included if samples included PLWD and the study examined the impact of HBPalC on hospital utilization (i.e., hospitalization and ED use) or health care costs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of eight studies were included. Overall, HBPalC provided core services such as symptom management and advanced care planning. PLWD-specific HBPalC focused on addressing neurobehavioral symptoms and supporting caregivers. HBPalC was consistently associated with reductions in hospitalization and associated costs, although evidence for changes in ED utilization was not available, with no studies reporting ED outcomes for PLWD specifically.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: HBPalC was associated with reduced hospitalization, but its impact on ED use was inconclusive for PLWD. Most studies had heterogeneous patient samples and did not report PLWD-specific outcomes. There is a lack of HBPalC specifically designed for PLWD, and more studies are needed to evaluate HBPalC's impact on ED use among PLWD.

articles.title: Impact of Hands-On Pediatric Emergency Training on Wound Suturing, Airway Management, and Orthopedic Casting Skills: Prospective Pre-Post Interventional Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Opportunities to practice low-frequency skills for high-acuity pediatric emergency procedures in clinical settings are limited. The Basic Emergency Skills Techniques 3N1 (BEST 3N1) workshop was designed as a structured, hands-on training program to support procedural skill development among pediatric emergency care practitioners.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to evaluate preworkshop to postworkshop changes in procedural performance and knowledge after a 3-day hands-on pediatric emergency skills workshop.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A quasi-experimental prospective pre-post interventional study was conducted during the 8th BEST 3N1 workshop, held from February 11 to 13, 2025, at the Simulation and Skills Development Centre, Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The workshop included 24 scheduled continuing medical education hours in 3 domains: wound suturing, pediatric airway management, and pediatric orthopedic emergencies and casting. Procedural performance was assessed using complete paired preworkshop and postworkshop data for each assessment. Day 1 wound suturing and day 2 airway management were assessed using 4-item checklists scored from 0 to 8. Day 3 orthopedic casting competence was assessed using a keyword-based rubric covering equipment, procedural steps, and postapplication care, with a total score range of 0 to 30. Written knowledge was assessed using a 30-item multiple-choice test.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The number of paired observations differed in assessments because the analysis was based on complete matched preworkshop and postworkshop data for each outcome. Day 1 wound suturing checklist mean scores increased from 4.14 (SD 1.72) to 7.72 (SD 0.68) among 88 paired participants, with a mean change of 3.58 (SD 1.71; P<.001) points. Day 2 airway management checklist scores increased from 5.47 (SD 1.88) to 7.81 (SD 0.56) among 77 paired participants, with a mean change of 2.34 (SD 1.96; P<.001) points. Day 3 orthopedic casting total competence scores increased from 4.20 to 6.39 among 77 paired participants, with a mean change of 2.19 (SD 1.72; 95% CI 1.80-2.58; P<.001). Written knowledge scores increased from 19.04 (SD 3.77) to 22.32 (SD 3.23) among 94 paired participants, with a mean change of 3.28 (95% CI 2.16-4.39; P<.001) points.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The BEST 3N1 workshop was associated with improved checklist-based procedural performance, orthopedic casting competence, and written knowledge among pediatric emergency care practitioners. These findings support the use of structured hands-on workshops for high-acuity, low-frequency pediatric emergency skills.

articles.title: How I Do It: An Intensivist's guide to RV Failure and Right Ventricular Assist Devices.
authors: Cardiology/CV Surgery Section, Pulmonary Vascular Disease and Cardiovascular Network.

abstract.text: Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a high-mortality form of cardiogenic shock frequently encountered in critical illness and is often underrecognized due to its heterogeneous presentation. This article presents a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to the diagnosis and management of acute RVF using a longitudinal case in the intensive care unit. We highlight practical bedside tools for recognition, including point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and review targeted strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, and contractility support. Special emphasis is placed on airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in appropriately selected patients. This bedside "How I Do It" guide is written for intensivists and pulmonary/critical care clinicians and translates advanced hemodynamic and device concepts into practical decision points for acute care management.

articles.title: Ultrasound Teaching in UK Undergraduate Medical Education: A National Survey.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Ultrasound teaching is increasingly incorporated into undergraduate medical education (UGME), yet its implementation within UK medical schools remains poorly described. This study aimed to provide the first comprehensive national overview of ultrasound teaching across UK UGME curricula.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in 2025 among UK medical schools. Respondents provided data on ultrasound curriculum integration, teaching delivery, faculty involvement, assessment methods and implementation barriers. Descriptive statistics were used to analyse responses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirty-nine of 43 eligible medical schools responded (91% response rate). Twenty-six schools (67%) currently include formal ultrasound teaching in their curriculum, and seven further schools planned to introduce it in the 2025/26 academic year (85% if implemented). Most (69%) deliver ultrasound teaching across both early/pre-clinical and later/clinical years. Anatomy (81%) and procedural skills (65%) were the most common domains. The median total ultrasound teaching time was 5hours (IQR 3-10; n = 24), with 88% of schools providing ≤10hours. Small-group hands-on sessions were the predominant teaching method (96%), and 69% of schools did not assess ultrasound knowledge/skills. The main implementation barriers were limited curriculum capacity and trained faculty shortage (54% each). Overall, 59% of respondents supported inclusion of ultrasound as a mandatory GMC competency for graduates.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Ultrasound teaching is gaining momentum within UK UGME. However, considerable variation exists in content, duration and assessment. Addressing faculty shortages, curriculum capacity and the absence of national competency standards will be essential to ensure consistent, high-quality ultrasound education across UK medical schools.

articles.title: Comparing behavioral outputs across automated tracking software reveals platform-dependent variability in zebrafish neurobehavioral analysis.

abstract.text: The zebrafish (Danio rerio) is a prominent vertebrate model in behavioral neuroscience, with the novel tank diving test (NTT) representing one of the most validated paradigms for assessing anxiety-like responses and vertical exploration. Although automated video-tracking software are widely used to quantify behaviors, the results obtained from different programs are rarely equivalent, representing a critical challenge for data comparability. Variations in detection algorithms and coordinate processing may compromise the interpretation of behavioral outcomes and reproducibility across studies. Here, we aimed to systematically assess the agreement, accuracy, and reproducibility of behavioral metrics across different video-tracking platforms, and to determine whether a standardized post-analysis approach could improve cross-system comparability. To achieve our goal, we compared four well-established systems: ANY-maze and EthoVision (closed-source software), and TrackR and ToxTrac (open-source software), using the zebrafish NTT paradigm. To enable comparison across platforms, an independent post-analysis approach was applied using the CartesianBehaviour package, which utilizes spatial coordinates to calculate movement patterns and minimize biases introduced by software-specific data processing. Our results revealed differences in tracking accuracy and intra- and inter-software data variability, demonstrating systematic discrepancies in behavioral parameters such as total distance traveled and time spent in the top area. Despite these differences, the use of a common post-analysis framework showed strong positive correlations across systems. Finally, our findings demonstrate the lack of direct equivalence between behavioral metrics obtained from different tracking platforms and reinforce the importance of standardizing post-analysis to ensure data reproducibility in neurobehavioral research.

articles.title: Apparent temperature, heat waves, and unintentional injury-related emergency medical service calls: A case-crossover study.

abstract.text: Evidence on apparent temperature, heat waves, and unintentional injuries remains limited. We aimed to examine the short-term associations of apparent temperature and heat waves with injury-related emergency medical service (EMS) calls and variation across injury types and population subgroups. We conducted a time-stratified case-crossover study of 170,538 unintentional injury-related EMS calls in Minhang District, Shanghai, from July 2021 to June 2025. Conditional logistic regression with distributed lag models evaluated apparent temperature and nine heat-wave definitions combining temperature percentiles and consecutive-day durations. Cumulative associations were summarized over lag 0-2 days for apparent temperature and lag 0-1 days for heat waves. The cumulative exposure-response curve generally increased with apparent temperature, with the estimated minimum at the lower boundary of the observed range. Comparing the 99th percentile (42.5 °C) with this minimum (-2.9 °C), the cumulative odds ratio (OR) was 1.21 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.12-1.31). The apparent-temperature association was largest for traffic injuries (OR 1.80, 95% CI: 1.56-2.07). Among adults aged 18-64 years, the OR was 1.38 (95% CI: 1.24-1.53), with evidence of overall heterogeneity across the three age groups (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted q = 0.001). For heat waves defined by daily mean temperature at or above the 95th percentile for ≥ 3 consecutive days, the cumulative OR was 1.07 (95% CI: 1.03-1.11). High apparent temperature was associated with increased odds of unintentional injury-related EMS calls. These findings support the inclusion of injury prevention in heat-health planning, although comparisons across exposure windows and heat-wave definitions remain exploratory.

articles.title: [Patterns of safety incident reporting in a paediatric department: a six-year analysis].

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Patient safety incidents are a global healthcare concern, and paediatric patients are particularly vulnerable. Although voluntary reporting systems cannot estimate the true incidence of these incidents, they help identify reporting patterns and opportunities for improvement. This study aimed to describe reports submitted from a hospital paediatric department and to analyse their association with incident type and severity, the reporter's professional category, and the clinical area.

abstract.label: MATERIALS AND METHODS
abstract.text: Observational, descriptive, retrospective study of 659 reports recorded in a centralised reporting system between 2019 and 2024. Year, type and severity of the reported incident, reporter's professional category, and clinical area were analysed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall, 87.4% of reports involved near misses or no-harm incidents. Medication/vaccines was the most frequently reported category (28.5%), followed by patient care and follow-up (25.8%). Adverse events were mainly concentrated in patient care and follow-up (42.2%) and diagnosis (32.5%). Nursing staff submitted the highest number of reports, whereas reports submitted by physicians included a higher proportion of adverse events (P<.01). The paediatric emergency department accounted for 47.5% of reports, with no significant differences in severity among clinical areas (P=.063).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The reporting system predominantly recorded reports of near misses and no-harm incidents, with differences in reporting patterns according to incident type, professional category, and clinical area. Analysis of these patterns can identify processes requiring further review and help guide feedback strategies tailored to different professional groups and clinical settings.

articles.title: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: SETTING
abstract.text: A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016-March 2024).

abstract.label: PATIENTS
abstract.text: Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day.

abstract.label: INTERVENTIONS
abstract.text: None.

abstract.label: MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
abstract.text: We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92-1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92-1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71-0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918-49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018-58,624) met the U.S. threshold.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

articles.title: Hallucinated Evidence and Real-World Risk-Physicians' Intent to Act on AI-Generated Abstracts in Emergency Medicine and Trauma Surgery: Cross-Sectional, Vignette-Based Diagnostic Accuracy Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in academic writing and can generate linguistically polished but factually incorrect scientific content. Such misinformation may distort evidence appraisal and, if translated into clinical practice, compromise patient care.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to estimate physicians' likelihood of misperceiving false information embedded in LLM-generated abstracts as true and reporting an intent to use that information in future practice. We also explored which features were associated with perceived credibility and intended clinical action.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a cross-sectional, vignette-based survey of physicians working in emergency medicine and trauma surgery across 4 hospitals in Germany. Each participant assessed 4 abstracts generated using GPT-5 Thinking mode, of which 2 contained intentionally false claims supported by plausible explanations and 2 contained accurate claims. The primary outcome was the proportion of physicians reporting an intent to use or act on recommendations contained in abstracts with false claims. Secondary outcomes included perceived accuracy, rejection of accurate claims, and ratings of precision, structure, and grammar.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty physicians provided 80 ratings of 4 abstracts. Overall, physicians reported that they would act on 68% (54/80) of abstracts. Using abstract truth status as the reference, the decision to act had a sensitivity of 78% (31/40), specificity of 43% (17/40), positive predictive value of 57% (31/54), and negative predictive value of 65% (17/26). The positive likelihood ratio was 1.35 (95% CI 0.98-1.85), the negative likelihood ratio was 0.53 (95% CI 0.27-1.04), and the diagnostic odds ratio was 2.55 (95% CI 0.96-6.73). True and false abstracts received similar ratings for perceived accuracy (mean 3.15, SD 0.89 vs mean 2.88, SD 1.04; P=.21), precision (mean 3.15, SD 0.89 vs mean 2.93, SD 1.00; P=.29), structure (mean 3.23, SD 0.77 vs mean 3.20, SD 0.88; P=.89), and grammar (mean 3.40, SD 0.59 vs mean 3.43, SD 0.68; P=.86). Abstracts that physicians intended to act on were rated substantially higher for perceived accuracy, precision, and structure than those they would not act on (all P<.001), whereas grammar ratings did not differ (P=.80).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Physicians frequently reported an intent to act on LLM-generated abstracts containing false claims, and true and false abstracts were not reliably distinguished on perceived quality measures. Perceived accuracy, precision, and structure were strongly associated with intended action, whereas grammar was not. These findings highlight the risk that persuasive scientific presentation may increase the credibility and potential clinical influence of fabricated or inaccurate AI-generated evidence.

articles.title: Task Force 11: Additional Cardiac Conditions and Considerations in Competitive Athletes.
articles.journal_full: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

abstract.text: The recently updated AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities provides a comprehensive framework for guiding clinicians in the evaluation and management of competitive athletes. Divided into 11 Task Forces, it covers a broad range of cardiovascular diseases and clinical scenarios. Task Force 11 was devoted to cardiac conditions and considerations in athletes not included in the other Task Forces. Here, we present the detailed rationale for the clinical considerations covered in this section of the Scientific Statement. These topics include hypertension, commotio cordis, pulmonary embolism, performance-enhancing drugs and supplements, exercise in extreme environments (specifically altitude and scuba diving), and pregnancy.

articles.title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
articles.journal_full: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

abstract.text: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

articles.title: Task Force 8: Care of Competitive Athletes with Arrhythmias and Sudden Cardiac Arrest: Clinical Considerations and Electrocardiogram Interpretations.
articles.journal_full: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

abstract.text: This document outlines recommendations for managing competitive athletes with arrhythmias and risks of sudden cardiac arrest, emphasizing individualized risk assessment, shared decision-making, and return-to-play protocols tailored to each athlete's cardiac profile and sport demands. It provides evaluation strategies for ventricular arrhythmias, implantable cardiac defibrillators, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern/syndrome, and syncope, alongside guidance for electrocardiogram interpretation in athletes. A key focus is placed on differentiating between low-risk and high-risk conditions, with recommendations for treatment strategies and ongoing monitoring to ensure athletes' safety.

articles.title: Task Force 5: Clinical Considerations for Myocarditis and Selected Cardiovascular Conditions, Including Valvular Heart Disease.
articles.journal_full: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

abstract.text: Athletes with myocarditis, pericarditis, valvular heart disease, and other acquired cardiovascular conditions require careful evaluation when considering competitive sports participation. This document outlines key clinical considerations, risk factors, and expert consensus, serving as the rationale for Section V of the recent AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are essential in determining return-to-play eligibility. This Task Force document addresses myocarditis, pericarditis, the cardiovascular impact of respiratory viral infections, incidental myocardial fibrosis, Kawasaki disease, infiltrative cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease.

articles.title: Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Challenging airways are common in the out-of-hospital setting, where delays or failure to secure the airway can result in significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, this pilot study aimed to determine whether training paramedics in the role of airway assistant improves intubation time during a simulated regurgitating airway using suction-assisted laryngoscopy and airway decontamination (SALAD).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Twelve qualified paramedics were randomly allocated to one of two groups (n = 6) and paired with intensive care paramedics (ICPs). Airway assistants in Group 1 completed a one-hour airway assistant training program, whereas airway assistants in Group 2 received no training. Participants completed a standardized, timed simulation using a continuously regurgitating mannequin designed to replicate the challenges of out-of-hospital intubation. The primary outcome was time to successful intubation, defined as passage of the endotracheal tube through the vocal cords with cuff inflation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Airway assistant training significantly reduced intubation time. The untrained group recorded a median intubation time of 102.5 seconds (IQR 36), compared with 53 seconds (IQR 19) in the trained group. Group comparisons demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in intubation time (p = 0.009) and corresponded to a very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86; Hedges' g = 1.72). No association was observed between intubation time and the age or experience of either the airway assistant or the ICP. No esophageal intubations occurred in either group.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this pilot study, training paramedics to perform the airway assistant role significantly reduced intubation time in a simulated regurgitating airway. These preliminary findings suggest that incorporating structured airway assistant training into prehospital education programs may improve airway management performance in challenging environments. Given the small sample size and simulated setting, larger studies are required to confirm these findings and determine whether the observed benefits translate to clinical practice.

articles.title: External validation of a decision rule for bacteremia vs contaminants in pediatric blood cultures.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Half of positive blood cultures in pediatric emergency departments (PEDs) represent contaminants, driving unnecessary hospitalization, antibiotic exposure, and repeat visits. A clinical decision rule derived at CHU Sainte-Justine showed 99% sensitivity and 60% specificity for distinguishing bacteremia from contaminants but had not been externally validated. We sought to validate this rule in an independent pediatric cohort.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective diagnostic study spanned from January 2015 to May 2025 at a tertiary PED in Switzerland, using positive blood cultures from patients younger than 16 years. The four predictors (Gram-negative organisms or Gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains; time to positivity <17 hours; indwelling device; suspected osteoarticular infection) classified each case as low, moderate, or high risk. The primary outcome was bacteremia, adjudicated by two independent reviewers, based on organism identity and infectious disease specialist's assessment. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed with 95% CIs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 130 children included (median age 3.8 years [IQR 0.9-9.9]; 61.5% male), 78 (60.0%) had true bacteremia. The rule yielded a sensitivity of 97.4% (95% CI, 91.0-99.7), specificity of 69.2% (95% CI, 54.9-81.3), positive predictive value of 82.6% (95% CI, 73.3-89.7), and negative predictive value of 94.7% (95% CI, 82.3-99.4). Both false-negatives were immunocompetent children with methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia without indwelling devices. Among contaminants, 71% received antibiotics under usual care versus 31% classified as moderate or high risk by the rule.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This first external validation supports the Sainte-Justine rule in a distinct pediatric population, preserving sensitivity with higher specificity. Multicenter validation is warranted before adoption.

articles.title: Successful management of arrow‑rebound‑induced transcervical penetrating trauma with major vascular and pharyngolaryngeal injuries: A case report.

abstract.label: RATIONALE
abstract.text: Penetrating neck injury involving major vessels is highly lethal. Long-trajectory transcervical penetration caused by rebounding arrows is exceptionally rare in civilians, posing significant diagnostic and management challenges.

abstract.label: PATIENT CONCERNS
abstract.text: A man in his early 50s presented to the emergency department approximately 2 hours after an arrow, rebounding from a nearby training target, penetrated his neck (entering above the left mandible, exiting on the right). He was conscious with minimal external bleeding but copious oropharyngeal secretions. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) revealed the arrow traversing the hyoid bone and oropharynx, abutting the right common carotid artery (CCA) and compressing the right internal jugular vein (IJV).

abstract.label: DIAGNOSES
abstract.text: Open neck injury; combined right CCA and IJV injury; hemorrhagic shock; pharyngolaryngeal trauma without aerodigestive perforation; and pulmonary infection with consolidation.

abstract.label: INTERVENTIONS
abstract.text: Initial stabilization included arrow shaft shortening by firefighters. Emergency exploration under general anesthesia involved tracheotomy, cervical exploration, primary repair of the right IJV and CCA, and foreign body removal. Postoperative management in the intensive care unit included damage-control resuscitation (transfusion of 7.0 U packed red blood cells, 1100 mL plasma, and 10.5 U cryoprecipitate), antimicrobial therapy (cefuroxime, guided by cultures showing Staphylococcus epidermidis), early individualized anticoagulation (enoxaparin transitioned to rivaroxaban), and systematic correction of coagulopathy and electrolyte disturbances.

abstract.label: OUTCOMES
abstract.text: The patient was discharged on postoperative day 12 with healed wounds. Follow-up at 1, 3, 6.5 months, 1, 2, and nearly 3 years showed intact neurological function. Imaging confirmed stable right IJV occlusion. Anticoagulation was discontinued at 1 month without subsequent bleeding or thromboembolism. Although long-term imaging was limited to a 6.5-month non-contrast computed tomography, the patient remained asymptomatic without signs of venous hypertension or neurological deficits throughout the follow-up period.

abstract.label: LESSONS
abstract.text: High-quality preoperative computed tomography angiography with 3D reconstruction is critical for defining the relationship between the foreign body and vital structures. In selected patients, early individualized anticoagulation after excluding active bleeding may mitigate venous thrombosis. Systematic intensive care unit management of coagulopathy, electrolytes, and pulmonary complications is pivotal for survival.

articles.title: Informal Digital Information Use in Hospital Mass Casualty Incident Management During Wartime: Multicenter Cross-Sectional Questionnaire Study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Managing mass casualty incidents (MCIs) during an active warfare environment presents unique challenges, including operating under extreme uncertainty. Traditionally, emergency communications rely on strict, hierarchical channels from prehospital services to receiving hospitals. However, informal digital communication streams, particularly instant messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram, are increasingly used within medical workflows. Despite international interest in public social media during disasters, empirical research regarding how hospital leadership echelons use informal messaging tools for real-time operational and clinical decision-making during active warfare remains sparse.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to characterize the adoption of social media and instant messaging platforms as early information sources among hospital-based MCI managers during wartime and to evaluate their specific impact on real-time operational and clinical decision-making.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A multicenter, cross-sectional study was conducted using a structured questionnaire distributed across all 24 national medical centers authorized to receive MCIs during wartime in Israel.
