Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Across eight countries, 76 studies met the inclusion criteria, primarily from Australia (n = 29) and Canada (n = 23). Air transport and medical evacuation was the most frequently described pathway (71%), followed by ground transport (51%). Explicit description of paramedic or emergency medical services (24%) and dispatch/9-1-1 (12%) were depicted less frequently. Additionally, pathways were commonly described but rarely evaluated: only 12/76 (16%) publications used an evaluative design, and no pathway was evaluated in more than 7 of 76 publications (9%). The most reported barriers were infrastructure and communications (92%), cost and jurisdiction (87%), and distance to definitive care (83%). All percentages describe how often a topic was reported across the 76 included publications, and not its prevalence in practice. An explicit cultural-safety framework was applied in 9% of the publications, and community-led governance of the research in 7%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The published evidence disproportionately described transporting patients out of their communities. Community first response and tele-support were described more often than their standing in the literature suggests; however, they were rarely evaluated, and Indigenous-led governance of the research itself was reported in 7% of publications. Low reporting frequency does not establish that these models are uncommon in application and practice. Future priorities include community-partnered evaluation of community-based capacity and telehealth-supported care, alongside the development of patient and family cultural safety.

articles.title: Navigating Uncertainty: 2026 AAST Presidential Address.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

articles.title: [Emergency medicine requirements for the resuscitation room and the resuscitation room team].

abstract.text: The resuscitation room is the central interface between prehospital emergency medical services (EMS) and in-hospital emergency care for critically ill and severely injured patients. From an EMS perspective, requirements are defined for activation, prenotification, team structure, handover, overload management and feedback. Written activation and allocation criteria are required that are applicable in the prehospital setting and agreed upon by hospitals, emergency dispatch centres and EMS providers. Prenotification must take place through a continuously available, reliable communication channel, be actively acknowledged and enable transparent feedback on capacity. Paramedics must be authorised to activate the resuscitation room independently of the presence of an emergency physician. On arrival, a qualified and operational team with clearly identifiable roles should be available. Handover should be structured and as interruption-free as possible. The exploratory online survey showed that trauma resuscitation care is predominantly guideline-based and more often includes a written minimum staffing requirement. In nontrauma resuscitation care, written activation criteria and binding team structures were less frequently available. Although handovers were mostly standardised, substantial deficits existed in overload and diversion protocols as well as in interprofessional feedback structures involving EMS. These findings indicate a need for coordinated procedures, transparent capacity management and binding quality-assurance measures.

articles.title: Unintended Exposure to Medical Aid in Dying Drug Mixtures: Principles of Emergency Care.

abstract.text: Medical Aid in Dying (MAID) is a legal medical option for terminally ill patients with decision-making capacity to self-administer prescription medication to cause death. MAID has expanded across the United States, with New York becoming the most recent state to legalize it in August 2026. As these medications become more available in the community, typically administered outside controlled medical settings, such as the home, rare but consequential unintended exposures can occur. MAID is distinct from euthanasia in that the patient must have decision-making capacity and must be able to self-administer the medication; this requirement contributes to the presence of highly lethal drug mixtures in nonclinical environments. Although MAID formulations are designed to be lethal, unintended recipients may ingest only a partial dose (eg, a "sip"), making survival possible with prompt medical care. We review the background and common components of MAID mixtures, which typically combine a sedative (benzodiazepine and/or barbiturate), an opioid, and cardiotoxic agents such as digoxin, β-blockers, and/or tricyclic antidepressants. We propose preliminary management guidelines for suspected unsanctioned MAID exposures: early regional poison center consultation; supportive resuscitation; activated charcoal when safe; targeted diagnostics, including serum digoxin concentration and serial electrocardiograms; gastric aspiration, when feasible; use of digoxin immune Fab when indicated; avoidance of flumazenil and naloxone in mixed ingestions; and substance-specific therapies, such as high-dose insulin for propranolol toxicity and sodium bicarbonate for tricyclic antidepressants-induced QRS widening.

articles.title: Building a HEARTSafe campus: A scalable model for cardiac arrest preparedness and response.
articles.journal_full: Journal of American college health : J of ACH

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Assess participant knowledge and comfort with cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and automated external defibrillator (AED) use following implementation of the American Heart Association CPR Anywhere® curriculum.

abstract.label: PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: 738 university students, faculty, and staff.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A pre-post study design assessed knowledge and comfort outcomes after participating in the CPR Anywhere® program.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Significant improvements at the α = .001 level were observed in both knowledge and comfort scores following the intervention. Mean knowledge scores increased from pre- to post-intervention by 1.73 points on the 7-question survey, and the percentage of participants feeling comfortable performing CPR increased from 63% to 97%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: A campus-wide CPR/AED educational initiative improved participants' knowledge and comfort with CPR/AED use and supported broader cardiac arrest preparedness efforts. The program was associated with increased AED availability across campus and the creation of a Cardiac Emergency Response Plan, underscoring the value of replicating such initiatives in university settings.

articles.title: Implementation of artificial intelligence-enabled, obstetric point-of-care ultrasounds into routine antenatal care in Lusaka Province of Zambia.
articles.journal_full: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Access to obstetric ultrasound remains limited in many countries owing to the limited availability of equipment and specialist operators. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled obstetric point-of-care ultrasound (OB POCUS) may expand access to reliable gestational age (GA) dating within routine antenatal care (ANC).

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate the feasibility and clinical utility of implementing AI-enabled OB POCUS for GA assessment across four public-sector facilities in Lusaka Province, Zambia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We integrated routine AI-enabled OB POCUS into ANC using a training-of-trainers model, followed by standardized competency-based training for facility healthcare providers and ongoing mentorship. We abstracted data from facility ANC registers for women scanned between September 2024 and March 2025. Among patients with both last menstrual period (LMP)- and AI-enabled OB POCUS-based dating, we calculated the discrepancy between the two estimates and applied American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) GA-specific thresholds to classify each patient according to whether the discrepancy was large enough to warrant revising the LMP-based estimated due date (EDD) to the AI-enabled OB POCUS-based EDD. We estimated the proportion meeting these re-dating criteria and used logistic regression to assess factors associated with meeting them.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 1068 ultrasound recipients, 859 (80.4%) had both a recorded LMP and a documented AI-enabled OB POCUS-based EDD. Of these, the median EDD discrepancy was 11 days (IQR = 5-29 days), and 51% met the ACOG criteria for EDD revision. The proportion meeting re-dating criteria did not differ by GA at presentation and was not affected by facility or demographic characteristics.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Implementation of AI-enabled OB POCUS within public-sector ANC in Zambia was feasible. Half of women scanned met the criteria for revising an LMP-based due date, indicating that such technologies could substantially change pregnancy care where ultrasound is otherwise unavailable.

articles.title: Evaluating Paediatric Surgery Consultations: Insights From a Tertiary Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Journal of paediatrics and child health

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: Paediatric surgical consultations constitute an important component of paediatric emergency department (PED) practice, yet detailed data on referral patterns and clinical outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the characteristics, urgency, timing and clinical outcomes of paediatric surgery consultations in a tertiary PED and to identify potential areas for improving referral processes and resource utilization.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective, single-centre, cross-sectional study included paediatric surgery consultations requested from the PED between January 1 and December 31, 2022. Consultations were classified as emergency, urgent, or elective and emergency referral indications were further categorized according to the suspected diagnosis or primary clinical concern at referral. Clinical outcomes were classified as discharge, hospitalization without surgery, or hospitalization with surgery. Consultation timing (working hours vs. after-hours) and seasonal trends were also analysed. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS v25, with p < 0.05 considered significant.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 5433 consultations were analysed; 86.3% were classified as emergency, 9.8% as urgent and 3.8% as elective. Among emergency consultations, trauma and burns (n = 1369) and suspected appendicitis (n = 1100) were the most frequent indications. Of patients referred with suspected appendicitis, 51.2% were discharged and 26.2% underwent surgery, whereas 76.7% of those with acute abdominal pain without a specific surgical diagnosis were discharged and none underwent surgery. Overall, 65.3% of patients were discharged and 16.2% underwent surgery. Most consultations (70.4%) occurred after-hours; however, neither urgency distribution (p = 0.133) nor clinical outcomes (p = 0.124) differed significantly according to consultation timing.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Paediatric surgery consultations encompassed a heterogeneous spectrum of conditions with substantially different clinical outcomes. Diagnosis-specific analysis identified potential opportunities for institution-specific refinement of referral and triage pathways. Although most consultations occurred after hours, their urgency and clinical outcomes did not differ significantly from those during working hours. Given the single-centre design and institution-dependent nature of referral practices, these findings should be interpreted within the context of the study setting.

articles.title: After the ambulance.
Adaptive Workforce Strategies in Public Health Emergencies: A Quasi-Experimental Study with a Historical Control Group.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Crisis-driven health care shortages require adaptive regulatory changes. Allowing advanced nursing students to provide clinical care could bolster surge capacity while enhancing professional competence.

abstract.label: STUDY OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The aim of this study was to evaluate the impact of crisis period clinical work on nursing students' academic and licensure outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A quasi-experimental study with a historical control group was conducted among 68 students enrolled in an academic career retraining track (an intensive first-entry nursing program for individuals holding a non-nursing bachelor's degree with no prior nursing background). During a major public health emergency (the COVID-19 pandemic), a work experience group (n = 23) received temporary clinical permissions before licensure, while a control group (n = 45) followed the standard curriculum without early clinical employment. Outcomes included final program grades and scores on the Governmental Licensing Examination in Nursing (GLEIN).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The work experience group demonstrated significantly higher mean final grades [79.92 (SD = 5.14) versus 76.9 (SD = 9.72); difference, 3.02 (95% CI, 0.28-5.76); P =.033] and higher GLEIN scores [81.85 (SD = 6.69) versus 73.9 (SD = 9.49); difference, 7.95 (95% CI, 0.70-15.20); P =.029] compared to the control group. Regression analysis identified crisis period clinical work experience as a significant predictor of higher licensing exam performance.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Temporary clinical employment of advanced nursing students during a crisis was positively associated with academic performance and higher licensing examination scores. Adaptive regulatory policies can support student academic readiness and licensure success during public health emergencies.

articles.title: The emergency department as a critical window for ADHD recognition in female adolescents.
articles.journal_full: The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science

articles.title: [Analysis of follow-up compliance in adult dental trauma patients presenting to a nighttime dental emergency service].
articles.journal: Zhonghua Kou Qiang Yi Xue Za Zhi
articles.journal_full: Zhonghua kou qiang yi xue za zhi = Zhonghua kouqiang yixue zazhi = Chinese journal of stomatology

abstract.text: Objective: To analyze the follow-up compliance and influencing factors of patients with dental trauma treated in the oral emergency department during evening hours, providing a scientific basis for improving patient prognosis and optimizing emergency service processes. Methods: The clinical data of 124 patients with dental trauma who presented to the Oral Emergency Department of Peking University School and Hospital of Stomatology during evening hours (18:00-24:00) between January 2024 and December 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Follow-up visit status was evaluated by tracing patient records via the electronic medical record (EMR) system. Univariate analysis and multivariate logistic regression analysis were performed to identify factors associated with follow-up compliance. Results: Among the 124 patients, 54.0%(67/124) returned for follow-up according to medical advice, while 46.0%(57/124) failed to return. Univariate analysis showed that patient age, injury type, insurance type, and residential distance were not significantly correlated with follow-up compliance (P>0.05). Insurance coverage was not identified as an independent promoting factor for compliance. Among the 24 patients with registered residential addresses, living more than 20 km from the hospital was not an independent risk factor. Conclusions: Evening dental trauma patients in oral emergency departments show low follow-up compliance. Improving patient follow-up adherence and optimizing dental trauma outcomes require strengthened oral health education, establishment of appointment reminder systems, and implementation of remote consultation services.

articles.title: Postoperative prophylactic and delayed oral antibiotics after total shoulder arthroplasty: a multi-institutional database analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic and delayed postoperative oral antibiotics following total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The TriNetX database was queried for primary TSA patients. Those with prior pathologic fracture, upper extremity malignancy, infection, prosthetic joint infection (PJI), or revision surgery within 6 months were excluded. After 1:1 propensity score matching, two comparisons were performed: (1) prophylactic oral antibiotics within 1 postoperative day versus controls (n=5,891 per cohort) and (2) delayed oral antibiotics on postoperative days 7-30 versus controls (n=3,087 per cohort). Outcomes at 30 and 90 days included acute kidney injury (AKI), emergency department (ED) visits, readmission, PJI, and revision surgery.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: At 30 days, prophylactic antibiotics were associated with fewer readmissions (2.78% vs. 3.73%; P=0.004), with no differences in AKI, ED visits, PJI, or revision surgery. At 90 days, they were associated with higher PJI (0.92% vs. 0.48%; P=0.004) and a trend toward lower ED visits (5.25% vs. 6.16%; P=0.032) and readmissions (3.70% vs. 4.67%; P=0.009), but higher revision surgery (1.17% vs. 0.73%; P=0.014). Delayed antibiotics were associated with higher rates of AKI, ED visits, readmissions, and revision surgery at both 30 and 90 days (all P<0.001), as well as higher PJI at 90 days (3.14% vs. 0.42%; P<0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Although residual confounding cannot be excluded, postoperative prophylactic or delayed oral antibiotics were not associated with reduced PJI or revision surgery and may be associated with antibiotic-related adverse effects. Level of evidence: III.

articles.title: Development and validation of an adjunctive diagnostic tool for Canadian CT head rule-positive patients: a pilot study.

abstract.text: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is among the most frequent causes of emergency department visits worldwide. Although the Canadian CT Head Rule (CCHR) and similar algorithms provide high sensitivity for detecting clinically significant injuries, their limited specificity results in overuse of computed tomography (CT), with associated costs, radiation exposure, and resource strain. This study investigated the value of routine laboratory biomarkers as adjunctive tools for CT decision-making in CCHR-positive patients with mTBI. Inclusion parameters were based primarily on their clinical significance and statistical performance. Two cohorts from a single tertiary center were analyzed: a development cohort of 110 patients and a temporal validation cohort of 127 patients recruited at the same institution during an earlier period. Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and glucose-to-potassium ratio (GPR) were significantly elevated in CT-positive cases. A multivariable logistic regression model including NLR, PLR, glucose, loss of consciousness, and repeated vomiting achieved strong performance in the original cohort (AUC 0.94, 95% CI 0.89-0.98; sensitivity 94.7%, 95% CI 88.1-97.7; specificity 62.5%, 95% CI 38.6-81.5; accuracy 90.0%; optimism-corrected AUC 0.90 on bootstrap internal validation). In the validation cohort the model retained high sensitivity (92.2%, 95% CI 83.4-96.2) but showed significantly lower overall discrimination (AUC 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.84). These findings suggest that combining simple, widely available biomarkers with established clinical criteria may provide a practical, low-cost triage tool for optimizing CT use in mild TBI, especially in resource-limited settings. Because the development cohort was recruited among high-risk patients and because the second cohort provides temporal rather than external validation, these results are preliminary and require confirmation in a prospective multicentre cohort.

articles.title: Drug-Induced Electrolyte Disturbances in Older Adults Presenting to the Emergency Department: Mechanisms, Recognition and Prevention.

abstract.text: Many older adults attending the emergency department (ED) take medications that interfere with water and electrolyte balance. This narrative review, based on a structured PubMed/MEDLINE search covering January 2016 to September 2026, summarizes evidence on drug-associated disorders of sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium in older ED patients. Thiazides, antidepressants, antiepileptic drugs, antipsychotics, proton pump inhibitors and desmopressin are associated with hyponatremia; with thiazides, the risk peaks in the first weeks of treatment and is highest in women aged 80 years or older. Lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which may persist after discontinuation and cause hypernatremia when water intake is inadequate. Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, trimethoprim and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs predispose to hyperkalemia, particularly in chronic kidney disease; diuretics and proton pump inhibitors are associated with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia; and denosumab can cause severe hypocalcemia in advanced kidney disease. Most of this evidence is observational, and drugs usually act together with comorbidities, acute illness and other medications. We propose a severity-based ED algorithm integrating medication history, laboratory, electrocardiographic and volume assessment (including point-of-care ultrasound) to guide stabilization, drug adjustment, safe correction and disposition. ED-based medication safety programs reduce inappropriate prescribing, but their effect on electrolyte-related outcomes remains unproven.

articles.title: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy and Female Infertility: A Systematic Review of Human Clinical Evidence.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Female infertility represents a major global health issue, and effective treatment remains challenging in several infertility-related conditions. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) has been proposed as a potential adjunctive intervention in reproductive medicine, although human clinical evidence remains limited. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the available human evidence regarding the association between HBOT and reproductive outcomes in women with infertility or infertility-related conditions. Potential biological mechanisms, including the hypothetical involvement of sirtuin-related signaling in adaptive responses to intermittent hyperoxia, were also considered. Methods: A systematic literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, LILACS and the Cochrane Library was updated through 10 May 2026. The search was restricted to studies published from 1 January 2016 to 10 May 2026, reflecting the review's prespecified focus on approximately the preceding decade of human clinical evidence. Original human studies investigating HBOT in women with infertility or infertility-related conditions and reporting reproductive outcomes were eligible. Study selection was conducted according to predefined eligibility criteria and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and the certainty of evidence for the main outcomes was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity and the absence of sufficiently comparable outcomes across studies, a pooled meta-analysis was not performed. Results: Seventy-six records were identified through electronic database searches, and 11 reports underwent full-text eligibility assessment. Two original human studies involving women with resistant thin endometrium or poor ovarian response met the eligibility criteria. In women with resistant thin endometrium undergoing frozen embryo transfer, endometrial thickness increased after HBOT (6.57 ± 1.23 vs. 5.76 ± 1.66 mm before HBOT; p = 0.002). Compared with propensity-score-matched concurrent controls, women receiving HBOT had a higher implantation rate (RR, 3.00; 95% CI, 1.26-7.14) and a higher intrauterine pregnancy rate after blastocyst transfer (RR, 2.96; 95% CI, 1.14-7.70). In women with poor ovarian response undergoing IVF/ICSI, fully adjusted analyses showed that HBOT was associated with a higher number of retrieved oocytes (β = 1.51; 95% CI, 0.92-2.10), available embryo rate (β = 24.29 percentage points; 95% CI, 7.27-41.31), and normal fertilization rate (β = 17.23 percentage points; 95% CI, 2.35-32.11). Clinical pregnancy occurred in 1 of 10 pre-HBOT cycles (10.0%) and 1 of 19 post-HBOT cycles (5.3%); one live birth was reported following HBOT. This single event does not provide a comparative estimate of live-birth rates. Certainty of evidence was very low for all outcomes assessed using GRADE: endometrial thickness, implantation, intrauterine pregnancy, number of oocytes retrieved, available embryo rate, and normal fertilization rate. Conclusions: Available human evidence reports associations between HBOT and selected reproductive outcomes in women with resistant thin endometrium or poor ovarian response. However, the evidence is based on only two small, non-randomized studies addressing different clinical populations and outcomes, and the certainty of evidence was very low for all outcomes assessed using GRADE. Current evidence is therefore insufficient to establish a causal therapeutic effect, support the routine use of HBOT for female infertility or define an optimal treatment protocol. Further well-designed prospective controlled studies are required.

articles.title: Sim-SEA: Integrating Significant Event Audit and In Situ Simulation to Support Patient Safety Learning and Organizational Change-A Prospective Single-Center Pilot Study in Pediatric Emergency Care.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Patient safety depends on healthcare systems' ability to learn from clinical experience and translate insights into system-level improvement. Significant Event Audit (SEA) is well established but may only partly capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of clinical performance. Although in situ simulation is increasingly used to explore team performance and system vulnerabilities, its routine integration into formal risk-management pathways remains limited. We developed Sim-SEA, a structured approach embedding in situ simulation within the SEA learning cycle.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Sim-SEA adapted the seven-phase SEA framework to incorporate in situ simulation as a core component. We conducted a 12-month single-center, uncontrolled pre-post pilot study in a tertiary pediatric emergency department, comprising 10 Sim-SEA cycles. Self-perceived competence in technical and non-technical domains was assessed at baseline and immediately after simulation using a 6-item ad hoc questionnaire. A follow-up assessment was conducted among participants who subsequently encountered a real emergency. Participants' perceptions, system vulnerabilities, and improvement actions were also examined.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Fifty-nine physicians, residents, and nurses participated. Self-perceived competence improved significantly from baseline to post-simulation across ABCDE assessment, teamwork, situational awareness, communication, speak-up behavior, and decision-making (all p < 0.01). At follow-up, available for 35/59 participants (59.3%) who subsequently encountered a real emergency, self-perceived scores remained significantly higher than baseline. Implemented changes included workspace reorganization, a cognitive medication aid, and a standard operating procedure for role allocation. Participants reported greater engagement, reflective learning, psychological safety, and awareness of risks and system vulnerabilities.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this single-center, uncontrolled pilot study, Sim-SEA was feasible as a structured method for embedding in situ simulation within clinical risk management and supported potential benefits for self-perceived learning and the identification and development of organizational and environmental improvement actions. Further studies should assess effects on objective competence and patient-safety outcomes.

articles.title: Community and EMS Interventions to Improve Survival in Cardiac Arrest.
articles.journal_full: The New England journal of medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Early cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but evidence from randomized trials about whether community-based implementation strategies improve outcomes is lacking.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a registry-based, cluster-randomized trial involving adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by emergency medical services (EMS) in North Carolina counties. The counties were grouped into clusters, which were then randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to implement a multifaceted intervention or administer usual care. The intervention included four components: training of 911 telecommunicators to improve rapid recognition of cardiac arrest, training of 911 telecommunicators to improve delivery of CPR instructions from telecommunicators to bystanders, community CPR training, and enhanced use of automated external defibrillators by first responders or bystanders before EMS arrival. Data were collected through the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome (Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2; range, 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating worse neurologic outcome).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: From July 1, 2022, to June 30, 2026, a total of 28 clusters comprising 11,615 patients were assigned to the intervention group, and 27 clusters comprising 10,844 patients were assigned to the usual-care group. The median age of the patients was 64.0 years, and 36.7% were women. The percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a good neurologic outcome was 9.0% (1048 of 11,608 patients) in the intervention group and 9.4% (1017 of 10,839 patients) in the usual-care group (adjusted odds ratio, 0.97; 95% confidence interval, 0.75 to 1.26; P = 0.80).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, implementation of a multifaceted strategy involving the community and EMS did not result in a greater percentage of patients who survived to hospital discharge with a favorable neurologic outcome than usual care. (Funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute of the National Institutes of Health; RACE-CARS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04660526.).

articles.title: The Scandinavian Neurotrauma Committee 2026 guidelines for initial management of minimal, mild and moderate head injuries in adults: a systematic review, meta-analysis and modified Delphi consensus study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Several clinical guidelines exist to identify intracranial injury (ICI) after head injury. The Scandinavian Neurotrauma Committee (SNC) published evidence- and consensus-based guidelines in 2000, updated in 2013. Since then, demographic changes, including an ageing population and increased use of antithrombotic therapy have prompted further revision. The aim of this study is to provide a clinically relevant update to the SNC guidelines for the initial management of adults with minimal, mild, or moderate head injury.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis addressed population, exposure, comparator, and outcome questions on which emergency department patients with minimal or mild head injury require head computed tomography (CT), direct discharge, in-hospital observation, or repeat CT. Evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. Recommendations were developed through a modified Delphi process with stakeholder review.

abstract.label: FINDINGS
abstract.text: Twenty-nine stakeholders participated in developing a seven-point recommendation set and updated management flowcharts. Key changes include reduced emphasis on routine CT in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants, incorporation of glial fibrillary acidic protein and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 biomarkers, and use of structured observation as an alternative to CT in selected risk groups.

abstract.label: INTERPRETATION
abstract.text: The updated guidelines support risk-adapted imaging and observation strategies that may reduce unnecessary CT scans and hospital admissions, although further validation of safety and effectiveness is needed.

abstract.label: FUNDING
abstract.text: No specific funding.

articles.title: Preoperative CT-derived psoas attenuation and correction loss after traumatic thoracolumbar fracture fixation: A construct-dependent association.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Postoperative correction loss remains a concern after posterior fixation of traumatic thoracolumbar fractures. Although bone quality and construct characteristics influence mechanical stability, the role of preoperative muscle quality remains poorly defined. We examined whether CT-derived psoas attenuation was associated with correction loss and whether fracture-level screw placement modified this association.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective single-center cohort included 78 adults who underwent posterior pedicle screw fixation for traumatic AO Spine A3 thoracolumbar fractures. Preoperative psoas and paravertebral attenuation and cross-sectional area were measured at L3. Correction loss was defined as the difference between final-follow-up and immediate postoperative Cobb angles measured on supine sagittal CT reconstructions. Multivariable linear regression tested the interaction between centered psoas attenuation and fracture-level screw placement, adjusting for age, sex, vertebral attenuation, instrumented levels, and follow-up duration. An extended model added vertebral height loss and canal compromise. HC3 robust variance estimation and sensitivity analyses were performed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Mean correction loss was 4.1 ± 5.4°, and 23 patients (29.5%) experienced loss greater than 5°. The psoas attenuation-by-fracture-level screw interaction was significant (B=0.311°/HU; 95% CI, 0.091-0.530; p = .006; HC3 p = .037). Without fracture-level screws, each 10-HU increase in psoas attenuation corresponded to approximately 2.6° less correction loss (B=-0.255°/HU; 95% CI, -0.440 to -0.071; p = .007), although HC3 inference crossed the null (p = .068). No clear association was observed with fracture-level screws. The interaction persisted after adjustment for vertebral height loss and canal compromise (B=0.342°/HU; 95% CI, 0.127-0.556; p = .002; HC3 p = .016), when short- versus long-segment fixation replaced instrumented-level count, and in patients with at least 12 months of follow-up. Paravertebral attenuation showed a similar pattern, whereas muscle cross-sectional area did not.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Preoperative psoas attenuation showed a construct-dependent association with correction loss after fixation of traumatic AO Spine A3 fractures. Lower attenuation may identify mechanical vulnerability when the fractured vertebra is not incorporated into the construct. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation before CT-based muscle assessment can guide construct selection.

articles.title: A Low-Cost Serratus Anterior Plane Block Phantom With a Thoracodorsal Artery Analogue and Pleural-Breach Feedback.

abstract.text: Ultrasound-guided serratus anterior plane block (SAPB) is an evidence-supported component of multimodal analgesia for rib fractures, but training requires learners to integrate chest-wall sonoanatomy with safe needle control near vascular and pleural structures. We describe a low-cost part-task trainer, meaning a simulator designed to rehearse selected components of a procedure rather than the entire clinical encounter, and propose a staged pathway from simulation to supervised patient practice. Four wooden stacking blocks support a tongue-depressor scaffold. Transverse tongue depressors represent ribs, and a water-filled examination glove sits immediately beneath them as a simulated pleural safety boundary. Two chicken fillets represent serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi, with a single layer of cling film creating the superficial fascial plane. A fluid-filled thermometer probe cover placed in this plane represents the thoracodorsal artery. The primary task is superficial SAPB, with in-plane needle visualisation, vessel avoidance and hydrodissection. An optional deep-plane station is designed to provide immediate visible feedback if an unsafe trajectory breaches the water-filled glove; it does not simulate pneumothorax physiology. One final prototype was evaluated in a proof-of-concept bench session. Post hoc estimates from archived ultrasound images placed the superficial target plane at approximately 8-10 mm, and the rib surrogates at approximately 18-22 mm depth. No validity, reliability, durability or learner-outcome testing was performed. The model and proposed seven-step pathway are therefore offered as a starting point for structured preclinical preparation, not as a stand-alone competency or entrustment tool.

articles.title: Mapping Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Other Prospective Risk Analysis Approaches in Intrahospital Transport Involving Critically Ill Patients: A Scoping Review.

abstract.text: Intrahospital transport exposes critically ill patients and their care teams to clinical and organizational vulnerabilities, and proactive risk analysis can inform preventive interventions. This scoping review mapped the use of failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), its variants, and complementary prospective risk analysis approaches in intrahospital transport pathways involving critically ill patients or critical care transitions. Studies of multi-area transfers, imaging pathways, and mixed adult and pediatric populations were included for their organizational relevance, not because all participants were critically ill. The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched on October 3, 2026, for studies published from 2002 to 2026. Three reviewers independently screened all records and full-text reports. All included studies were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018, and the six studies with quantitative comparisons were also appraised with the JBI checklist for quasi-experimental studies. Of the 789 records identified, 689 were screened after the removal of 100 duplicates. Fourteen studies, reported in 15 publications, were included. Seven studies used FMEA, five used healthcare failure mode and effects analysis (HFMEA), and one used failure modes, effects and criticality analysis (FMECA); the remaining study used the bow-tie model. Recurring vulnerabilities involved communication and handoff, patient identification, medication management, equipment readiness, device security, and monitoring. Four studies reported fewer adverse events after implementation, one reported improved perceived preparedness, and one reported a lower risk priority number (RPN). Designs and outcomes were heterogeneous. The mapping can inform local risk analysis and the design of interventions, but the reported associations do not establish causal effectiveness. Controlled multicenter evaluations with measures of fidelity, sustainability, and cost are needed. The vulnerabilities and preventive strategies identified are particularly relevant to nursing practice, given the central role of nurses in patient preparation, monitoring, device protection, medication continuity, and interprofessional handoff. No dedicated studies have addressed transport from the intensive care unit or emergency department to the operating room or between intensive care units, and research is needed in underrepresented regions, such as the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Latin America, and most of Europe.

articles.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.journal_full: The New England journal of medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: In patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be performed to establish reperfusion. Data comparing prehospital ECPR with conventional care regarding survival until hospital discharge among patients who are 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest are limited.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, we evaluated the outcomes in young adults who were attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) that were equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR (intervention group) as compared with those attended by HEMS without ECPR capability (conventional group). The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 144 patients were included in the intervention group, and 87 were included in the conventional group. In the intervention group, 57 of 144 patients (40%) survived until hospital discharge, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.59 to 4.66; P = 0.002). At 6 months, a favorable neurologic outcome was reported in 51 of 141 patients (36%) in the intervention group and in 11 of 85 patients (13%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 4.22; 95% CI, 2.82 to 6.32). There were 32 adverse events in the intervention group and 11 in the conventional group.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among patients who were 50 years of age or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating ECPR into HEMS was associated with improved survival until hospital discharge, as compared with conventional care. (Funded by the Dutch Ministry of Health; OnScene ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04620070.).

articles.title: Workplace Violence Against Physicians in Bangladesh: A Contemporary Systems-Based Narrative Review of Current Evidence.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Workplace violence against physicians is an occupational and public health challenge in resource-constrained healthcare systems. In Bangladesh, physician shortages, overcrowding, service delays, inadequate security, and institutional constraints may increase exposure to clinical environments. This narrative review synthesized evidence on forms, perpetrators, determinants, consequences, institutional responses, and prevention using a systems-based and socio-ecological perspective.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A narrative review was conducted with reference to the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for peer-reviewed publications from January 2022 to May 2026. The primary evidence comprised studies reporting workplace violence among physicians or physician-specific findings in Bangladeshi healthcare settings. Contextual evidence was considered separately to inform interpretation. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Findings were synthesized thematically because methodological heterogeneity precluded quantitative pooling.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twelve studies constituted the evidence base. Psychological and verbal violence were most common, with patients' relatives or attendants frequently identified as perpetrators. Younger and early-career physicians, emergency department staff, and night-shift workers appeared particularly vulnerable, although demographic associations varied. Recurring determinants included treatment delays, overcrowding, staffing constraints, communication difficulties, inadequate security, weak reporting mechanisms, governance limitations, and health-system pressures. Workplace violence was associated with psychological distress, burnout, reduced job satisfaction, defensive medical practice, workforce instability, and disruption of healthcare delivery. Institutional reporting, investigation, and post-incident support remained inadequate.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Workplace violence against physicians in Bangladesh is a systems-level occupational, governance, and healthcare-resilience challenge arising from interacting individual, interpersonal, organizational, health-system, and societal conditions. Prevention should extend beyond reactive security measures to workforce strengthening, standardized reporting and accountability, legal protection, occupational support, communication and de-escalation, and public engagement. Future research should prioritize standardized measurement, longitudinal and intervention studies, and underrepresented healthcare settings.

articles.title: Rethinking Mild Therapeutic Hypothermia After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Dead End or Missed Opportunity? An Expert Viewpoint.

abstract.text: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains associated with high mortality and neurological disability. Mild therapeutic hypothermia has been questioned after large trials failed to demonstrate superiority over controlled normothermia with fever prevention. In this expert viewpoint, we argue that these neutral findings should not be interpreted as proof of biological futility in every patient and setting. The clinical effect of hypothermia may depend on patient phenotype, timing of initiation, cooling technique, temperature-control quality, and integration with contemporary post-resuscitation care. This may be particularly important in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention, in whom hypothermia can impair the pharmacokinetics and antiplatelet effects of oral P2Y12 inhibitors. Current evidence does not support routine hypothermia in all comatose survivors. However, uncertainty remains regarding its value in selected patients. Patients with an intermediate degree of ischemic brain injury may represent a plausible target for neuroprotection, but this remains an unproven hypothesis. Future trials should investigate whether injury severity modifies the effects of early, precisely delivered hypothermia, using standardized protocols, active normothermia as the comparator, and prespecified antithrombotic and post-resuscitation strategies.

articles.title: Exploring Esophageal Widening in Computed Tomography Performed in Critically Ill Patients.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Early diagnosis and therapy stratification represent central factors in the management of critically ill patients, today often assisted by clinical scores, which also include laboratory testing results. The aim of this study was to further characterize computed tomography-detected abnormal esophageal widening, which we often observe in critically ill patients in our emergency department when reading CT examinations. We expect this factor to be potentially meaningful for clinical evaluation and prognosis of critically ill patients. Methods: In this retrospective observational study, critically ill patients receiving CT trauma room imaging in our hospital's emergency department were included. In the first part of the analysis, esophageal diameter at four anatomical landmarks were compared between patients who survived and those who died within 28 days in all critically ill patients presenting with AEW. In the second exploratory part of the study, the relevance of the laboratory parameters and AEW in predicting mortality were analyzed. In part three, the correlation between the 28-day mortality of all critically ill patients and the presence of esophageal widening was assessed. Results: Esophageal widening was detected in 98 of all 1683 included patient examinations. Nineteen of these patients have died (19.4%), and ten of them (52.6%) suffered primarily from a cerebrovascular event. In the group of patients with AEW, cervical AEW was more frequent among deceased patients (63.2% vs. 27.8%; p = 0.0064), and mean maximal esophageal diameter was also greater among deceased patients (19.2 vs. 16.4 mm; p = 0.0392). Multiple laboratory parameters were also found to correlate with mortality in all patients with AEW. No significant correlation of AEW alone with 28-day mortality in all critically ill patients that received ED-CT could be demonstrated in our retrospective sample. Conclusions: Esophageal widening, especially in the upper segment, was found in a substantial proportion of critically ill patients, with increased width correlating with mortality risk in the group of patients with AEW. Future studies should include much larger patient cohorts and a prospective design to evaluate if AEW might be a candidate to serve as a potential parameter of clinical scores which aim at early patient stratification.

articles.title: Modified pneumonia risk score using lung ultrasound for the prediction of radiographic pneumonia in children.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The diagnosis of pneumonia in children based on clinical findings is challenging. The Pneumonia Risk Score (PRS), a clinical prediction tool, estimates the risk of radiographic pneumonia. Most children are classified as moderate-risk and are recommended to undergo chest x-ray (CXR). We hypothesized that lung ultrasound (LUS) may add diagnostic value beyond the PRS for predicting radiographic pneumonia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We studied a convenience sample of children 6 months to 18 years old enrolled in a prospective LUS registry who presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory complaints and underwent CXR and LUS. The primary outcome was radiographic pneumonia. Logistic regression included the five PRS clinical predictors, and LUS consolidation ≥1 cm with bronchograms was added to create the PRS + LUS model. We compared the area under the curve (AUC) of the PRS to the PRS + LUS, evaluated risk re-classifications, and proposed a novel diagnostic algorithm.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 275 children, 58 (21%) had radiographic pneumonia. LUS consolidation was strongly associated with pneumonia (OR 28.68 [95% CI, 9.98 to 82.43]). The PRS + LUS demonstrated greater diagnostic accuracy than the PRS alone (AUC 0.85 [95% CI, 0.77 to 0.89] versus 0.70 [95% CI, 0.61 to 0.76]; P < 0.001). Using our proposed novel two-step diagnostic algorithm, the PRS + LUS was calculated for patients assigned a moderate-risk score by PRS, resulting in assigning an additional 120 (44%) patients a high- or low-risk score, decreasing the moderate-risk category.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Adding LUS to the PRS improves prediction of radiographic pneumonia and may reduce CXR use, particularly among patients with moderate risk.

articles.title: Private Equity Acquisitions and Home Health Agency Use, Expenditures, and Quality.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: Over the past 2 decades, the number of private equity (PE) acquisitions of Medicare home health agencies (HHAs) has increased considerably, with 6% of HHAs currently owned by PE firms.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To examine the impact of PE acquisitions of HHAs on home health use, costs, and quality measures.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This cohort study used Medicare fee-for-service claims data from 2011 to 2022 and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services HHA Cost Reports to measure home health visits, expenditures, and health outcomes among Medicare-certified HHAs. The sample included only Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries 65 years and older with any HHA use. These data were linked to a novel dataset of PE acquisitions of HHAs. A stacked difference-in-differences design was applied to compare outcomes before and after PE acquisition to a matched set of non-PE HHAs. Data analyses were performed from June 2025 through May 2026.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: The primary outcomes included (1) home health use (ie, total number of HHA visits per episode), (2) type of service use (ie, skilled nursing, home health therapy, home health aide, social work), (3) patient quality outcomes (ie, 30-day rehospitalizations, emergency department visits), and (4) HHA financial outcomes (ie, revenue, expenses, and profits).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 165 PE-acquired HHAs, serving 71 610 beneficiaries, and 422 matched for-profit non-PE HHAs, serving 170 066 beneficiaries, were identified. PE acquisition was associated with an absolute decrease of 1.11 HHA visits per episode (95% CI, -1.68 to -0.54 ; relative decrease, 8.3%) and an 11.3% decrease in total net expenses (log coefficient, -0.12; 95% CI, -0.22 to -0.01), while operating margins were 7.9 percentage points higher (95% CI, 5.1-10.7 percentage points). There were no statistically significant changes in net patient revenue, 30-day rehospitalizations, or emergency department visits. Heterogeneity analyses indicated that results were primarily driven by a single, large PE acquisition.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: In this cohort study with a difference-in-differences design, PE ownership of HHAs appeared to reduce service use and was associated with higher operating margins, with no statistically significant changes in patient quality outcomes, suggesting PE's use of cost-containment strategies rather than revenue generation to increase profits. The effects appear to be driven by 1 large acquisition, highlighting the heterogeneity of the impact of PE across HHA deals.

articles.title: Strategic solutions for the daily challenges of qualified intensive care unit beds and team shortages in hospitals.

abstract.text: No single, universal solution addresses the growing problem of hospital boarding amid constrained critical care resources. Throughout this text, we explored practical strategies aligned with this philosophy: early stabilization in Emergency Departments through specialized critical care teams; structured use of intermediate care units; tele-critical care networks extending intensivist oversight; hospital-based palliative care integration; automated early warning systems; robust rapid response systems and outreach teams; optimized perioperative triage; and governance reforms through closed or semi-closed intensive care unit models.

articles.title: Predictors and clinical outcomes of extubation failure in patients with cervical spinal cord injury.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Respiratory compromise is common in cervical spinal cord injury (SCI) and poses a challenge in deciding whether to extubate or perform a tracheostomy. This study evaluated the characteristics of failed extubations and hypothesized that those with unsuccessful extubation attempts would have a higher trauma burden and worse weaning parameters.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This was a retrospective review of intubated cervical SCI at a Level 1 trauma center from 2018 to 2024. Demographics, injury, surgical and airway management data were collected. Location of intubation and extubation, weaning parameters, and time to airway event or failure were tabulated. Statistical analysis was completed using Stata with p < 0.05 as significant.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Seventy patients with SCI were analyzed with a mean age of 54 years (range 18-89) and 62 (89%) males. Twenty successful extubations (SE) were compared to 36 failed extubations (FE), excluding the direct to tracheostomy (10) or terminally extubated (4) patients. Frequency of TBI (5% FE vs 14% SE, p = 0.3), blunt cerebrovascular injury (25% vs. 32%, p = 0.63) and ISS (30 vs 23, p = 0.13) were not statistically different. Documented weaning parameters - rapid shallow breathing index and negative inspiratory force were similar, although more FE patients were extubated in the OR/PACU. FE patients had significantly fewer hospital and ICU-free days; however, mortality differences did not reach statistical significance.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Failed extubation in SCI is associated with longer length of stay. Trauma burden and weaning parameters were not correlated with FE; however, extubation outside of the ICU may increase the risk of failure.

articles.title: Comparative mortality of pelvic ring fractures vs. hip fractures in adults ≥55 years: A propensity-matched cohort study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hip and pelvic fragility fractures are associated with substantial mortality in older adults. While standardized care pathways are established for hip fractures, management of pelvic fragility fractures remains less defined. This study compared mortality between matched hip and pelvic ring fracture patients managed operatively or nonoperatively.

abstract.label: HYPOTHESIS
abstract.text: Pelvic and hip fractures would demonstrate comparable mortality within operative and nonoperative treatment groups.

abstract.label: PATIENTS AND METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX network to identify adults aged ≥ 55 years with hip or pelvic ring fractures. Patients were stratified by operative or nonoperative management, and cohorts were propensity score matched 1:1 based on demographic and clinical characteristics. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were mortality at 30 days, 90 days, and 2 years. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated 1-year mortality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: After matching, 255,202 patients per cohort were included in the nonoperative subgroup and 11,448 per cohort in the operative subgroup. Among nonoperative patients, 1-year mortality was higher after hip than pelvic fracture (11.13% vs 10.68%; HR 1.123, 95% CI 1.105-1.141). Among operative patients, 1-year mortality was also higher after hip fracture (8.84% vs 5.94%; HR 1.424, 95% CI 1.314-1.545). However, 30-day mortality was higher after operative pelvic fracture (3.11% vs 2.49%; p = 0.004). Male sex, older age, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease were associated with increased mortality.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Hip fractures were associated with greater 1-year mortality across management strategies; however, operative pelvic fractures demonstrated greater early mortality. These findings highlight pelvic fragility fractures as high-risk injuries warranting further evaluation of standardized geriatric care pathways.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: III.

articles.title: Longitudinal trajectories of non-suicidal self-injury, suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts following standardized outpatient emergency management in adolescents.
articles.journal_full: Child and adolescent psychiatry and mental health

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency presentations for non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts in youth have increased markedly. Behavioural and ideational components of self-injury and suicidality may follow partially dissociable courses, underscoring the need for longitudinal evaluation after emergency care.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To examine longitudinal changes in NSSI behaviour, NSSI thoughts, suicidal ideation, and suicide attempts after standardized outpatient emergency management; identify psychological and familial predictors; and assess the perceived benefit of safety planning.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Participants were 105 adolescents (mean age = 14.9 years) presenting in acute crisis to an outpatient emergency service with NSSI and/or suicidal ideation/suicide attempt, followed up twice. Measures included NSSI and suicidal thoughts and behaviour, emotional reactivity, psychological distress, patient and parental motivation, parental stress, and perceived benefit of the safety plan. Changes over time were analysed using non-parametric tests of both frequency and prevalence, and predictors using linear mixed-effects models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Changes differed by dimension: suicide attempts declined in both frequency and prevalence, NSSI behaviour declined in frequency, and NSSI thoughts and suicidal ideation in prevalence while overall frequency was unchanged. Emotional reactivity, general psychological distress, and patient motivation improved. Higher patient motivation was independently associated with lower NSSI behaviour over time, while no variables significantly predicted NSSI thoughts. Parental, but not adolescent, perceived benefit of the safety plan was associated with reduced NSSI behaviour at follow-up.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Following emergency management, self-injurious behaviour and ideation followed partially dissociable courses. Behavioural improvement was linked to adolescent motivation and parental engagement, whereas ideation improved less completely: fewer adolescents reported suicidal or NSSI-related thoughts, but their frequency did not decline. Ideation therefore warrants continued, targeted monitoring even when behaviour improves.

articles.title: A bedside score using arrival data to identify major hemorrhage after blunt pelvic ring fracture: Development and validation.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Early recognition of major hemorrhage after blunt pelvic ring injury could guide mobilization of transfusion and hemorrhage-control resources. We developed an arrival-based bedside score and compared its performance with shock index.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We studied 239,736 adults with documented blunt pelvic ring fractures in the 2019-2024 National Trauma Data Bank. Major hemorrhage was defined as a hemorrhage-control procedure, hemorrhagic death, or transfusion of ≥ 1000 mL or ≥ 4 units of red blood cells within 4 h. Penalized logistic regression selected arrival variables for an integer score. We assessed performance in a held-out test set (n = 79,912) and at approximately matched alert volume. A model refitted on 2019-2022 admissions was evaluated in 2023-2024. Subgroup analyses were post hoc.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Major hemorrhage occurred in 26,479 patients (11.0%); 31.0% were aged ≥ 75 years, and 45.9% had fallen. In the test set, the score achieved an AUROC of 0.882 (95% CI, 0.879-0.886), exceeding shock index by 0.060 (95% CI, 0.055-0.064; P < 0.001). At approximately 15.6% of patients flagged, the score identified 678 additional major hemorrhage cases with 684 fewer false-positive alerts. The temporally validated model achieved an AUROC of 0.885 (95% CI, 0.881-0.888). Discrimination exceeded shock index for pelvic ring disruption (0.830 vs 0.778) and high-energy mechanisms (0.811 vs 0.764), but was lower after falls (0.779 vs 0.800).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In patients with documented blunt pelvic ring fractures, an arrival-based score identified major hemorrhage more accurately than shock index at a similar alert burden. Reduced performance after falls and uncertain applicability to suspected fractures warrant caution. External validation and prospective impact assessment are needed before clinical use.

articles.title: Does the number of debridement procedures impact risk of infection in open fractures?

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to evaluate the relationship between the number of debridements and risk of infection, while stratifying by degree of wound contamination. It was hypothesized that patients with severe contamination, a higher number of debridements would be associated with lower risk of infection.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This is a retrospective secondary analysis of prospectively collected data in the PREP-IT trial (Program of Randomized trials to Evaluate Preoperative antiseptic skin solutions in orthopaedic Trauma). The primary outcome measure was adjudicated surgical site infection. Independent variables were number of debridement procedures and time from injury to definitive wound closure. Analysis was stratified by degree of contamination and multivariable analyses were performed to control for confounders.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: 3502 total open fractures corresponding to 3222 patients with a median (interquartile range, IQR) age of 42 (29-58) years (2199 [62.8%] men; median (IQR) body mass index 27.7 [24.3-32.6]) were included in this analysis. 2199 patients were included in the non/minimal contamination group, 970 in the surface contamination group, and 333 in the embedded contamination group. After controlling for patient-level characteristics there was a 27% increase in the risk of infection for each debridement performed in the overall patient cohort (OR 1.27 [1.12-1.43] p < 0.001), and a 45% increase in the embedded contamination group (OR, 1.45 [1.12-1.88] p = 0.004). There was no statistically significant difference between minimal contamination groups and the surface contamination group.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The results of this study indicate that increased number of debridement procedures was not associated with lower infectious rates. Patients with the highest degree of contamination demonstrated significantly increased risk of developing an infection with each additional debridement. These findings support the importance of limiting unnecessary additional debridement procedures to reduce infection risk and optimize outcomes.

articles.title: Cone-Beam CT-Guided SpineJack® vertebral augmentation: A reproducible technique for accurate pedicular access and implant deployment.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: SpineJack® vertebral augmentation requires precise bilateral transpedicular access and accurate implant deployment. This study evaluated the feasibility, safety, and technical performance of cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-guided SpineJack augmentation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective single-institution, two-site study included consecutive CBCT-guided procedures performed between May 2021 and April 2026. Technical success required planned bilateral implantation, expansion, and cement augmentation without pedicle breach or implant malposition on final CBCT. Secondary outcomes included immediate vertebral height restoration, complications, procedure duration, radiation exposure, and treatment setting.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The analysis included 178 procedures; median age was 45 years (interquartile range [IQR], 27-59), and 158 procedures (88.8%) involved traumatic fractures. Technical success was 100% (178/178), including 64 procedures (36.0%) with pedicle-implant clearance < 0.8 mm. Median absolute vertebral body height gain was 4.1 mm (IQR, 2.7-6.1), and median restoration of baseline height loss reached 77% (IQR, 47-98). All 24 cement leaks (13.5%) were asymptomatic. No neurological, vascular, infectious, or implant-related complications occurred. Median procedure duration was 60 min (IQR, 50-90), and median dose-area product was 33.2 Gy·cm² (IQR, 19.4-53.1). One hundred procedures (56.2%) were performed on an outpatient basis.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: CBCT-guided SpineJack augmentation achieved accurate bilateral implant deployment and substantial immediate vertebral height restoration without major procedure-related complications. These findings support CBCT as a reliable guidance strategy for vertebral augmentation, with demonstrated feasibility in outpatient practice.

articles.title: The MIS-Diamond fixation: A minimally invasive diamond-shaped construct for spinopelvic dissociation in polytrauma patients.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Sacral fracture with spinopelvic dissociation (SPD) is a rare, high-energy injury associated with substantial mortality and morbidity. Surgical stabilization is technically challenging and has historically been associated with relatively high rates of construct failure. The present study describes and evaluates a novel minimally invasive spinopelvic diamond-shaped construct (The MIS-Diamond fixation), designed to improve rigid triangular stabilization while minimizing soft-tissue morbidity and facilitate the fracture reduction.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective observational study was conducted including patients who underwent MIS-Diamond fixation for AO Type C3 sacral fractures at a single Level-I Trauma Center between January 2014 and December 2024, with a minimum follow-up of 12 months. Neurological status, operative parameters, perioperative complications, and radiological outcomes were systematically assessed. Fractures were classified according to the AO Spine Sacral Injury Classification System.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Thirty-two patients (mean age 39 years) were included. Surgery was performed at a median of 5 days post-injury, with a mean operative time of 115.8 min and mean estimated blood loss of 82.7 mL. No intraoperative complications occurred. One patient developed a postoperative S1 motor impairment attributed to indirect radicular injury during reduction. Implant-related complications were recorded in 4 patients (12.5%), including one late-onset surgical site infection and three cases of asymptomatic iliac screw loosening. No soft tissue or wound healing complications were observed. Implant removal was successfully completed in 28 patients (87.5%) at 12 months postoperatively.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: MIS-Diamond fixation demonstrated a favourable safety profile while enabling early postoperative mobilization. The incorporation of a 5.5 mm transverse iliac rod converts the classical triangular construct into a rigid box-like configuration, enhancing rotational stability and preventing coronal diastasis during vertical distraction. Limiting instrumentation to L4-L5 reduces the number of immobilized motion segments compared to previously described longer constructs, potentially mitigating long-term degenerative sequelae.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The MIS-Diamond fixation represents a safe and effective minimally invasive surgical option for SPD, providing reliable multiplanar stabilization with a low complication profile. Routine implant removal at 12 months is feasible and recommended to preserve motion segment function. Prospective multicentre studies are warranted to further validate these findings.

articles.title: Effect of extreme heat on fall risk in older adults in a rural state.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Falls are common in older adults and may result in decreased functional ability, hospitalization, and death. Extreme temperature events, expected to worsen as a result of changing climates, have systemic impacts on the body, many of which overlap with the risk factors for falls in older adults. Our objective was to quantify the association between temperatures of 32°C (90°F) and greater and fall risk in older adults in a rural population.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We analyzed emergency medical services (EMS) patient care report data (2019-2023, n = 26,266) and hospital discharge data (emergency department visits (2011-2022, n = 96,658); hospitalizations (2011-2022, n = 31,407) on falls among adults aged 55 years and older at the ZIP Code level in Montana using case-crossover conditional logistic regression models. Heat was categorized based on daily temperature minimums and maximums (0°C and below, 0°+ to <32°C [reference], ≥32°C) as well as cumulative exposure (0 [reference], 1, 2, or 3+ days of ≥32°C), adjusted for daily precipitation and maximum daily humidity.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Daily temperatures ≥32°C were associated with increased odds of falls requiring hospitalization (odds ratio [OR]: 1.08, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.00, 1.15), as were two consecutive days of ≥32°C (OR: 1.14, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.29). Daily temperatures ≥32°C were also associated with increased odds of EMS calls related to falls and lift assists (OR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02, 1.13).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: We found evidence of associations between extreme heat and fall-related hospitalizations and EMS utilization among older adults. As hospitalizations for falls significantly impact both individual health and healthcare systems, understanding and addressing heat-related fall risk is critical, especially as extreme heat events are projected to increase.

articles.title: Combining a Modified Emergency Severity Index Score with Chief Complaints - Validation of a New Allocation Algorithm for Integrated Emergency Centers.
articles.journal: J Am Coll Emerg Physicians Open
articles.journal_full: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Current health policy reforms in Europe aim to synchronize emergency departments and acute outpatient clinics (AOC)/primary care services through the establishment of Integrated Emergency Centers (IECs). A central challenge of this model is the upstream triage at a central point of assessment (CPA). To date, there is a lack of standardized concepts for a single-stage assessment conducted by emergency-qualified staff that also facilitates cross-sectoral allocation. To address this gap, this study introduces the optimized leading-symptom-weighted modified Emergency Severity Index (L-mESI opt.) triage instrument. This tool aims to safely distribute the clinical workload between emergency departments (EDs) and AOCs by linking a modified emergency severity index (mESI)-omitting vital signs-with the patient's chief complaint (CEDIS).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective analysis of walk-in emergency patients was conducted at two university hospitals in 2024 (training dataset: n = 26,845). Outpatient treatment rates were determined for combinations of chief complaints and mESI categories. These probabilities informed an optimized allocation algorithm (L-mESI opt.) via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and the maximum Youden Index. The model was verified using a separate validation dataset (n = 11,512).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The pretest probability for AOC allocation was identified at 74%. The optimized L-mESI-opt. algorithm correctly allocated 54.2% of patients to the AOC, the ED workload was reduced by 46.9%. Compared with standard ESI-based steering, the L-mESI-opt. significantly improved sensitivity for inpatient care from 54.5% to 69.5% and achieved a negative predictive value of 85.4%. Although 14.6% of AOC-allocated patients required subsequent ED admission ("Upstream") in the validation set, critical outcomes remained minimal (observation unit transfer: 0.3%; mortality: 0.1%). Validation confirmed consistent quality and safety.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: L-mESI opt. model demonstrates the potential to effectively reduce ED workload while maintaining high patient safety in a simulated environment. These results show that its adaptability could allow for broad application in IECs. However, the successful implementation of such an algorithm will likely depend on close spatial and organizational links between EDs and AOCs to manage bilateral patient flow efficiently. Prospective clinical trials are warranted to confirm these findings in real-world settings.

articles.title: Complete Symptom Resolution After Rest in Acute Dizziness: Implications for Selective Magnetic Resonance Imaging Use and Patient Out-of-Pocket Costs in Japan.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: We examined the association between symptom resolution after rest and causative central lesions on initial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and the patient-perspective economic implications of hypothetical MRI omission. Methods: This exploratory, single-center, retrospective observational study included 170 patients with dizziness who underwent MRI between April 2022 and March 2024. Symptoms were reassessed after 10 min of supine rest. Among patients discharged home, MRI-related charges were hypothetically omitted for those with complete resolution, with other care unchanged. Sensitivity analyses examined the impact of hypothetical additional outpatient revisit costs. Results: Causative central lesions were detected in 0 of 90 patients with complete resolution (0.0%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.0-4.0%) and 12 of 80 with residual symptoms (15.0%; 95% CI, 8.0-24.7%; p < 0.001). Among 89 discharged patients, hypothetical MRI omission in 54 (60.7%) reduced estimated initial medical expenditures by JPY 909,300 (22.6%); the median estimated patient-payment reduction was JPY 3552. In sensitivity analyses limited to additional outpatient revisits, estimated reductions remained positive across the principal scenarios but diminished as assumed revisit use increased. Conclusions: Complete symptom resolution was associated with a lower observed proportion of causative central lesions and warrants evaluation as information complementary to established assessment. Hypothetical selective MRI use reduced estimated initial expenditures and patient payments. These exploratory findings do not establish the safety of MRI omission; prospective validation incorporating clinical outcomes and downstream healthcare use is required.

articles.title: Whole blood transfusion in adult patients with traumatic brain injury: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Whole blood (WB) transfusion may improve outcomes in trauma patients compared with component therapy, but evidence in traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains limited. We evaluated the clinical effectiveness of WB transfusion in adults with TBI requiring transfusion.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP for studies published from January 2006 through August 31, 2026. Eligible studies included randomized trials and observational studies using propensity score matching or inverse probability of treatment weighting. Random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustment was performed for mortality. Component-specific transfusion requirements were summarized qualitatively.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Five studies were included in the systematic review, and four studies were included in the mortality meta-analysis.
