Study Design: A descriptive study. Place and Duration of the Study: Department of Emergency Medicine, Beijing Jingmei Group General Hospital, Beijing, China, from January 2019 to October 2025.

abstract.label: METHODOLOGY
abstract.text: Adults admitted within 24 hours of SICH onset who underwent repeat computed tomography within 72 hours were included. Haematoma expansion was defined as an increase in haematoma volume by >20% or >6 mL. Clinical, radiological, and laboratory variables were analysed using multivariable binary logistic regression. Model discrimination and apparent calibration were assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis and the Brier score; 1,000 bootstrap resamples were used for internal assessment.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Haematoma expansion occurred in 87 (31.1%) of 280 patients. Higher admission Glasgow Coma Scale scores were unexpectedly associated with expansion [odds ratio (OR) 1.20, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.09-1.31; p <0.001]. Lower serum magnesium was associated with expansion (OR 0.41, 95% CI: 0.28-0.60; p <0.001). Ionised calcium, reported per 0.1 mmol/L, was also inversely associated with expansion (OR 0.58, 95% CI: 0.43-0.77; p <0.001). Apparent model performance included an area under the curve of 0.832 (95% CI: 0.779-0.879), sensitivity of 0.805, specificity of 0.746, and a Brier score of 0.147.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Lower admission serum magnesium was independently associated with haematoma expansion. The model showed good apparent discrimination but requires external validation before clinical use. Key Words: Cerebral haemorrhage, Haematoma, Magnesium, Nomogram, Risk assessment.

articles.title: Determinants of Pre-Hospital Delay in Patients with ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction in Dera Ismail Khan.
articles.journal_full: Journal of the College of Physicians and Surgeons--Pakistan : JCPSP

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To assess the association between sociodemographic factors and healthcare-seeking behaviour, and pre-hospital delay (>6 hours) in patients diagnosed with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

abstract.label: STUDY DESIGN
abstract.text: An analytical cross-sectional study. Place and Duration of the Study: Department of Cardiology, Gomal Medical College, Dera Ismail Khan, Pakistan, from September 2025 to April 2026.

abstract.label: METHODOLOGY
abstract.text: A total of 255 patients diagnosed with STEMI were included using non-probability consecutive sampling. A predesigned pro forma was used to collect data on sociodemographic variables, symptom interpretation, healthcare-seeking behaviour, first medical contact, and distance from the healthcare facility. Pre-hospital delay was defined as presentation to the coronary care unit more than 6 hours after symptom onset. Data were analysed using SPSS version 27. Bivariate analyses were performed using the chi-squared test and independent samples t-test, while multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The mean age of the 255 patients was 58.28 ± 11.2 years; 155 (60.8%) were male. Fifty-nine (23.1%) patients fulfilled the criteria for pre-hospital delay. The strongest independent predictors were misguided healthcare-seeking behaviour (aOR 9.43; 95% CI: 3.33-26.69; p <0.001) and symptom misinterpretation (aOR 3.47; 95% CI: 1.48-8.13; p = 0.004). Reduced delay was observed in patients who were at a shorter distance from the healthcare unit.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In STEMI, pre-hospital delay is mainly caused by misguided healthcare-seeking behaviour and misinterpreted symptoms. To reduce delays, public awareness and reinforcement of primary healthcare referral systems are essential.

abstract.label: KEY WORDS
abstract.text: Prehospital delay, ST-elevation myocardial infarction, Risk factors, Treatment delay, Rural population.

articles.title: Bezold Abscess: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: A Bezold abscess is a neck abscess characterized by inflammation and infection of the mastoid process that can invade deep into local anatomical musculature and vasculature.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We highlight the case of a 62-year-old man who presented with ongoing left-sided neck pain, headache, and tinnitus that started two weeks prior to arriving at the emergency department. Physical examination showed tenderness to the left trapezius muscle, left-sided mastoid tenderness, and pearly tympanic membranes bilaterally. A computed tomography angiogram of the head and neck was performed due to concerns of vertebral dissection, which eventually led to a diagnosis of Bezold abscess.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Although Bezold abscess has been described in the medical literature, it is rarely encountered in modern clinical practice because the widespread use of antibiotic therapy prevents acute mastoiditis from progressing to abscess formation. We highlight the complexity of clinical presentation that can easily be mistaken for other medical conditions, such as occurred with our patient who presented with symptoms more consistent with vertebral dissection: neck pain; tinnitus; and headache, without associated ear pain or discharge.

articles.title: Prehospital Ultrasound to Identify Endotracheal Tube Dislodgment in an Infant: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is well established as a useful adjunct for airway management in both adult and pediatric patients, including confirmation of successful endotracheal intubation. While suprasternal ultrasound of the trachea is the most described method for confirming endotracheal tube (ETT) placement, a focused lung exam can be used to rapidly identify appropriate ventilation in otherwise apneic patients.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: This case involves a one-month-old male infant who experienced an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest secondary to suspected sudden infant death syndrome. During resuscitation, an accidental extubation occurred after an attempt at securing the ETT with a commercial pediatric tube holder. Loss of end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) waveform was recognized immediately; however, emergency medical services clinicians questioned the device's accuracy due to earlier failures of the ETCO2 monitor and the ETT remaining secured at an expected depth. A rapid POCUS lung examination demonstrated absence of bilateral lung sliding. The patient was immediately extubated, revealing a kinked ETT in the oropharynx with the distal tip positioned above the vocal cords. A supraglottic airway device (SGA) was placed with a successful return of ETCO2 waveform, followed shortly by successful reintubation because of difficulty ventilating through the SGA.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Lung ultrasound is a rapid and effective alternative for identifying ETT dislodgment when conventional verification methods are unreliable or unavailable. As ultrasound becomes increasingly available in prehospital and resource-limited settings, it may be effectively used by nonphysician clinicians to confirm airway placement and detect airway complications.

articles.title: From Staple Removal to Startle-The Unexpected Discovery of a Scalp Pseudoaneurysm: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) allows emergency physicians to rapidly diagnose vascular abnormalities, including pseudoaneurysms. Although commonly identified following vascular catheterization, traumatic pseudoaneurysms of superficial scalp arteries are rare.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: An 85-year-old woman receiving anticoagulation presented to the emergency department (ED) for removal of a scalp staple placed during treatment of a previously bleeding scalp wound. Physical examination revealed a persistent scalp hematoma. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated a hypoechoic collection with Doppler flow consistent with a pseudoaneurysm. Computed tomography angiography confirmed the diagnosis. Ultrasound-guided compression attempted in the ED resulted only in transient thrombosis. The patient subsequently underwent elective percutaneous embolization.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Emergency physician-performed POCUS can rapidly identify traumatic scalp pseudoaneurysms and facilitate timely consultation and treatment.

articles.title: Focal Hepatic Hot Spot Sign Mimicking Active Extravasation on CT Angiography in Superior Vena Cava Syndrome: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Caused by portosystemic venous shunting, the focal hepatic hot spot sign (or hot quadrate sign) is a radiologic finding most commonly associated with superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction. On contrast-enhanced imaging, this finding may mimic active hepatic extravasation or focal hepatic pathology, posing a diagnostic challenge in the emergency department (ED).

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We report a case of a 70-year-old man with progressive cognitive decline and hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring intubation. Computed tomography (CT) angiography of the chest demonstrated a focal area of intense contrast enhancement in the left hepatic lobe, initially concerning for active extravasation. Further review of the imaging revealed a right upper lobe lung mass and a large mediastinal mass causing high-grade SVC stenosis. The hepatic finding was subsequently identified by the reading radiologist as a focal hepatic hot spot sign representing a vascular pseudolesion due to collateral venous flow. The patient was diagnosed with SVC syndrome secondary to malignancy and underwent chemotherapy before transitioning to comfort care.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The focal hepatic hot spot sign represents a hepatic pseudolesion resulting from altered venous return and collateral circulation, most commonly in the setting of SVC obstruction. In the ED, this finding may be misinterpreted as hemorrhage or focal hepatic pathology, potentially leading to unnecessary diagnostic or therapeutic interventions. Recognition of the focal hepatic hot spot sign is essential for emergency physicians to avoid misdiagnosis and identify underlying central venous obstruction. Awareness of this imaging pitfall can improve diagnostic accuracy and guide appropriate management in patients undergoing contrast-enhanced CT imaging.

articles.title: Soft Palate Perforation with Endotracheal Tube During Video Laryngoscopy.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 57-year-old man with a history of obesity-hypoventilation syndrome, diabetes mellitus, and chronic renal insufficiency was intubated with an 8.0-mm endotracheal tube under video laryngoscopy in the emergency department due to respiratory failure. After successful intubation, bloody secretions were noted in the patient's mouth. Subsequent examination revealed that the endotracheal tube had caused a through-and-through perforation at the junction of the soft palate and the anterior tonsillar pillar. Because the intubation had been successful, the endotracheal tube was not removed, and the soft palate was transected to free the tube. The patient made an uneventful recovery.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Soft palate perforation is an uncommon injury that has been reported more frequently with video laryngoscopy than direct laryngoscopy. To prevent this injury and ensure its rapid recognition, it is recommended that the clinician sequentially look at the "5 M's" during intubation: Mouth-Monitor-Mouth-Monitor-Mouth.

articles.title: Delayed Revascularization in Rural Acute STEMI Patient on Direct Oral Anticoagulation: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Acute ST-elevated myocardial infarction (STEMI) is a medical emergency requiring timely revascularization to preserve myocardial injury. Rural populations often experience delays in treatment leading to increased risk of complications and mortality. Emergent treatment of STEMI in a patient on long-term direct oral anticoagulation facing delays to revascularization is a complex scenario for rural physicians.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 55-year-old male presented to the emergency department in rural Alaska and was diagnosed with acute inferior STEMI. The patient's history was notable for pulmonary embolism with long-term direct oral anticoagulation. Thrombolytic therapy was not recommended and prompt revascularization via percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was needed; however, the nearest PCI-capable hospital was hundreds of miles away, increasing the risk of ischemic cardiomyopathy and death. The patient achieved revascularization after transport and, in the following year, experienced multiple episodes of ventricular tachycardia leading to ablation and need for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case illustrates a complex but not uncommon scenario that rural physicians face. In rural patients requiring acute STEMI treatment but without timely access to a PCI-capable hospital, systemic thrombolysis and immediate transfer of care is often the only option for revascularization. There is a need for clear STEMI management guidelines in anticoagulated patients who present in rural settings.

articles.title: A Rare Presentation of Pneumococcal Meningitis with Acute Bilateral Vision Loss: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Bacterial meningitis affects about 1.2 million people worldwide each year. Streptococcus pneumoniae is responsible for the majority of cases of bacterial meningitis in the United States and Europe, with visual impairment seen in 6.3% of patients. The etiology of acute vision loss in the setting of bacterial meningitis remains wide-ranging, most often occurring in the setting of endogenous endophthalmitis, optic neuropathy, and cortical blindness. Retinal necrosis is rare, and typically associated with viral meningitis, but has not been reported in bacterial meningitis.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 66-year-old man with headache, malaise, and intermittent blurry vision, initially diagnosed with viral upper respiratory infection and presumed trigeminal neuralgia, presented to the emergency department with altered mental status, meningismus, and progressive bilateral vision loss. He was diagnosed with bacterial meningitis, and subsequent cerebrospinal fluid and blood cultures were positive for S pneumoniae. Ophthalmologic evaluation demonstrated bilateral nonreactive pupils, retinal ischemia, optic nerve pallor, and retinal necrosis but no intraocular inflammation. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed multifocal cortical ischemic infarcts thought to be of embolic source. His hospitalization was complicated by mitral valve regurgitation, endocarditis, and cardiac tamponade requiring extensive surgical repair.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case represents a rare presentation of bilateral retinal ischemia and necrosis in the setting of S pneumoniae meningitis without evidence of endophthalmitis. Awareness of atypical ocular presentations and differential diagnoses is vital in providing early diagnosis, treatment and specialist involvement.

articles.title: Spontaneous Cardiac Tamponade in a Patient with Severe Hemophilia A: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder characterized by deficiency of factor VIII. The clinical features of this disease are hemorrhage and can be life-threatening when major organ systems are involved.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We report the case of a 13-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A and factor VIII inhibitors who presented with fever and septic arthritis, later developing refractory shock with tachyarrhythmia. Despite initial suspicion of sepsis-related myocarditis, point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) revealed massive hemorrhagic pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. Recombinant factor VIIa was transfused as hemostatic rescue therapy; the patient was subsequently started on fresh frozen plasma and emicizumab. Ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis resulted in rapid hemodynamic recovery.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the importance of considering obstructive shock in unstable hemophilia patients and demonstrates that timely POCUS-based diagnosis and factor-supported pericardiocentesis can be lifesaving.

articles.title: Gaze-Evoked Vomiting After Minor Orbital Trauma: White-Eyed Blowout Fracture.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 16-year-old girl presented to the emergency department after being struck in the right eye by another player's elbow during a basketball game. She had only minimal periorbital swelling but developed persistent nausea, repeated vomiting, and diplopia with upward gaze. Visual acuity, visual fields, and pupillary light reflexes were normal. Extraocular movement testing showed mild limitation of upward gaze of the right eye, and upward gaze reproducibly provoked diplopia, marked nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) showed no intracranial hemorrhage, and orbital CT was initially interpreted as showing no obvious orbital floor fracture or extraocular muscle entrapment. Given the discrepancy between the mild external appearance and the severe ocular symptoms, white-eyed blowout fracture with trapdoor-type entrapment and an oculocardiac reflex was suspected. She underwent emergent surgery, after which her vomiting, diplopia, and ocular motility disturbance improved immediately.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: White-eyed blowout fracture is a trapdoor-type orbital floor injury seen mainly in children and adolescents and may present with minimal external signs and subtle or negative-appearing CT findings. Gaze-evoked nausea or vomiting, diplopia, and relative bradycardia are important bedside clues to extraocular muscle entrapment with an oculocardiac reflex. This case highlights that white-eyed blowout fracture may be detected by careful bedside examination even when CT does not clearly show an orbital floor fracture. Emergency physicians should recognize this entity as a clinically important, easily missed diagnosis in pediatric orbital trauma.

articles.title: Exercise-Induced Diaphragmatic Rupture with Intrathoracic Gastric Herniation: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: While abdominal pain is a common complaint in the emergency department (ED), it is key to obtain a diligent history and maintain a broad differential diagnosis. The development of exercise-induced diaphragmatic hernia is rare but can result in a high risk of morbidity and mortality.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: This is a case of a 24-year-old man who presented to the ED with acute-onset epigastric abdominal pain that began while performing "burpee" (squat thrust) exercises. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed diaphragmatic rupture with gastric herniation into the left hemithorax. The patient underwent emergent surgical intervention to reduce the intra-abdominal contents and repair the diaphragmatic defect.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: There are no prior reports of diaphragmatic hernia due to burpee exercises in the emergency medicine literature. Consideration of exercise-induced diaphragmatic hernia is necessary due to the high morbidity of this condition.

articles.title: Case Report of Orthopedic Screw Migration Presenting as Abdominal Pain in the Emergency Department.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Hip fractures are a concern in older adults, with incidence expected to rise as the population ages. Despite advances in surgical technique and hardware design, complications remain, influenced by patient factors and surgical choices. Rarely, hardware migration into the pelvis occurs, which poses serious risks. In the emergency setting, abdominal pain is a common complaint, and when evaluating patients with complex histories or prior orthopedic surgeries, clinicians must maintain a broad differential. This case details the discovery of a medially displaced hip screw into the pelvis as the cause of abdominal pain in a patient in the emergency department (ED).

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 44-year-old female with end stage renal disease on hemodialysis, anemia, and osteoporosis presented to the ED with sudden-onset, bilateral lower quadrant abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. The patient reported undergoing left hip open reduction and internal fixation seven months prior. Imaging of the abdomen noted medial displacement of the cephalomedullary nail through the left acetabulum into the pelvis with associated extraperitoneal hematoma. She underwent hardware removal and exploratory laparotomy without bowel injury.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Orthopedic screw migration is a rare but serious complication, with limited documentation in the literature. Risk increases in patients with poor bone quality and healing, often due to chronic conditions. In patients with multiple comorbidities, careful history and a thorough exam when presenting to the ED are critical to identifying complications. Strategic use of imaging and clinical judgement can help emergency physicians refine their differential diagnosis.

articles.title: Subacute Microperforation of Right Atrial Pacemaker Lead Presenting with Shock due to Cardiac Tamponade: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Delayed cardiac tamponade is a rare but life-threatening complication following permanent pacemaker placement and may present with non-specific symptoms.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We report the case of a 66-year-old woman on oral anticoagulation who presented with generalized weakness, nausea, and profound hypotension four days after dual-chamber pacemaker placement. Initial evaluation demonstrated atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, a normal chest radiographic findings, prerenal azotemia, and no evidence of device malfunction on interrogation. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) performed in the emergency department revealed a large pericardial effusion with right atrial and right ventricular collapse and a plethoric inferior vena cava, consistent with cardiac tamponade. Emergent pericardiocentesis yielded 400 mL of sanguinous pericardial fluid with rapid hemodynamic improvement. Subsequent imaging revealed a 2-mm protrusion of the right atrial lead into the myocardium, which was suspected to be the source of the effusion, but pacemaker revision was not necessary.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the limitations of routine diagnostic testing following permanent pacemaker placement and emphasizes the importance of early POCUS in patients with atypical presentations, particularly in the setting of anticoagulation.

articles.title: A Case Report of Meningitis due to Borrelia Species in Arizona.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Lyme disease is most prevalent in the Northeast and Midwest regions of the United States, as well as northern California; however, cases have been reported in nonendemic areas, including the Southwestern United States. Atypical presentations or underreporting can cause delay in diagnosis.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We present the case of a 22-year-old previously healthy man, who presented to our emergency department in metropolitan Phoenix with five days of headache, fever, meningismus, and photophobia, and later developed focal neurologic deficits consistent with Lyme meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid was notable for lymphocytic pleocytosis, and Western blot for Borrelia burgdorferi Immunoglobulin-M antibodies was positive, which led us to Lyme meningitis as the unifying diagnosis. He was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and his symptoms resolved.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the importance of considering this pathology in nonendemic areas.

articles.title: Tension Pneumopericardium from a Gastrojejunal-Pericardial Fistula Causing Tamponade: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Cardiac tamponade typically develops from the accumulation of blood and other fluids, although it can occur from pneumopericardium.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with chest pain and was found to have a pneumopericardium on computed tomography. He developed signs of obstructive shock with hypotension refractory to intravenous fluids and vasopressors. The patient stabilized with bedside pericardiocentesis and pericardial drain placement.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Gastrointestinal-pericardial fistulae are a rare cause of pneumopericardium. Emergency physicians typically rely on cardiac point-of-care ultrasound to evaluate for tamponade and guide pericardiocentesis. However, air artifacts interfere with images, complicating diagnosis and procedures.

articles.title: Inferior Vena Cava Cement Migration with Pulmonary Cement Embolism: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Vertebral augmentation procedures, including vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty, can result in cement extravasation, which is often clinically silent. Less commonly, cement may migrate intravascularly into the inferior vena cava (IVC) and pulmonary arterial circulation, resulting in pulmonary cement embolism, a potentially life-threatening complication. Early recognition in the emergency department (ED) is essential to guide appropriate imaging, specialty consultation, and timely management.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 76-year-old woman with recent third lumbar vertebral augmentation presented to the ED with acute worsening low back pain and burning bilateral radicular symptoms approximately one week after the procedure. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast demonstrated linear hyperdense material extending from the treated vertebral body into the IVC, concerning for intravascular cement migration. Additional CT of the chest demonstrated multiple bilateral subsegmental pulmonary cement emboli. Interventional radiology was consulted emergently, and the patient was transferred for endovascular retrieval of the IVC cement fragment, which was successfully removed. The pulmonary cement emboli were small, peripheral, and asymptomatic and were managed conservatively. The patient remained hemodynamically stable and was discharged after monitored hospitalization.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Inferior vena cava cement migration with pulmonary cement embolism is a potentially life-threatening complication of vertebral augmentation. Emergency physicians should maintain suspicion for this diagnosis in patients with acute pain or new cardiopulmonary symptoms following recent spinal procedures. Early imaging, multidisciplinary consultation, monitored admission, and endovascular retrieval when indicated may reduce morbidity.

articles.title: Diagnosing a Fractured Pedunculated Osteochondroma Using Point-of-Care Ultrasound in the Emergency Department: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: This case report discusses the use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in the diagnosis of a fractured pedunculated osteochondroma in an 8-year-old boy after minor trauma. Although osteochondromas are the most common benign bone tumors, especially in this age, historically only radiographs have been obtained in the emergency department to diagnose these benign bone tumors.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: An 8-year-old boy reported ongoing pain for 2 months but had an acute onset worsening of his pain after minor trauma to the medial distal right femur. Point-of-care ultrasound was used to diagnose a fractured pedunculated osteochondroma prior to radiographic imaging.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: We demonstrated the practicality and ease of POCUS in assisting with the diagnosis of an osteochondroma and the subtle fracture of the base. Both POCUS and radiographic imaging may be beneficial when used in conjunction for the diagnosis of benign bone tumors in this age group.

articles.title: Luxatio Erecta with Complex Medical Decision-Making Regarding Reduction: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Luxatio erecta is a rare glenohumeral dislocation. The standard treatment is reduction under procedural sedation; however, decision-making becomes more nuanced in patients with comorbidities. This report describes a hyperglycemic patient with type 1 diabetes with luxatio erecta.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: An 18-year-old man resented with a traumatic inferior shoulder dislocation. Laboratory tests indicated severe hyperglycemia without diabetic ketoacidosis. The emergency department team performed a risk-benefit assessment before proceeding with procedural sedation. Closed reduction was successful, and hyperglycemia was managed with intravenous fluids.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Inferior shoulder dislocations are rare; severe hyperglycemia in diabetics is not an absolute contraindication to procedural sedation, but the patient may need individualized risk-benefit assessment.

articles.title: Intracardiac Placement of Needle Thoracostomy Catheter by Paramedics Due to Anatomic Variation: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Needle thoracostomy is the only procedure in the United States for paramedic treatment of suspected tension pneumothorax within the most recent emergency medical services (EMS) national scope of practice model. We present a rare complication of an out-of-hospital left needle thoracostomy performed by paramedics after intracardiac placement of the catheter. The patient's imaging studies in the receiving emergency department (ED) confirmed that the needle thoracostomy insertion location was correct, but the catheter entered the heart due to the patient's existing atypical anatomy.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 64-year-old unrestrained male driver in a roll-over motor vehicle accident was found in respiratory distress with difficulty auscultating left-sided lung sounds, left chest wall pain on palpation, and confusion. The first-arriving paramedics performed a left needle thoracostomy for suspected tension pneumothorax in advance of helicopter EMS transport. However, pulsatile blood flow from the catheter suggested intracardiac placement, which was confirmed on multiple imaging modalities in the ED. Imaging showed the catheter in the anterior second intercostal space at the midclavicular line. It was also revealed that the patient's heart was prominently superior and nearly extended to the left chest wall with a majority of his left lung positioned posteriorly within the thorax. There were no signs of pneumothorax, hemothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, diaphragmatic injury, sternotomy wires, or other evidence that his atypical anatomy was the result of an exogenous process.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Intracardiac placement of a needle thoracostomy catheter is a rare complication. In this case, the patient's atypical anatomy contributed to asymmetric lung sounds and suspicion of tension pneumothorax. Regardless of which insertion site was chosen, the likelihood of intracardiac placement was potentially high due to the patient's anatomy. Anatomical variation can cause lung sound asymmetry that mimics a pneumothorax, which emergency clinicians and paramedics must consider when assessing for tension pneumothorax.

articles.title: Emergency Department Use of Genicular Nerve Block for Sickle Cell Pain Crisis: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Acute pain crises are a common emergency department presentation in patients with sickle cell disease. Pain management typically relies on multimodal analgesia, with opioids often playing a central role. We propose incorporating regional anesthesia techniques into the pain management regimen.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We present a case of a young patient with sickle cell disease experiencing an acute pain crisis with severe knee pain. A genicular nerve block was performed, resulting in significant pain reduction in the affected knee.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Regional anesthesia, including isolated nerve blocks, may be safe and effective as part of a multimodal pain approach for patients suffering from acute pain crises due to sickle cell disease. This may help reduce the need for opioid or other sedating pain medications, as well as the inherent risks associated with increasing doses, such as respiratory depression.

articles.title: Use of Point-of-Care Ultrasound to Confirm and Manage a Morel-Lavallée Lesion in the Emergency Department: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Morel-Lavallée lesions are closed, soft tissue degloving injuries that occur when shearing forces separate the subcutaneous tissue from the underlying fascia. This creates a potential space for hemolymphatic fluid accumulation. Morel-Lavallée lesions are frequently under-reported and often misdiagnosed as hematomas or abscesses, leading to potential mismanagement. While magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is considered the gold standard for diagnosis, point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has been shown to be an effective adjunct that can rapidly confirm sonographic features consistent with Morel-Lavallée lesions, support MRI-established findings, and guide procedural intervention in the emergency department (ED) setting.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We describe a 20-year-old woman presenting to the ED with persistent right-sided hip pain two months after a pedestrian-motor vehicle collision. Initially misdiagnosed as a hematoma, an outpatient follow-up MRI identified a large Morel-Lavallée lesion, with POCUS confirming subcutaneous anechoic fluid collection in the ED. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded 150 mL of serosanguinous fluid, with real-time imaging confirming decompression. Laboratory analysis demonstrated elevated red blood cell and nucleated cell counts consistent with Morel-Lavallée lesion.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the integrated diagnostic and therapeutic role of point-of-care ultrasound as an adjunct to MRI, confirming sonographic features of a Morel-Lavallée lesion, guiding aspiration, and providing real-time postprocedural assessment within a single ED encounter in a patient presenting two months after injury.

articles.title: Bedside Sonography Brings the Weiss Ring into Focus: Rapid Diagnosis of Posterior Vitreous Detachment.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 51-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with blurred vision and a large, dark floater in her right eye. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) revealed a Weiss ring, strongly suggesting a diagnosis of a posterior vitreous detachment.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Identifying a Weiss ring with POCUS may be a reasonable and easier alternative for emergency clinicians when used in conjunction with a slit-lamp examination and may aid in timely ophthalmologic management of posterior vitreous detachments.

articles.title: Prehospital Cold-Water Immersion for Undifferentiated Heat Stroke: A Case Series.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Heat stroke is a time-sensitive condition that requires early intervention to prevent morbidity and mortality. Heat-related deaths are also increasing. Multiple studies have evaluated various cooling methods and assessed their effectiveness, safety, and practicality across diverse settings and populations. Earlier and faster cooling leads to improved patient outcomes. The National Association of Emergency Medical Services Physicians recommends initiating prehospital cold-water immersion before emergency medical services (EMS) transport.

abstract.label: CASE SERIES
abstract.text: This case series evaluated the feasibility and effectiveness of prehospital cold-water immersion initiated before and continued during EMS transportation from the scene to emergency department arrival in this critically ill patient population.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Rapid initiation and maintenance of prehospital cold-water immersion in undifferentiated heat stroke was both feasible and effective. Over the course of the case series, no deaths were reported, and all patients were eventually discharged home.

articles.title: Behavioral Trigger Identification in Recurrent Postpartum Chest Pain After Negative Cardiopulmonary Evaluation: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Recurrent chest pain in postpartum patients frequently results in repeated emergency department (ED) visits despite negative cardiopulmonary investigations, creating diagnostic uncertainty and increasing healthcare resource utilization. We report a case highlighting the value of a structured postexclusion assessment to identify clinically relevant behavioral triggers after life-threatening causes have been excluded.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 33-year-old woman, six weeks postpartum, presented repeatedly with nocturnal chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea. Serial electrocardiograms, cardiac biomarkers, chest imaging, and transthoracic echocardiography were consistently normal, excluding acute cardiopulmonary pathology. Careful reassessment of symptom chronology and behavioral history identified a reproducible temporal association between symptom onset and nocturnal binge-eating episodes. Following outpatient psychiatric and clinical psychological evaluation confirming Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, diagnostic criteria for binge-eating disorder, targeted behavioral counseling led to a marked reduction in symptom frequency and no further ED presentations during follow-up.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case demonstrates that, after exclusion of life-threatening cardiopulmonary disease, a structured assessment emphasizing symptom temporality and behavioral triggers can uncover clinically actionable mechanisms underlying recurrent postpartum chest pain. Incorporating this approach into emergency department evaluation may facilitate appropriate management while reducing unnecessary repeat investigations and ED utilization.

articles.title: A 30-Year-Old Man With Rapid Floor-of-Mouth Swelling After Facial Trauma.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 30-year-old man presented to the emergency department with severe blunt facial trauma following a fall from height. Examination revealed extensive floor-of-mouth ecchymosis and a large tense sublingual hematoma causing tongue elevation, dysarthria, and swelling mimicking Ludwig's angina, producing a traumatic pseudo-Ludwig appearance with marked airway crowding. Three-dimensional computed tomography demonstrated severely displaced bilateral mandibular fractures. Owing to pronounced segmental instability with mobile dentoalveolar fragments, temporary interdental bridle wire stabilization was performed in the emergency department. Despite the dramatic anatomical findings, serial airway reassessments confirmed sustained airway stability, permitting delayed definitive open reduction and internal fixation.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Traumatic pseudo-Ludwig angina secondary to bilateral mandibular fractures is an uncommon presentation that may closely mimic life-threatening infectious floor-of-mouth swelling. Hemorrhage within the confined sublingual space can rapidly elevate and posteriorly displace the tongue, resulting in progressive airway compromise. This case highlights the importance of dynamic airway assessment, serial airway reassessment, and early multidisciplinary management, including temporary interdental bridle wire stabilization, in carefully selected patients with traumatic hemorrhagic floor-of-mouth emergencies.

articles.title: From Pain to Clarity: A Case of Pneumoperitoneum Diagnosed by Point-of-care Ultrasound.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Acute abdomen is a common emergency presentation, and gastrointestinal perforation can be rapidly fatal if not promptly identified. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) offers a rapid bedside alternative when advanced imaging is delayed or unavailable.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We report a 40-year-old man presenting in cardiac arrest, resuscitated after ten minutes, with subsequent findings of abdominal distension and prior epigastric pain. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated classic signs of pneumoperitoneum, and intestinal perforation was confirmed by the drainage of feculent fluid. Despite intervention, the patient expired.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case underscores the value of POCUS in diagnosing perforation in unstable patients, guiding emergent decisions when transfer or definitive imaging is not feasible.

articles.title: From Frenulum Tear to Transfusion-An Unexpected Diagnosis of Hemophilia in a Toddler: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Labial frenulum tears in infants are commonly associated with minor trauma but may raise concern for nonaccidental injury. These injuries are typically benign and self-limiting; however, persistent or excessive bleeding should prompt evaluation for an underlying bleeding disorder. Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency with clinical symptoms that vary based on the level of severity.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A previously healthy 14-month-old male presented to the pediatric emergency department three times within 10 days for persistent bleeding from a superior labial frenulum tear sustained after minor trauma. Initial examination was reassuring, and he was discharged without laboratory evaluation. On repeat presentation, he was found to have normocytic anemia and isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Despite topical and oral antifibrinolytic therapy, he returned with worsening anemia, melena, hematemesis, pallor, and tachycardia. He required a packed red blood cell transfusion, intravenous aminocaproic acid, and hospitalization. Further hematologic evaluation revealed a low factor VIII activity level, confirming mild hemophilia A. There was no prior personal or family history of abnormal bleeding.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights that hemophilia A may initially present with disproportionate bleeding from a minor mucosal injury, even in the absence of a known bleeding history. Persistent bleeding after minor trauma warrants prompt coagulation evaluation to prevent diagnostic delay and serious complications.

articles.title: Polysubstance-Induced Vasoplegia Managed with Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: While the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) becomes increasingly commonplace in overdose, questions about its role in various shock states remain. The application of VA-ECMO with impaired myocardial function is well established, and use in cardiogenic shock precipitated by poisoning has continued to increase. In poison-induced vasoplegia with preserved myocardial function, the role of VA-ECMO remains undefined. Many atypical antipsychotic and antidepressant agents are known to cause mild hypotension via alpha-1 adrenergic blockade. Intravenous fluids and vasopressors alone are generally effective for single-substance ingestions. In the setting of polysubstance intoxication, synergism leading to bradycardia and refractory vasoplegia refractory to conventional therapies may result, prompting consideration for extracorporeal support.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 71-year-old woman presented to the emergency department (ED) after being found obtunded near bottles of quetiapine, olanzapine, trazodone, mirtazapine, levomilnacipran, eszopiclone, and clonazepam. She underwent prehospital intubation and received push-dose epinephrine for hypotension. In the ED, the patient remained hypotensive with a relative bradycardia, requiring escalating doses of norepinephrine, vasopressin, epinephrine, angiotensin II, and methylene blue infusions. Her extremities remained warm, and point-of-care echocardiography revealed hyperdynamic function, consistent with vasoplegic shock. She subsequently underwent VA-ECMO cannulation, which was followed by a rapid decrease in vasopressor requirements and decannulation on hospital day 3. The patient recovered and was transferred to inpatient psychiatry neurologically intact. Urine mass-spectrometry revealed large peaks for quetiapine, olanzapine, milnacipran, mirtazapine, trazodone, and zopiclone.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: While overdose data are limited, levomilnacipran may precipitate or potentiate relative bradycardia with hypotension and a preserved ejection fraction. Significant ingestions and synergism with other agents causing peripheral alpha-1 antagonism may lead to hemodynamic instability refractory to conventional therapies. Extracorporeal life support may aid in recovery.

articles.title: Atypical Presentation of Extensive Stanford Type A Aortic Dissection Initially Misattributed to Aspiration Pneumonia: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Acute aortic dissection is a life-threatening emergency that may present with nonspecific symptoms, particularly in older adults, leading clinicians to anchor on more common diagnoses.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: An 85-year-old man presented with four days of cough, weakness, and constipation after a recent emergency department (ED) visit due to food impaction after he choked on a carrot. A chest radiograph obtained the day before admission showed left basal consolidation, prompting referral for suspected aspiration pneumonia. In the ED, he appeared comfortable with no complaints of chest pain. Physical examination noted mild tachycardia and wheezes bilaterally and treatment was initiated with antibiotics and bronchodilators. A low-voltage electrocardiogram led to immediate point-of-care echocardiography, which demonstrated a large circumferential pericardial effusion, a markedly dilated aortic root, and right ventricular collapse. Computed tomography angiography confirmed an extensive Stanford Type A aortic dissection.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights how deceptively calm presentations can mask catastrophic disease and why clinicians must be ready to abandon their first diagnosis when the data demands it.

articles.title: Locked-In Syndrome from Delayed Vertebral Artery Dissection After Strangulation: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Vertebral artery dissection is a rare but life-threatening complication of strangulation. Symptoms are often nonspecific and may not manifest immediately, complicating diagnosis. If prior neck trauma is not elicited during assessment, clinicians may miss a mechanistic link to prompt vascular imaging, leaving patients at risk for irreversible outcomes, as illustrated in this case.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 24-year-old woman presented to a critical access emergency department (ED) with nonspecific neurological symptoms that had largely resolved upon arrival. Her only reported history was vague head and neck pain, which she attributed to stress after leaving an abusive relationship several weeks earlier. Hours later, while still in the ED, the patient experienced abrupt neurological deterioration. She was transferred to a regional medical center, where magnetic resonance imaging eventually revealed vertebral artery dissection with basilar artery hypoperfusion and extensive pontine infarction. Collateral history obtained from family revealed a preceding strangulation event. Police at the scene had documented neck injury, but the patient declined their offer of a medical assessment. By the time vertebral artery dissection was diagnosed, she had developed irreversible neurological damage leading to locked-in syndrome. She survived in this state for years before succumbing to complications of quadriplegia. The death was certified as a homicide due to inflicted blunt force neck injury.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case underscores the importance of timely, skilled medical assessment after strangulation and highlights the need for targeted screening of patients with vague neurological symptoms or disclosure of intimate partner violence.

articles.title: Status Epilepticus in a Patient Prescribed Theophylline: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Seizures are a frequent reason for emergency department (ED) evaluation, and new-onset events carry a wide differential in which medication toxicity can be overlooked. Toxicity from seldomly prescribed drugs, such as theophylline, can be particularly challenging to recognize because they can cause nonspecific adverse effects, including palpitations, nausea, vomiting, and seizures. Although theophylline use was widespread in the 1980s, current prescribing patterns are unknown. Nevertheless, theophylline toxicity continues to result in ED visits and poison center calls. Because adverse effects may be acute or chronic, identifying theophylline toxicity remains difficult.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 74-year-old woman presented to the ED with status epilepticus. After thorough history and extensive medical work-up, medication toxicity was suspected as the cause of her seizures. Upon further investigation, the patient was found to have theophylline toxicity. Prompt treatment was initiated resulting in cessation of seizures, highlighting the importance of considering medication toxicity in geriatric patients with new-onset seizures.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Theophylline toxicity can present with vague, multisystem symptoms, with status epilepticus being one of its most severe complications. Rapid identification of the underlying toxic etiology is essential to guide treatment and stop the seizures. Moreover, clinical suspicion should be elevated in the geriatric population related to frequent polypharmacy. In this case, confirming the medication history with a family member raised concerns for medication misuse, enabling timely intervention. Although rarely prescribed, physicians should counsel patients on the risks and adverse effects of theophylline and emphasize close monitoring.

articles.title: Subarachnoid Pneumocephalus Following Endoscopic Transsphenoidal Surgery.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: CASE PRESENTATION
abstract.text: A 26-year-old man with past medical history of prolactinoma presented two weeks status post endoscopic transsphenoid prolactinoma excision with a positional headache and cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea; he was found to have diffuse subarachnoid air.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: There are few reports of subarachnoid pneumocephalus in the emergency medicine literature. Pneumocephalus, particularly tension pneumocephalus, typically occurs in the setting of traumatic skull fractures. However, emergency physicians should be aware of subarachnoid pneumocephalus in the setting of endoscopic skull base surgeries.

articles.title: Partial Segmental Thrombosis of the Corpus Cavernosum Following Valsalva Maneuver: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavernosum is a rare vascular condition that may present with nonspecific groin or pelvic pain and mimic more common surgical or urologic emergencies.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 33-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute left-sided groin and pelvic pain after straining during defecation. Initial history and evaluation raised concern for incarcerated inguinal hernia, epididymo-orchitis, renal colic, lymphadenopathy, and soft tissue infection. Computed tomography demonstrated asymmetric enlargement of the left corpus cavernosum, while penile ultrasound showed diminished cavernosal flow. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed segmental thrombosis of the left corpus cavernosum. The patient was treated conservatively with rivaroxaban and analgesia, resulting in symptomatic improvement.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavernosum should be considered in patients presenting with unexplained groin or perineal pain when standard abdominal, penile, testicular, and hernia evaluations are unrevealing. Magnetic resonance imaging may be necessary for definitive diagnosis, and conservative management is frequently successful.

articles.title: Retrocaval Ureter Diagnosed Following Point-of-Care Ultrasound Detection of Hydronephrosis: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Retrocaval ureter (RCU) is a rare congenital anomaly resulting from abnormal development of the inferior vena cava, leading to ureteral obstruction and hydronephrosis. Patients often present with nonspecific symptoms, making diagnosis challenging. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is frequently used in the emergency department (ED) to evaluate abdominal pain and may identify clinically important abnormalities requiring further investigation.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 30-year-old woman presented to the ED with a two-day history of nonspecific abdominal pain. Physical examination was notable only for mild epigastric tenderness. Abdominal POCUS performed by the emergency physician demonstrated moderate right-sided hydronephrosis. The patient had no urinary symptoms and normal renal function. Follow-up renal ultrasound confirmed hydronephrosis and proximal hydroureter without nephrolithiasis. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography subsequently revealed a RCU with the characteristic fish-hook configuration. Renography demonstrated preserved renal function with delayed drainage secondary to ureteral obstruction. The patient underwent surgical correction with ureteral reconstruction and stent placement.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the value of POCUS in the evaluation of patients with nonspecific abdominal pain. Detection of hydronephrosis prompted further diagnostic evaluation and led to the diagnosis of a rare congenital urologic anomaly requiring surgical intervention. Emergency physicians should consider further investigation when hydronephrosis is identified on POCUS, even in the absence of urinary symptoms.

articles.title: Cauda Equina Syndrome Secondary to Seizure-Induced Spinal Fracture During Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy carries a risk of central nervous system oxygen toxicity, which can result in seizures. Seizure-induced spinal fractures are uncommon complications that occur during generalized convulsive activity. While often benign, lumbar vertebral body burst fractures may result in cauda equina syndrome. Additionally, patients with beta-thalassemia may have decreased bone mineral density due to ineffective erythropoiesis and bone marrow expansion increasing the risk for pathologic and traumatic fractures.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: A 35-year-old man with beta-thalassemia major presented to the emergency department after a witnessed, first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure during hyperbaric oxygen therapy for chronic venous ulcers. Initial evaluation revealed severe low back pain and midline lumbar tenderness. Computed tomography revealed an acute third lumbar vertebra (L3) burst fracture with retropulsion. The patient rapidly developed progressive right lower-extremity weakness and acute urinary retention. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed 70% loss of height of L3, severe thecal sac stenosis at L2-L3 and L3-L4, and a ventral dural hematoma resulting in stenosis at L4-L5. The patient was diagnosed with cauda equina syndrome and underwent emergent neurosurgical decompression.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This case represents a rare convergence of multiple complications: central nervous system oxygen toxicity during hyperbaric oxygen therapy, seizure-induced lumbar burst fracture with retropulsion, and traumatic cauda equina syndrome in a patient with beta thalassemia. Physicians must maintain a high index of suspicion for vertebral fractures and monitor for evolving neurological deficits when managing the patient with acute back pain following seizure activity.

articles.title: Initial management of mild traumatic brain injury in emergency departments and walk-in clinics in Argentina. Proposal by the Emergency Council of the Argentine Medical Society (SAM) and the Argentine Scientific Society of Emergency Medicine (SCEA).
authors: Sociedad Científica de Emergentología de Argentina

abstract.text: Mild traumatic brain injury (MTBI) has traditionally been defined by a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score between 13 and 15 points. It accounts for 80-90% of head injuries treated in emergency departments. While most patients have a favorable outcome, up to 16% have intracranial injuries, although less than 1% will require critical interventions, justifying systematized diagnostic strategies. The overuse of computed tomography (CT) scans leads to unnecessary exposure to ionizing radiation, avoidable costs, and overcrowding in emergency departments. Clinical decision rules standardize the use of neuroimaging with high sensitivity for relevant lesions; however, their limited specificity and low adherence limit their impact on daily practice. Serum biomarkers have demonstrated sensitivity of 96-100% and negative predictive values of 95-100% for ruling out intracranial lesions within 12 hours after trauma, thereby reducing the number of unnecessary CT scans. This review proposes an update focused on a stepwise diagnostic model that integrates structured clinical assessment, warning signs, decision rules, and biomarkers, adapted to different levels of complexity, including centers without access to CT scans-a common reality in our setting. New paradigms in follow-up after mild traumatic brain injury (MTBI) are also analyzed: early identification of persistent symptoms, patient education, and telemedicine.

articles.title: Bilateral renal infarction unmasking rheumatic mitral valve disease with left atrial appendage thrombus in sinus rhythm: a case report.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Acute renal infarction mimics pyelonephritis and is frequently missed at first presentation. Rheumatic mitral stenosis can cause systemic embolism even in sinus rhythm.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 47-year-old Thai man presented with four days of evolving abdominal pain, previously attributed to gastroenteritis and treated symptomatically at a first emergency visit. He had fever without chills, left costovertebral-angle tenderness, and a bland urinalysis. Point-of-care ultrasound was atypical for pyelonephritis; computed tomography showed bilateral wedge-shaped cortical defects with a cortical rim sign but could not exclude focal bacterial nephritis. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrated an avascular left upper pole, confirming bland infarction, supported by lactate dehydrogenase 1194 U/L, procalcitonin 0.28 ng/mL, and sterile cultures. Echocardiography revealed rheumatic mitral valve disease with clinically significant stenosis (valve area 1.34 cm2 by planimetry; diastolic doming, commissural fusion, fish-mouth orifice) and moderate regurgitation. The left atrium was dilated, with dense spontaneous echo contrast and a left atrial appendage thrombus despite sinus rhythm. Enoxaparin with overlapping warfarin was started; a direct oral anticoagulant was avoided. At 2 months the patient was in New York Heart Association class II without recurrent embolism, but the international normalized ratio had not yet reached target; repeat transoesophageal echocardiography is scheduled at 3 months.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound can resolve the computed tomography ambiguity between infarction and focal bacterial nephritis at the bedside. In mitral stenosis, a prior embolic event or left atrial thrombus mandates vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation irrespective of rhythm, and an appendage thrombus and coexisting mitral regurgitation defer balloon commissurotomy.

articles.title: On-Scene Time-Dependent Probabilities of Return of Spontaneous Circulation and Favorable Neurological Outcome in Cases of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with an Initial Shockable Rhythm: A Retrospective Study Using the National Utstein Data in Japan.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with an initial shockable rhythm, the likelihood of achieving on-scene return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and favorable neurological outcomes changes with elapsed resuscitation time. We aimed to describe these time-dependent patterns under existing Japanese emergency medical services (EMS) practice. Methods: We conducted a nationwide retrospective descriptive cohort study using linked Japanese Utstein and emergency transport data from 2017-2022. Adults with cardiogenic OHCA and an initial shockable rhythm were included. For each time point after EMS contact, we calculated the observed probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC and, among patients achieving on-scene ROSC, the probability of a favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2 at 1 month) according to ROSC timing. Results: Among 22,383 eligible patients, 5095 achieved on-scene ROSC and 3182 had favorable neurological outcomes. The probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC was 6.97% (1295/18,583; 95% CI, 6.61-7.34%) at 10 min and 0.50% (87/17,375; 95% CI, 0.41-0.62%) at 20 min. At 10 min, favorable neurological outcomes occurred in 50.0% of patients aged <75 years and 20.5% of those aged ≥75 years who achieved on-scene ROSC at or after that time point. A sensitivity analysis restricted to 3128 patients receiving first EMS defibrillation within 1 min showed broadly similar temporal patterns. Conclusions: Under existing Japanese EMS practice, subsequent on-scene ROSC and favorable neurological outcomes became less frequent with later ROSC timing. Younger patients showed more favorable neurological outcomes at later ROSC times, but these findings do not establish age-based criteria for prolonged resuscitation or transport decisions.

articles.title: Vegetarian dietary patterns are not associated with lower odds of noncommunicable diseases among patients presenting to a tertiary care center in North India: a cross-sectional survey.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) present a huge global burden, accounting for approximately 7.3 trillion cases and 43.8 million deaths in 2021. In India, 68% of all deaths are caused by NCDs. Carbohydrate intake has been associated with NCD development. Standard Indian diets mainly comprise carbohydrates. In this study, we aimed to analyze the association of vegetarian versus omnivorous diets with the odds of developing NCDs in patients visiting the emergency department.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Over 18 months, a cross-sectional epidemiological survey-based study was conducted among patients aged >18 years presenting to our department with documented comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus [DM], hypertension, heart disease, hypothyroidism, Alzheimer disease, and cancer). These patients completed a 32-item questionnaire survey regarding dietary and lifestyle choices. Associations between comorbidity status and dietary variables were evaluated by bivariate analysis. Additionally, unadjusted odds ratio (OR) and adjusted OR for DM, hypertension, and heart disease were calculated.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: This study included 11,011 patients, of which 55.31% were males and 68.91% were >55 years old. Furthermore, 65.87% were vegetarians, whereas 28.97% were omnivores. Hypertension, DM, and heart disease were found in 62.6%, 49.9% and 26.0%, respectively, while 58% had combinations of NCDs. Adjusted for age, sex, smoking, sugar, alcohol, exercise, and packaged food, OR (omnivore vs. vegetarian) was 0.94 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.86-1.03; P=0.180), 0.91 (95% CI, 0.83-1.00; P=0.052) and 1.02 (95% CI, 0.92-1.13; P=0.690) for DM, hypertension, and heart disease, respectively.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Most patients with NCDs followed a vegetarian dietary pattern, which was not associated with lower odds of developing NCDs.

articles.title: Priapism Got You Down? A Novel Method to Build Your Own Moderate Fidelity Task Trainer.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: This task trainer was designed to instruct emergency medicine (EM) residents and faculty at all levels of training.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Priapism management is time-sensitive, and the clinical opportunities to perform dorsal penile nerve block and corporal aspiration are seldom practiced. Despite knowledge of the importance of prompt recognition and management of priapism, many emergency physicians may not actually perform the recommended procedures to manage it for a variety of reasons.1 Due to the sensitive nature of the condition, physicians are eager to learn about and practice these intimate maneuvers in the safe setting of simulation; however, there is not a commercial task trainer available.2 Some low-fidelity creations have been published as solutions, but they are less realistic and time consuming to make, limiting feasibility and usability.3-7 One published creation inspired this task trainer, but the main structure is no longer available to be purchased, underscoring the need for a model that can be reproduced and recreated by the educator with flexible starting materials.3 Others are more time-consuming to make and require specific simulation equipment4 or may not be easily reused.5, 6 Other published low-fidelity creations are less anatomically accurate, limiting the fidelity of practice regarding the most intimate aspects of the procedure.7, 8.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of this educational session, participants should be able to: 1) identify indications, contraindications, and potential complications of priapism management, 2) gather appropriate supplies and describe relevant landmarks, anatomy, and patient positioning for management of priapism, 3) demonstrate a dorsal penile nerve block, aspiration of corpus cavernosum, and intracavernosal phenylephrine administration to treat priapism, and 4) develop an approach to manage common pitfalls of priapism care.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: We developed a more realistic and replicable priapism task trainer using materials readily accessible in a simulation lab. Emergency medicine faculty and simulation center staff collaborated to create a task trainer constructed from silicone and internal tubing, using the mold of a phallic-shaped candle (see attachment). This model was then used in a 30-minute training session, which included ten minutes of interactive discussion reviewing the steps of dorsal penile block and priapism management with PowerPoint images as a visual aid. Next, learners performed the procedure from start to finish with faculty guidance, followed by an opportunity to ask questions. The training session was open to EM residents, pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) fellows, EM community physicians, and EM academic faculty.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: This study was approved as exempt status by the Indiana University Institutional Review Board. Following the educational session, participants completed a voluntary survey evaluating the task trainer's realism, its usefulness as a teaching tool, and their change in confidence in performing priapism management.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The mixed group included 14 EM residents, five PEM fellows, four EM community physicians, and four EM academic physicians. Of 27 participants who used the task trainer, the majority (92.6%) of survey respondents agreed or strongly agreed that the task trainer was realistic. Learners reported increased confidence in knowledge of the procedural steps and increased confidence in potentially performing the procedure in the clinical setting (Table 1). Most participants would recommend the training to a provider of a similar level of training.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Overall, the educational content was effective since learners reported an increase in knowledge of the steps of the procedure in addition to improved confidence to perform the procedure safely and successfully in the clinical environment. While many learners had never performed this procedure before in the clinical setting, the majority would recommend this training to a colleague of the same level of training. While the need for training in this procedure is clear,1-2 the options for available task trainers have remained limited. There is no commercial priapism task trainer, and published creations have varied strengths and weaknesses in balancing fidelity, cost-effectiveness, reproducibility, and reusability.3-7 The main takeaway from this training is that a realistic, durable, and low-cost task trainer can be developed to effectively teach how to treat a rare and sensitive procedure.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Priapism, penile nerve block, dorsal nerve block, urology, aspiration, decompression.

articles.title: All In: A Casino-Themed Emergency Medicine Conference Day.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: The target audience includes individuals involved in the education and training of emergency medicine (EM) residents, such as program directors, assistant program directors, core faculty, and academic attendings, as well as learners including residents, physician assistant (PA) fellows, and medical students (MS).

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Gamification has increasingly been incorporated into emergency medicine (EM) residency education to enhance learner engagement, motivation, and active participation. Prior studies have demonstrated benefits of game-based learning across multiple areas of medical education, including improved knowledge retention, teamwork, communication, and learner satisfaction.1-4 However, most gamification interventions in EM involve isolated activities rather than comprehensive, multi-station conference curricula. To address this gap, we developed a casino-themed, multi-station educational conference designed to reinforce core EM knowledge, procedural skills, and clinical reasoning through competitive, team-based learning. The intervention incorporated simulation, rapid-response scenarios, board-style trivia, and wagering poker chips during a protected half-day residency conference.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of this educational intervention, participants will be able to: 1) demonstrate airway management skills through simulation, including equipment setup and timely interventions for both adult and pediatric cases, 2) interpret various electrocardiograms (EKGs) in high-pressure scenarios, 3) analyze cases and apply evidence-based management in various rapid-response scenarios, 4) demonstrate rapid recall of EM knowledge by answering board-style trivia questions, and 5) demonstrate increased confidence in team-based decision-making, effective communication under pressure, and leadership in high-stress emergency situations.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective educational innovation was delivered as a single, four-hour casino-themed EM conference session featuring interactive stations modeled after casino games and held during the residency program's weekly Wednesday educational conference. The session featured interactive, competition-based stations designed to replicate high-pressure ED scenarios. Learners rotated through four game-based stations: "Play Your Cards Right" for rapid-recall trivia using EM board-style questions, "Diagnostic Craps" for EKG interpretation and management, "High Stakes Airways" for hands-on airway management using mannequins and rapid sequence intubation scenarios, and "Rapid Response Roulette" for discussion of ED cases focusing on team dynamics, leadership, resuscitation, and escalation of care. The games were designed to reflect real-world ED challenges, with content and expectations tailored to postgraduate years (PGY) levels. Participants wagered poker chips based on confidence in their responses, reinforcing self-assessment and accountability. This method encouraged active participation, peer-to-peer learning, and application of clinical reasoning in high-pressure scenarios.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: The casino-style conference featured six tables each with an EM attending facilitator. Participants included EM residents, physician assistant (PA) fellows, and medical students. Learners started with 15 poker chips and engaged in four game-based sessions over four hours. The games "Play Your Cards Right," "High Stakes Airways," "Diagnostic Craps," and "Rapid Response Roulette" incorporated either case-based simulation, procedural skill stations, rapid decision-making, EKG interpretation, and/or evidence-based medicine (EBM) trivia. Learners wagered chips based on confidence, with gains/losses tied to performance. Faculty provided real-time feedback and facilitated discussions. Pre- and post-conference surveys (Appendix A) assessed educational value, skill improvement, confidence, and clinical applicability. Instructors also evaluated feasibility and effectiveness. The study was Institutional Review Board exempt.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of the 33 learners who attended the conference, 32 completed surveys (97% response rate) including 26 EM residents (10 PGY-1, 8 PGY-2 and 8 PGY-3), 4 medical students, and 2 physician assistants. One hundred percent of participants answered "yes" when asked if they would recommend this type of conference to peers and 100% preferred this learning style to traditional didactics. Eighty-eight percent of the respondents reported they are "very likely" to incorporate skills learned from this activity into future practice.Facilitators rated the game-based learning activities as highly effective teaching tools, with 92% rating 4 or 5 (on a 5-point scale). Facilitators were also asked if they found the games easy to implement, and 83% answered rating a 4 or a 5 (on a 5-point scale). Responses derived from the open-ended questions emphasize the conference's effectiveness in engaging participants, providing meaningful learning experiences and fostering a positive and well-organized environment.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This casino-style, game-based learning conference was highly rated for both educational value and engagement. Participants reported increased confidence in managing emergency scenarios, particularly in EKG interpretation and team-based critical decision-making. The format was viewed as feasible and effective, with most participants preferring game-based learning over traditional didactics, supporting its continued use in EM education.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Gamification, EM education, simulation, active learning, residency training.

articles.title: Point-of-Care Ultrasound Findings of Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome: A Case Report.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of assisted reproductive technology (ART). Prompt recognition and management are essential to reduce morbidity.1 This case describes a 30-year-old woman undergoing ART who presented to the emergency department (ED) with abdominal pain, distention, lightheadedness, nausea, vomiting, and shortness of breath following transvaginal oocyte retrieval. Physical examination revealed a tense, diffusely tender abdomen, and point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) demonstrated enlarged ovaries bilaterally with multiple follicles and moderate peritoneal free fluid, confirming the diagnosis of OHSS. Laboratory findings included leukocytosis, hemoconcentration, and hypoproteinemia.
