The patient received supportive care with intravenous fluids and analgesia and, during admission, underwent therapeutic paracentesis, resulting in the removal of roughly three liters of ascitic fluid. Her symptoms resolved, and she was discharged on hospital day three with complete recovery noted at follow-up. This case highlights the diagnostic value of POCUS in the emergency setting for early identification of OHSS. As the use of ART increases, emergency clinicians should be aware of OHSS presentations and consider bedside ultrasound as a key diagnostic tool to expedite care and improve outcomes.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Assisted reproductive technology, point of care ultrasound, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

articles.title: Cadaveric Model of Pneumothorax (the GASP model): A Realistic, Reusable and Cost-Effective Simulator for Chest Drainage Training.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: The gastrostomy-assisted simulated pneumothorax (GASP) model is designed to train residents in emergency medicine, anesthesiology, pulmonology, cardiothoracic surgery, and paediatric surgery in the various techniques used to perform chest drainage (CD).

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency, particularly in the case of a tension pneumothorax. Failure to perform timely CD can rapidly result in cardiorespiratory arrest.1 Needle decompression, chest tube insertion, and finger thoracostomy are the three main CD procedures that healthcare professionals must master. However, these are technically challenging procedures with potentially severe and sometimes fatal complications. The literature reports significant complication rates (19%) and failure rates (18-21%).2,3Synthetic simulators for CD are commonly used in simulation centres due to their availability. While they are useful in the early stages of training to teach the fundamental steps of the procedure, they lack realism, are expensive, and do not provide the tactile feedback essential for safe and effective performance. The GASP model was developed to provide a realistic, easily reproducible, and accessible pneumothorax simulation tool aimed at improving CD training for medical trainees.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of this educational session using the GASP model, learners should be able to: 1) identify the two main thoracic anatomical landmarks commonly used in clinical practice for CD: the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line, and the fifth intercostal space at the midaxillary line, 2) become familiar with the tactile sensation of palpating the superior border of the rib, a key landmark for directing the chest tube safely and with the correct angulation, 3) mastering the three main techniques of CD: needle decompression, chest tube insertion, and finger thoracostomy, and 4) demonstrate proficiency while performing the procedure within a complex simulation scenario.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: The GASP model utilises fresh cadavers prepared with an insufflation device and a gastrostomy button to simulate pneumothorax or haemopneumothorax. Manual or automated ventilation may be added to enhance realism. This model can be used to teach residents how to perform the three main CD procedures effectively and safely. Each learner can perform multiple repetitions on each cadaver.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: At the Institute of Anatomy and Surgical Simulation (IASC) in Toulouse, France, 10 fresh cadavers preserved by refrigeration were used for this study. Each donor had provided informed and written consent during their lifetime for the use of their body in experimental research. Demographic data related to the cadavers, such as age, sex, and body mass index, were collected.The GASP model was tested on 20 hemithoraces from the 10 cadavers. The presence and quality of the pneumothorax were assessed via ultrasound by an experienced radiologist. The two main CD approaches commonly used in clinical practice (axillary and anterior) were tested, along with several CD techniques: needle decompression, direct insertion using a Pleurocath® drain and Monod trocar, the Seldinger technique with a Fuhrman-Cook drain, and finger thoracostomy.The GASP model was subsequently introduced to first-year residents in anesthesiology, emergency medicine, and pulmonology. Participants used Likert scales to evaluate the model's realism, its transferability to clinical practice, and its overall educational value. Additionally, the study assessed learners' perceived self-efficacy and the level of discomfort associated with performing simulations on cadaveric specimens.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In all 20 hemithoraces (10 right and 10 left), a large pneumothorax was confirmed by ultrasound. All major CD techniques were successfully performed, using a variety of drainage devices appropriate to different clinical scenarios. The model provided a realistic simulation of the procedure, offering the same tactile sensation as on a live patient. It enabled repeated CD in each hemithorax (exceeding 40 procedures per side) without compromising the structural integrity of the model.Eight first-year residents (from anesthesiology, emergency medicine, and pulmonology) were enrolled in the first CD course on cadaver-based training at our faculty, using the GASP model. Pre- and post-training assessments based on 10-point questionnaires demonstrated significant improvements in baseline confidence in technical skills, stress management, and overall performance. The GASP model was also evaluated by participants using a 5-point Likert scale, revealing high levels of realism, strong transferability to patient care, and increased perceived self-efficacy among learners. Finally, the cadaveric model was associated with minimal discomfort for participants.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The GASP model is realistic, easy to implement, reproducible, low-cost, and reusable multiple times. It serves as a valuable tool for enhancing skill acquisition among a wide range of healthcare professionals who need to master this procedure, providing a level of tactile realism that is often lacking in synthetic models. Its successful integration within our medical simulation centre supports the development of additional cadaveric simulation models for other emergency procedures.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Pneumothorax, chest drainage, emergency medicine, simulation, anatomy.

articles.title: Physical Wellbeing Scavenger Hunt.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: This small group session is appropriate for any level of medical student, emergency medicine resident physicians, and faculty.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Burnout is a major issue in medicine, with over half of physicians experiencing burnout at some point in their career.1 Physicians who regularly participate in self-care activities, such as regularly exercising, having a well-balanced diet, and appropriate amount of sleep, experience less burnout.2,3,4 As a resident, it is difficult to find time to practice self-care.2 This session sought to combine education on how to implement appropriate self-care as a trainee and how to carry that forward after training in a way that was fun, provided a period of physical exercise, and provided time outdoors for those participating.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of this session, the learner will be able to: 1) implement basic ways to improve sleep quality, 2) avoid common pitfalls in diet and nutrition, 3) incorporate more physical activity into their lives.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: Learners were divided into teams of three to four. A scavenger hunt was created using Google Forms and QR codes. The initial QR code was displayed in the lecture hall at the start of the session. Fifteen other QR codes were either physically distributed throughout the Emergency Medicine Offices and the Emergency Department or provided to participants via text message when they completed certain tasks. Each QR code led to a different Google Form with a question about physical wellbeing. Participants were allowed to use any resource they had with them, including their mobile devices. After the question was answered correctly, an explanation was provided in the Google Form. A riddle was also provided to help locate the next QR code. An incorrect answer required the participants to try to answer the question again. Participants were not given any hints after answering incorrectly. There were no formal penalties for incorrect answers. However, incorrect answers increased the time it took to complete the task. At the end of the session, each question was debriefed by the instructor.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: Participants completed a five-question pre-survey to rate their level of physical wellbeing using a 1-5 Likert Scale. Participants also completed a 10-question post survey that asked them the same initial 5 questions to rate their physical wellbeing on the same scale as the pretest, as well as additional questions asking how likely they were to change their physical habits based on the session and how much they enjoyed the session on a different 1-5 Likert Scale. They were also asked to provide recommendations for future changes. Pre- and post-test Likert scores were compared using the Mann-Whitney U Test.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twelve participants, all resident physicians, took part in the exercise. Twelve completed the pre-survey, and ten completed the post-survey. There was no difference in physical wellbeing score (median 3 before vs median 2.5 after, P=0.62). All participants except one were at least moderately likely (3 or above on a 1-5 Likert scale) to change their sleep habits based on the exercise. All were at least moderately likely (3 or above on a 1-5 Likert scale) to change their eating and exercise habits based on the activity. All respondents found the activity to be at least moderately enjoyable (3 or above), with 8 of 10 finding it extremely enjoyable (5).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This wellbeing scavenger hunt effectively taught learners how to incorporate simple changes into their lives to improve the self-care habits. This model could be applied to other educational topics to incorporate a component of physical wellbeing and exercise and has been used during new resident orientation and wilderness education within our department.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Wellbeing, physical wellbeing, exercise, nutrition, sleep habits, self-care.

articles.title: Physical Frailty and End-of-Life Care Small Groups.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: This module was developed for emergency medicine (EM) residents, though may also be used for medical students on an emergency medicine clerkship or attending physicians.

abstract.label: LENGTH OF CURRICULUM
abstract.text: This frailty and end-of-life care module consists of two 60-minute small group sessions.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency medicine physicians often care for patients with significant comorbidities, physical frailty, and acute and chronic life-limiting conditions, including those at end-of-life. Over 60% of emergency department (ED) patients older than 65 years old meet established criteria for physical frailty, and at least half of older adults present to the ED in their final month of life.1,2 Therefore, it is critical that EM physicians understand end-of-life trajectories and adopt a thoughtful approach to end-of-life communication, clinical decision-making and symptom management to support both patients and their caregivers.3 To address this need, we developed a flipped-classroom case-based small group discussion session for emergency medicine learners that augments self-learning, followed by a small group discussion with peers.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: At the end of this module, learners should be able to: 1) recognize and classify end-of- life trajectories, 2) define physical frailty, including risk factors, prevalence and prognosis in ED patients, 3) develop a differential diagnosis and diagnostic and treatment plan for a patient with metastatic cancer presenting with fatigue, constipation, labile mood, and diffuse osseous pain, 4) review Medicare Hospice Benefit eligibility, 5) understand the differential diagnosis and medical management of chemotherapy-related nausea, 6) discuss the assessment and management of dyspnea in end-of-life patients, and 7) review how to estimate and communicate prognosis using practical timeframes.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: This exercise consists of two 60-minute small group sessions (two clinical cases per session) using a "flipped classroom" design.4-20 The facilitator should distribute the learner responsible content one week in advance. Learners are instructed to complete the assigned readings and review four cases to prepare for an in-person discussion guided by the facilitator. Questions are included to guide their learning and structure the subsequent discussion. The facilitator uses the Physical Frailty and End-of-Life Care Preceptor Notes, which is organized around the handout questions, to stimulate discussion and answer questions.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: Learners evaluated the content using end-of-session anonymous feedback forms. Faculty small-group facilitators assessed learner participation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We received open-ended responses from 11 learners. All felt the workload to prepare for the small-group session was reasonable and beneficial to their residency education. Some respondents requested additional sessions to discuss personal and/or difficult patient care experiences based on this "bite-sized" introduction to frailty and end-of-life care.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Overall, this split two-hour flipped classroom educational activity was an effective method to introduce the concept of frailty and end-of-life care to emergency medicine residents. Following the initial session, the authors added an additional case to expand the curriculum into two sessions to allow more time for free-form discussion.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Emergency medicine, flipped classroom, medical education, teaching, end-of-life, frailty, hospice, palliative care, terminal dyspnea, malignant hypercalcemia, chemotherapy-induced nausea.

articles.title: Meeting the Milestones through Simulation: Disclosing a Medical Error.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: This simulation is intended for medical students, interns, junior residents, and senior residents.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Patient safety event reporting and disclosure of medical errors to patients and families are critical components of high-quality, transparent care and a necessary skill for emergency medicine (EM) physicians. Accurate reporting of errors, near misses, and unsafe conditions provides institutions with the data needed to investigate vulnerabilities, implement system-based solutions, and prevent recurrence. Disclosure of medical errors fosters trust, supports just culture principles, and reinforces professional accountability.1 Physicians have historically reported few adverse events, accounting for only 1-2% of all reports.2 To address this gap, the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) now emphasizes patient safety and quality improvement as a part of resident education.The ACGME Emergency Medicine Milestones have established clear expectations for resident education in patient safety.3 Residents, fellows, and faculty must know their responsibilities for event reporting. The milestones include ability to identify patient safety events, understand the system factors that lead to events, and how to complete institutional safety event reports.3 ACGME requires residents to participate in real or simulated interprofessional patient safety events and quality improvement activities as part of systems-based practice milestones.3 These requirements underscore the importance of experiential learning, feedback, and practice in order to achieve true competence in identifying causes and enacting sustainable safety interventions.Medication errors, particularly dosing errors, are among the most common patient safety threats in the emergency department (ED).4 The ED environment-with high patient volumes, time-sensitive decision-making, and frequent weight-based dosing-places EM physicians at especially high risk for ordering or administering incorrect doses. In this simulation, the wrong concentration of a sedation medication is administered and creates a scenario in which the learner must recognize the error, disclose it to the patient/family, and complete a patient safety report (PSR). This approach integrates clinical management with communication and systems-based practice and provides an avenue for residency programs to facilitate ACGME requirements while preparing residents for real-world patient safety responsibilities in scenarios that otherwise may not yet be encountered during the period of residency.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of this simulation activity, learners will be able to: 1) disclose a medical error to a patient and/or their family, 2) understand the different types of patient safety events that should be reported, 3) locate the form for disclosing a patient safety event at their institution, and 4) appropriately complete a patient safety report at their institution.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: The simulation was conducted with a high-fidelity pediatric mannikin. A total of 19 residents and three medical students participated in the simulation during their monthly didactic session. Afterwards, they were guided through completing a patient safety report for their institution.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: Learners completed a survey before and after the simulation case assessing their comfort with disclosing medical errors and completing an institutional patient safety report form. The survey questions were formatted in a Likert scale where 1 = strongly disagree, 2 = disagree, 3 = neither agree nor disagree, 4 = agree, 5 = strongly agree. Results collected were analyzed using Wilcox rank-sum test.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The participants completed a survey before and after the experience, and there was a statistically significant improvement in the learners' comfort level after completing the simulation. The free text responses were also universally positive.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Overall, the learners received the simulation well. General feedback was positive; the consensus was that there was increased confidence in patient safety reporting.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Patient safety, medical error, disclosing error.

articles.title: Acute Neurologic Decline in the ED: A Case Report on Recognizing ARIA in the Age of Anti-Amyloid Therapy.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Anti-amyloid beta (Aβ) immunotherapies are an emerging treatment for Alzheimer's disease (AD) with a rare but significant risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA). This visual case report describes a patient with lecanemab-induced ARIA to familiarize emergency providers with this critical adverse effect of novel anti-amyloid therapies. An 85-year-old female receiving lecanemab infusions presented to the emergency department (ED) with abruptly worsening confusion, an unsteady gait, and new left-sided deficits, including homonymous hemianopia and hemineglect. A non-contrast head computed tomography (CT) revealed extensive right parieto-occipital vasogenic edema, prompting magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which confirmed extensive ARIA with edema (ARIA-E) on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences and microhemorrhages (ARIA-H) on T2-weighted sequences. Lecanemab was discontinued, and the patient experienced partial neurologic recovery after a four-day admission. However, she was discharged with persistent functional limitations, including an inability to drive and a need for caregiver assistance. This case underscores the need for emergency physicians to maintain a high index of suspicion for ARIA in patients on anti-Aβ immunotherapies who present with new neurologic symptoms. Definitive diagnosis requires MRI, and management warrants prompt neurologic consultation.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Alzheimer's, dementia, neurology, medication adverse effects, ARIA.

articles.title: Shockingly Unreliable: A Case Report of Failure of Synchronized Cardioversion Device to Capture, Resulting in Ventricular Fibrillation and Cardiac Arrest.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Synchronized cardioversion is a standard treatment for unstable ventricular tachycardia. While modern defibrillators are designed with safety mechanisms, synchronization failure can result in catastrophic complications. We present the case of a 65-year-old woman with unstable wide-complex tachycardia with a pulse who underwent emergent synchronized cardioversion. Despite activation of the "sync" mode, the device failed to capture appropriately and delivered a shock on the T-wave, precipitating ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. After 26 minutes of resuscitation and multiple defibrillations, return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved. The patient ultimately recovered and was discharged home in stable condition. This case underscores the rare but serious risk of synchronization failure, particularly in obese patients where pad placement and capture may be impaired,1 and emphasizes the importance of visually confirming synchronization prior to shock delivery.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Cardioversion, ventricular fibrillation, defibrillator malfunction, ACLS, emergency medicine.

articles.title: Case Report: Sonographic Detection of Chorionic Hemangiomas in Sturge-Weber Syndrome.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is used frequently in the emergency department (ED) as a non-invasive diagnostic tool. Ocular POCUS is utilized in patients with vision changes to detect pathologies including retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage and central retinal artery occlusion. This case demonstrates the capability of POCUS to detect choroidal hemangiomas, a pathology strongly associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS). A 31-year-old male with no significant medical history presented with two years of progressive vision changes and headaches. A large right-sided facial birthmark was noted, though the patient had no prior diagnosis. Examination revealed right eye blindness and an afferent pupillary defect. Ocular POCUS revealed retinal detachment and choroidal thickening, which were interpreted as choroidal hemangiomas. Findings were corroborated by MRI. Together with input from our ophthalmology and neurology specialists, a diagnosis of SWS was made. This case demonstrates the utility of POCUS in the rapid identification of choroidal hemangiomas in an adult patient, facilitating an expedited diagnosis of SWS. Because there is no cure for SWS, early diagnosis and management by a multidisciplinary team, including ophthalmology and neurology, is essential to limit the progression of the disease and mitigate its effects.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Ocular, hemangiomas, chorion, Sturge-Weber, POCUS.

articles.title: Awaiting Stress: An Interprofessional In-situ Simulation to Optimize Team Management of Cardiac Arrest in an Emergency Department Observation Unit.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: This simulation is intended for interprofessional clinical decision unit (CDU) teams.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) observation units or clinical decision units (CDU) are a common care model found in many hospitals due to their ability to provide high-quality care and reduce length of stay while also minimizing costs.1,2,3 Despite initial clinical stability, deterioration while in the CDU may occur. Due to the unique environment of the CDU, it is essential that the interprofessional team is prepared to manage unstable patients; yet there is minimal literature on how to best train observation unit teams.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of this simulation session, learners will be able to: 1) prioritize and coordinate team-based tasks within the CDU environment upon recognizing patient decompensation and cardiac arrest, 2) optimize clinical decision unit (CDU) team member roles and interprofessional communication, 3) adapt resuscitation principles in the resource-variable setting of a CDU to manage a critically ill patient.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: This is run as an in-situ simulation with an interprofessional team as an experiential learning intervention. The in-situ format enables exploration of the team-specific and unit-specific context during the debrief.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: Participants completed a pre- and post-self-assessment via QR code along with responses to three program evaluation questions.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-five team members participated in six in-situ CDU simulations. On the pre-assessment, participants had a median of 4 (scale of 1- strongly disagree to 5 - strongly agree) across all categories including confidence in their role during a Code Blue, roles of team members, team priorities, trust in team members, equipment location, and comfort in providing hand-off. On the post-assessment, team priorities and trust in team members increased to a median of 5. In the program evaluation, participants found the experience valuable, particularly the debrief.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Team members started the simulation with confidence in cardiac arrest management, but participation increased their understanding of trust in team members and team priorities within the CDU context. This simulation and debrief session could help support team performance during cardiac arrest within the distinct clinical and interprofessional environment of the CDU.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Simulation, Clinical Decision Unit, CDU, short stay unit, interprofessional, cardiac arrest, debriefing.

articles.title: Intentional Pencil Ingestion - A Case Report of a Sharp Ingested Foreign Body.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: UNLABELLED
abstract.text: Treating foreign body ingestion in the emergency department (ED) is common; however, certain ingestions may be immediately life-threatening, depending on the object because sharp objects pose the greatest risk for gastrointestinal injury, including perforation and obstruction.1 This is a case of an adult male who arrived at the ED with suicidal ideation and reported ingesting a pencil two days prior. He presented with abdominal pain and hematochezia. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis identified the pencil in the distal ileum. The patient was admitted for surgical evaluation and monitoring. Remarkably, the pencil was passed spontaneously in the stool on hospital day six without signs of colonic perforation. This case illustrates how selected cases of high-risk foreign body ingestion may be managed conservatively, though close monitoring is critical given the risks of perforation, obstruction, or failure of progression.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Abdominal pain, CT, foreign body ingestion, mental health.

articles.title: How to Place a Central Line: Preparing Your Kit & Performing the Procedure.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: Senior Medical Students and Interns.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Central venous catheter (CVC) placement is a critical, high-risk procedure, and it is considered a core component of emergency medicine training.1 Iatrogenic complications from improper technique-including arterial dilation, pneumothorax, and line-associated bloodstream infections-can significantly impact patient outcomes.2-7 Therefore, emergency medicine trainees should ideally demonstrate procedural competence and adherence to safety practices before performing CVC insertion in clinical settings. These videos serve as part of a mastery-based curriculum designed to reinforce standardized, evidence-based techniques and institutional safety protocols for internal jugular CVC placement.8 The procedural preparation video focuses on sterile technique, ultrasound setup, and CVC kit preparation, and the procedural performance video focuses on sterile technique, the leapfrog technique for ultrasound-guided needle cannulation, and the safe insertion of the central venous catheter.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of these videos, learners will be able to:Identify and gather all necessary materials for internal jugular (IJ) CVC placement.Describe the appropriate positioning of the patient, ultrasound machine, and proceduralist for CVC placement.List common complications of IJ CVC placement.Demonstrate sterile field preparation, including donning personal protective equipment (PPE), placing a sterile drape, and placement of a sterile ultrasound probe cover.Perform a proper pre-procedural time-out including at least two patient identifiers and site verification.Prepare and organize CVC kit components for efficient procedural flow.Identify key anatomical landmarks and optimal patient positioning for right IJ CVC placement using ultrasound guidance.Demonstrate stepwise needle insertion with real-time ultrasound visualization to safely cannulate the internal jugular vein.Verify proper guidewire placement using both short- and long-axis ultrasound views before vessel dilation.Perform safe dilation and catheter advancement using standard procedural technique.Exhibit best-practice behaviors, including port flushing, line securement, and sterile dressing application.Document the procedure and identify post-placement safety steps such as confirmatory chest imaging.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: These videos were watched by emergency medicine-bound, fourth-year medical students as asynchronous study material prior to their mastery-based central venous catheter assessment. Students watched these videos, underwent individual pre-test (baseline) assessments using a 58-item checklist, witnessed a faculty member perform a group demonstration, and then performed deliberate observed practice. The previously published, procedure checklist was developed by a multidisciplinary team of experts, and minimum passing standards were determined using the Mastery-Angoff Technique.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: Efficacy of the videos may be inferred through baseline assessment scores, since students were given access to the videos prior to completing their baseline assessment. Utilizing a quasi-experimental design, these scores were compared to previously published data from the previous 2 years in which students completed the baseline assessment without access to the videos.9.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Ten fourth-year emergency medicine-bound medical students participated in a simulation-based mastery learning procedural course in March 2025. As part of their asynchronous preparation, they watched these two instructional videos: 1. Preparation to Place a Central Venous Cather and 2. Placement of a Central Venous Catheter. Learners were individually assessed in a simulation lab using a 58-item checklist. Pre-test scores ranged from 17 to 89% correct, with a median score of 67%. Previous cohorts from 2022 and 2023 had scores ranging from 19 to 84% with a median score of 43%. After deliberate practice, first post-test scores improved for participants and ranged from 89 to 98% correct.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: These educational videos were an effective component of a broader simulation-based mastery learning curriculum for central venous catheter placement. These videos provided a standardized introduction to both general and institution-specific patient safety practices related to CVC kit setup and CVC insertion. Although video views were not tracked, learners demonstrated significant improvement between pre- and post-testing, indicating the combined instructional approach was effective. Compared to previous years' cohorts, the students who had access to the instructional videos scored better on the baseline assessment, though the small number of participants kept this difference from reaching statistical significance. The videos also allowed students to engage with the material at their own pace, reinforcing safety principles and procedural preparation in a consistent and accessible way.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Procedural Education, Central Venous Catheter, Emergency Medicine.

articles.title: Based Interprofessional Didactic for Emergency Management of Snakebites.
articles.journal_full: Journal of education & teaching in emergency medicine

abstract.label: AUDIENCE
abstract.text: This simulation is intended for Post-Graduate Level 1-4 Residents and Attending Physicians.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Although uncommon in the Northeastern United States, emergency physicians may encounter exotic envenomation through zoological institutions, research facilities, or privately owned exotic reptiles.1 These cases present unique diagnostic and logistical challenges because management frequently requires species-specific antivenom and early consultation with regional toxicology experts.1,2,3 Emergency providers may be unfamiliar with such presentation, evaluation, and treatment steps. Simulation-based education can bridge this gap by allowing interprofessional teams, including residents, attendings, nurses, and pharmacists, to practice coordinated management in a safe environment.4,5 This project evaluates the feasibility, learner-reported preparedness, and educational outcomes associated with a multidisciplinary snakebite simulation.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: By the end of the simulation, participants will be able to recognize and appropriately manage neurotoxic snakebite envenomation, including initiating first-line management and toxicology consultation, coordinating antivenom administration, recognizing and treating antivenom-associated anaphylaxis, assessing and managing progressive respiratory failure, demonstrating effective interprofessional communication using TeamSTEPPS principles,4 and coordinating timely consultation, handoff, and disposition with toxicology, pharmacy, and the critical care team.

abstract.label: EDUCATIONAL METHODS
abstract.text: High-fidelity simulation will be used to provide an immersive environment. TeamSTEPPS (team strategies and tools to enhance performance and patient safety), an evidence-based communication training toolkit, will be used.4 High-fidelity simulation for snakebite education has been shown to enhance clinical skills, foster teamwork, and enable more timely and proficient provider care in snakebite cases.5 The simulation will depict an Indian Cobra snakebite case with evolving neurotoxicity and potential anaphylaxis after antivenom. Teams will manage airway, antivenom reconstitution, and anaphylaxis using TeamSTEPPS principles.4 Scenario branches depend on learner actions; facilitators will provide physiologic cues accordingly.

abstract.label: RESEARCH METHODS
abstract.text: The study consisted of a prospective, single-center, pre/post simulation-based educational pilot study. Physician participants completed pre- and post-surveys and objective multiple-choice tests. Observers used checklists to assess performance. Given the pilot nature of the simulation, no a priori sample size calculation was performed. The simulation was conducted using an interprofessional team model that included emergency medicine physicians, bedside nurses, pharmacists, and a toxicologist. Although all disciplines participated in the simulation to replicate real-word emergency department management of snakebite envenomation, only physician participants completed the pre- and post-intervention knowledge and confidence assessments. The educational study was designed to evaluate physician learning outcomes.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Seven emergency medicine physicians from varying training levels participated in the simulation, with a post-test response rate of 85.7% (n=6). Participants demonstrated significant improvements in self-reported knowledge regarding overall snakebite management (p = 0.042), appropriate first aid (p = 0.010), antivenom complications (p = 0.010), and recognition of both neurotoxic (p = 0.012) and hemotoxic envenomation patterns (p = 0.010). Confidence in administering antivenom (p = 0.025) and working effectively within a team during high-stress emergencies (p = 0.042) improved as well. No significant improvement was observed in objective multiple-choice knowledge scores. Critical action checklists demonstrated that all members were able to identify key clinical findings, communicate with toxicology, and recognize anaphylaxis, although adherence to antivenom preparation steps varied.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The simulation-based didactic was feasible and associated with improvements in self-reported knowledge, confidence, and perceived teamwork related to snakebite management among physician participants. However, objective knowledge scores did not significantly improve, highlighting the need for continued reinforcement of cognitive knowledge and anti-venom related procedural and systems-based skills. Given the pilot design and limited sample size, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Future iterations of the simulation will include larger sample sizes, expand emphasis on antivenom logistics, and incorporate deliberate practice stations to ensure both cognitive and procedural fidelity.

abstract.label: TOPICS
abstract.text: Snakebite, antivenom, anaphylaxis, neurotoxicity, communication, teamwork.

articles.title: Predicting survival in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Development and internal validation of risk scores.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in the pediatric population is associated with poor survival and neurological outcomes. We aimed to develop and internally validate risk scores to predict survival to discharge in pediatric OHCA patients.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We included pediatric OHCA patients in the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival from 2013 to 2023. We used logistic regression (LR) and classification and regression trees (CART) to develop risk scores using 70% of the data and validated them using the remaining 30% of the data. We used discrimination and predictive accuracy to evaluate model performance.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We included 26,895 pediatric patients, of whom 27.8% survived to hospital admission and 11.9% survived to hospital discharge. We developed three separate risk scores for i) infants ii) preschool and school-age children, and iii) adolescents. The most important predictor variables were gender, arrest location, witness status, etiology of arrest, bystander CPR, use of prehospital AED, and first rhythm. Models developed using both LR and CART approaches had good classification accuracy (AUROCC for LR: 0.81, 0.77 and 0.82, AUROCC for CART: 0.78, 0.76, 0.82 for the three age groups) However, we found CART models to be the most useful because they are simpler to follow, classified more patients in low and high survival categories using a smaller number of predictors. The average survival probability in infants for each risk group was 3%, 13%, and 33%, for preschool and school-age children it was 4%, 11%, and 29%, whereas for adolescents it was 4%, 13%, and 48% for the low, moderate, and high survival categories.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Pediatric patients experiencing OHCA can be classified into low, moderate, and high survival categories using a simple risk score and easily identified prehospital variables. These risk scores can facilitate research, monitor the quality of medical services and can potentially support clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Built environment and emergency medical services response time in a high-density megacity: multilevel evidence from urban-suburban.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Emergency medical services (EMS) response time is a key indicator for evaluating the performance of public health system and is closely associated with patient survival rates. However, empirical evidence on the potential relationship between the built environment and EMS response time remains limited, restricting the development of spatially informed strategies for improving EMS system operations.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This study employed 2024 ambulance dispatch data from the Beijing Emergency Center Office Management System, combined with multi-source data on the built environment, to construct a multilevel regression model examining the influence of subdistrict (township)-level built environment factors on EMS response time and investigating the heterogeneity between urban areas and suburbs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The results indicate that, at the citywide level, lower residential facility density and denser arterial and local road networks significantly reduced EMS response time. Specifically, while in central urban areas, high densities of residential facilities were associated with longer response time, in suburban areas, higher densities of local roads enhanced EMS efficiency.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: These findings provide valuable evidence to guide built environment interventions aimed at shortening EMS response time and improving service efficiency across different areas.

articles.title: Spatial optimization of vaccine supply networks in complex terrains: balancing economic feasibility and public health equity.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Vaccine supply planning in hazard-prone terrains faces compounding geographic, socioeconomic, and operational barriers. Conventional models relying on planar distances and static metrics often fail to capture true accessibility disparities, often driving inefficient infrastructure allocation and exacerbating health inequities.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: This study develops an integrated decision-making framework coupling spatial equity, economic feasibility, and multi-scenario resilience to systematically reconfigure the vaccine supply network across 183 counties in Sichuan, China.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Using high-resolution road network data from the AMap Application Programming Interface (API), we model actual geographic impedance based on travel time. An adapted two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method, embedded with socioeconomic vulnerability indicators, pinpoints baseline accessibility disparities. Candidate hubs are selected via entropy-weighted Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) combined with spatial-equity quotas, and a candidate-pool capacity-sufficiency check (α coefficient) determines the final candidate-pool size. A multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MO-MILP) model then co-optimizes hub configuration, capacity scaling, and cross-regional dispatch, endogenously balancing operational efficiency, equity penalties, and capacity expansion costs.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Under entropy-weighted TOPSIS ranking with spatial-equity quotas, the initial 61-hub pool (including 21 existing CDC anchors) provides aggregate capacity equal to 82% of total demand. The capacity-sufficiency rule therefore expands the pool to C* = 103 hubs that satisfy Cap(C*) ≥ 1.2 × total demand. The optimized baseline network (103 candidate hubs, 99 with positive flows) achieves zero unmet demand through endogenous capacity expansion and single-source assignment, with a total objective value of 18,510,357. Sensitivity analysis across α = 1.0-1.4 shows that higher sufficiency coefficients increase the candidate pool (76 → 150 hubs) while reducing required capacity expansion by 63%. Fixed-topology resilience tests indicate zero shortages under all structural failure scenarios when emergency expansion is permitted, whereas zero-expansion stress tests bound shortage-free surge tolerance between +10% and +20% demand growth.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Integrating spatial equity and capacity sufficiency at the candidate-pool stage limits the risk that pool-level capacity deficits are later compensated through node-level expansion. The α coefficient serves as a planning parameter for balancing network redundancy and expansion needs. The α = 1.2 configuration provides a robust and equitable vaccine supply network for mountainous regions under the model's cost assumptions.

articles.title: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest as the First Manifestation of ALCAPA in a 9-Week-Old Infant: Survival to Discharge After Emergency Repair and VA-ECMO.

abstract.text: Background and Clinical Significance: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) usually presents with heart failure at 2-3 months of age; cardiac arrest as the first manifestation is rare and often recognized only at autopsy. Case Presentation: A previously healthy girl collapsed at home at 65 days of age. After dispatcher-assisted parental resuscitation, the emergency team found asystole and achieved return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 4 min of professional resuscitation; the total low-flow time was not recorded. She was in cardiogenic shock (left ventricular ejection fraction 19.8%, high-sensitivity troponin T 2620 ng/L) with acute kidney injury and coagulopathy consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Echocardiography showed a dilated right coronary artery and no flow from the aorta into the left coronary artery. Emergency repair on day 1 was followed by venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for 4 days and continuous renal replacement therapy. The Simpson ejection fraction reached about 50% by day 9, fell to 37-40% during respiratory deterioration and was 45-50% on day 27; mitral regurgitation, graded as massive during VA-ECMO, regressed to trace without valve surgery. She was discharged on day 42 with impaired diastolic indices; no formal neurological assessment was documented. Conclusions: ALCAPA should be considered in every infant with unexplained cardiac arrest, and post-resuscitation echocardiography should assess the coronary origins. Emergency repair with VA-ECMO can achieve survival to discharge despite multiorgan failure, but long-term cardiac and neurodevelopmental follow-up is required.

articles.title: Effect modification by arterial pH on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with shockable rhythm: A multicenter registry study.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of emergency medicine
authors: Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium Investigators

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Arterial pH on emergency department (ED) arrival predicts outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but its effect on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) and neurological outcomes is unclear. We evaluated this association in patients with an initial shockable rhythm and assessed whether pH modified it.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We retrospectively analyzed the Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium registry. Adults with presumed cardiac-origin OHCA, an initial shockable rhythm, ED cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and arterial blood gas data measured after ED arrival were included. Exposure was ECPR initiated in the ED; the primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome at discharge (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2). Arterial pH was categorized as low (≤6.85), medium (>6.85 and <7.05), or high (≥7.05). Multivariable logistic regression assessed ECPR-by-pH interaction, with optimal 1:2 propensity score matching as a sensitivity analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 2183 patients, 213 (9.8%) received ECPR and 154 (7.1%) had a favorable neurological outcome. The association between ECPR and favorable outcome differed across pH categories (p for interaction = 0.004): adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 7.34 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.84-18.98) in the low-pH group, 2.07 (95% CI, 1.06-4.03) in the medium-pH group, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.37-1.94) in the high-pH group. The propensity score-matched analysis showed a similar pattern (p for interaction = 0.036).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Initial arterial pH modified the association between ECPR and neurological outcome after OHCA with an initial shockable rhythm. The association was strongest at low pH and not observed at high pH. Arterial pH may inform ECPR evaluation but should not determine treatment thresholds.

articles.title: Prehospital recognition and differentiation of seizure presentations by paramedics and ambulance nurses: A scoping review.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: The aim of this scoping review was to identify and map the literature examining prehospital clinician recognition and differentiation of seizure presentations.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Scoping Review.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews. A literature search was conducted in January 2026 across five electronic databases.

abstract.label: DATA SOURCES
abstract.text: Medline, Emcare, ProQuest, CINAHL, and SCOPUS.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The search yielded 1264 citations, with 32 full-text articles assessed for eligibility and 18 studies included, six of them identified or re-assessed during peer review. Studies examined paramedics (n = 16) and ambulance nurses (n = 2), with the largest proportion of publications between 2019 and 2021. Across studies reporting diagnostic performance, measured against variable reference standards, sensitivity ranged from 54.0 to 58.5% and specificity from 95.9 to 96.6% using the principal diagnostic definitions reported. Recognition rates ranged from 56.8 to 89.7%, while non-recognition reached 55.3% in one study. Non-convulsive seizures were particularly challenging, with non-recognition rates of 53.0-81.4%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This scoping review indicates that prehospital seizure recognition and differentiation remain suboptimal, particularly for non-convulsive presentations. However, variation in emergency medical services (EMS) workforce configurations and scope of practice limits generalisability across settings. Future research should prioritise outcomes-focused evaluations of seizure recognition and differentiation from key mimics.

articles.title: Admission arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a single-centre retrospective cohort study.
articles.journal_full: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Admission arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) is readily available after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but its independent prognostic value is uncertain and prior evidence is conflicting. We evaluated the association of admission PaCO2 with one-month mortality and neurological outcome, and quantified its incremental prognostic value.

abstract.label: MATERIAL AND METHODS
abstract.text: In a single-center retrospective cohort of 617 adults resuscitated from OHCA (2014-2023), patients were stratified by admission PaCO2 (≤50, >50-70 and >70 mmHg). The primary outcome was one-month all-cause mortality; the secondary outcome was neurological status at one month by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC), analyzed as a dichotomous, ordinal and survivor-restricted endpoint. Associations were estimated with multivariable logistic and ordinal regression adjusted for age, sex, witnessed arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), call-to-arrival time, initial shockable rhythm, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and arrest etiology. PaCO2 was modelled continuously (per 10 mmHg) and categorically; sensitivity analyses used alternative cut-points, and discrimination was quantified by the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC). A simplified Directed Acyclic Graph was used heuristically for variable selection; however, we explicitly acknowledge that post-resuscitation physiology represents a complex feedback system. Therefore, formal causal effect estimation was not attempted, and all analyses are strictly associational and prognostic.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: One-month mortality was 73.6% (454/617) and rose across PaCO2 groups (49.7%, 81.1%, and 90.7%; p < 0.001). Each 10-mmHg increase in PaCO2 was associated with higher mortality after adjustment for measured confounders (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.45, 95% CI 1.24-1.70; p < 0.001), with a concordant gradient for the ordinal CPC outcome (common aOR 1.53, 95% CI 1.31-1.79) and among survivors (aOR 1.91, 95% CI 1.25-2.91). The graded association was robust across categorization schemes but was attenuated after additional adjustment for concurrent acid-base and gas-exchange markers (lactate, base excess, PaO2; aOR 0.80, 95% CI 0.64-1.01; p = 0.063), consistent with strong collinearity between PaCO2 and acid-base status. Adding PaCO2 to a clinical model produced a minimal incremental improvement in discrimination of uncertain clinical utility (AUC 0.794 to 0.816; ΔAUC 0.022, 95% CI 0.002-0.043; optimism-corrected AUC 0.802). Calibration was assessed via bootstrap validation (calibration slope: 0.98, 95% CI 0.89-1.07; calibration-in-the-large: -0.04, 95% CI -0.21 to 0.13), indicating adequate agreement between predicted and observed risks.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this decade-long cohort, higher admission PaCO2 was associated with increased one-month mortality and worse neurological outcome after OHCA, but added minimal discrimination beyond established clinical factors. Because admission PaCO2 is a treatment-dependent exposure - determined by CPR duration and quality, airway and ventilation management, ventilator settings and the ROSC-to-sampling interval, none of which were available - independent prognostic value cannot be established from these data, and the association is most plausibly a signal of arrest severity and of the resuscitation delivered. Attenuation after adjustment for metabolic acidosis is consistent with shared pathophysiology, although mediator overadjustment cannot be excluded. Admission PaCO2 is immediate, inexpensive and universally available, but prospective studies capturing resuscitation timings, CPR quality and standardized ventilation are required before any prognostic role can be claimed.

articles.title: Circadian rhythmicity in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: a scoping review.
articles.journal_full: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) are time-critical events that exhibit circadian patterns, which influence their incidence and clinical outcomes.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To determine whether circadian rhythmicity influences the time of onset of OHCA and STEMI, as well as related clinical outcomes, in patients requiring prehospital emergency care and subsequent hospitalization.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: A scoping review.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The search process included four online databases: MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL Plus with Full Text, ScienceDirect, and ProQuest. The review included original articles published between January 2010 and December 2024.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eighteen studies met the inclusion criteria. These revealed that the incidence of OHCA and STEMI exhibits significant circadian variability, with the highest incidence in the morning. OHCA often has a secondary afternoon/evening peak. The nighttime hours are associated with the lowest incidence. Patients with nighttime OHCA or STEMI have a lower probability of return of spontaneous circulation and worse one-month and one-year survival and neurological outcomes. This less favorable prognosis is not due to the time of day when the event occurs but rather due to limited bystander availability, lower rates of bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation, and longer times to hospital intervention. Additionally, these events were more frequently recorded in winter, while weekly variations were insignificant.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Circadian and seasonal factors influence the occurrence and clinical course of OHCA and STEMI, with worse outcomes for nighttime cases being more a consequence of limited availability than the time of the event itself.

articles.title: Arterial blood gas parameters as mortality predictors in critically ill patients admitted from the emergency department: a prospective observational cohort study.
articles.journal_full: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis is rapidly available in emergency and intensive care settings and constitutes a core component of many critical illness scoring systems. Although ABG parameters are incorporated into many multidimensional critical illness scoring systems, their independent contribution to mortality prediction remains uncertain because these variables may change rapidly during the early course of critical illness and resuscitation. This study evaluated the prognostic performance of ABG parameters and validated severity scoring systems for predicting 28-day mortality in critically ill patients admitted from the emergency department (ED) to the intensive care unit (ICU).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this prospective observational cohort study, 242 adult patients admitted from the ED to the internal medicine ICU between January 2012 and March 2013 were enrolled. Admission ABG parameters (pH, PaCO2, PaO2, and HCO3 -) and severity scores (APACHE II, APACHE IV, and SAPS II) were recorded. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. Prognostic discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall 28-day mortality was 47.1%. Non-survivors had significantly higher APACHE II, APACHE IV, and SAPS II scores than survivors (all p < 0.001). SAPS II demonstrated the best prognostic performance (AUC 0.720; 95% CI 0.659-0.776), significantly outperforming APACHE II and APACHE IV. In contrast, none of the individual ABG parameters independently predicted 28-day mortality (all p > 0.05).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Multidimensional severity scoring systems, particularly SAPS II, provide superior prognostic discrimination compared with isolated ABG parameters in critically ill ED patients. Although ABG analysis remains essential for acute physiologic assessment, isolated blood gas variables appear insufficient as standalone mortality predictors in heterogeneous ICU populations.

articles.title: Performance of the National Early Warning Score 2 for diagnosing bacterial sepsis: a prospective single-center study in Vietnam.
articles.journal_full: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Early recognition of sepsis is vital for enhancing patient outcomes. While the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) has demonstrated good performance for identifying sepsis in emergency departments, its diagnostic accuracy in other clinical environments remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of NEWS2 for bacterial sepsis at an infectious diseases department.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This prospective diagnostic accuracy study consecutively enrolled adult patients admitted to the Department of Infectious Diseases (DID), Military Hospital 175, Vietnam, between March and July 2025. Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years and had suspected bacterial infection. NEWS2 was assessed within the first 24 hours of hospitalization. For patients admitted from the Emergency Department, NEWS2 was calculated using the initial clinical data recorded there; for those admitted from the Outpatient Clinic, it was assessed on admission to the DID. Sepsis was defined according to Sepsis-3 criteria. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, and specificity.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 741 patients screened, 120 were included in the final analysis, 83 patients (69.2%) were diagnosed with sepsis, including 1 case of septic shock. NEWS2 demonstrated moderate discrimination for identifying sepsis, with an AUROC of 0.75 (95% confidence interval: 0.66-0.84). The optimal cut-off was ≥5, yielding a sensitivity of 71.1% and a specificity of 73.0%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: NEWS2 demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance for identifying sepsis in this setting and may serve as a useful adjunctive tool for early risk stratification, particularly in resource-limited infectious diseases departments.

articles.title: Neurologic outcomes following intubation with non-depolarizing vs. depolarizing paralytics in status epilepticus: a target trial emulation.
articles.journal_full: Journal of critical care medicine (Universitatea de Medicina si Farmacie din Targu-Mures)

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Significant controversy exists regarding the optimal pharmacologic approach for endotracheal intubation in patients suffering from status epilepticus (SE).Study Aims: To evaluate post-hospitalization neurologic sequelae and other patient-centered outcomes in SE patients receiving neuromuscular blockers (NMBs). We hypothesized that ability to more rapidly reassess neurologic exam with depolarizing-NMBs (D-NMBs) would mediate improved neurologic outcomes compared to non-depolarizing-NMBs (ND-NMBs).

abstract.label: MATERIAL AND METHODS
abstract.text: We analyzed a cohort of SE patients in a large, quaternary academic system from May 2000 to March 2024. Measured confounders were addressed using propensity score methods and inverse probability of treatment weighting. 480 qualifying adults across closely-affiliated health system hospitals undergoing their first intubation for suspected SE with documented paralytic choice were identified via proprietary institutional database using the key search phrase "status epilepticus" in emergency medicine notes. (Exposure: Paralytic selection during rapid sequence intubation - intervention (D-NMB) vs. control (ND-NMB)). As a surrogate towards functional neurologic outcomes, need for "escalation in level of care" at hospital discharge was assessed as primary outcome of interest. Secondary outcomes included major hyperkalemia-related events (ventricular or pulseless arrhythmias) and 30-day survival.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: D-NMB use relative to ND-NMB use was associated with increased odds of escalation in level of care upon discharge (30.4% vs. 24.4%, odds ratio [OR] 1.35, 95% CI 1.01-1.81) in addition to decreased odds of home disposition upon hospital discharge (61.7% vs. 69.6%, OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.54-0.94). There was no difference in life-threatening peri-intubation cardiac events such as ventricular or pulseless arrhythmias (0.6% vs. 0.8%, p=0.64).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Across 480 SE patients, ND-NMBs were associated with lower need for escalation in level of care upon hospital discharge compared to D-NMBs.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of herbal medicine for Hymenoptera stings: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hymenoptera stings can cause severe anaphylaxis and venom-induced multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. Although conventional medicine (CM) can effectively control acute symptoms, its ability to prevent delayed venom-related organ injury remains limited. Therefore, herbal medicine (HM) combined with CM has been investigated to enhance venom detoxification and elimination. However, comprehensive evidence-based syntheses evaluating these interventions remain limited. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of HM + CM in mitigating venom-induced toxicity.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials was conducted. Major electronic databases were searched for studies comparing HM + CM and CM alone. Outcomes included total effective rate and biomarkers of hepatic, renal, cardiac, and inflammatory responses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall, 11 randomized controlled trials involving 1443 patients were included. While the total effective rate was statistically higher in the HM + CM group than in the CM-alone group (risk ratio, 1.03), this represents a modest 3% relative improvement with limited clinical relevance for acute symptom control. Instead, adjunctive HM was significantly associated with lower levels of biomarkers of hepatic injury (aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and total bilirubin), cardiac injury (creatine kinase and creatine kinase-myocardial band), systemic inflammation (C-reactive protein or high-sensitivity C-reactive protein), and renal dysfunction (serum creatinine), reflecting favorable changes in laboratory biomarkers associated with multi-organ toxicity. Although no adverse events were reported among the limited number of studies that formally assessed safety, the available evidence is insufficient to establish the definitive safety of HM.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: HM combined with conventional care appears to be a potentially useful adjunctive approach for Hymenoptera stings. While its additive effect on acute symptom resolution is clinically modest in the context of standard emergency care, adjunctive HM may offer a broader therapeutic scope. Specifically, it may complement clinical recovery while attenuating venom-induced systemic inflammation and improving related laboratory biomarkers.

articles.title: Initial shockable rhythm detection among patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest by arrest location: A population-based cohort study in Japan.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: We described the patient characteristics, bystander interventions, and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) according to arrest location, focusing on initial rhythm and automated external defibrillator (AED) use.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We analyzed medical-origin OHCAs from a population-based registry (2016-2024) by arrest location: home, nursing home, or other locations. Patient characteristics, bystander interventions, and outcomes were summarized descriptively. Multivariable logistic regression examined the association between arrest location and initial shockable rhythm.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 2478 OHCA cases, initial shockable rhythm was identified in 36.3% (221/609) in nursing homes, 7.1% (113/1582) at home, and 33.4% (96/287) in other locations. After adjustment, the odds of an initial shockable rhythm were higher in nursing homes than at home (adjusted OR, 12.35; 95% CI, 8.93-17.24) and than in other locations (adjusted OR, 2.35; 95% CI, 1.60-3.45). In nursing homes, 96.8% (214/221) of patients with an initial shockable rhythm received an AED shock. One-month survival with favorable neurological outcomes was the lowest in nursing homes (0.8% [5/609]).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Initial shockable rhythm was identified in more than one-third of arrests occurring in nursing homes, and 97% of these patients received an AED shock. This finding may partly reflect earlier AED access, potentially increasing the likelihood of detecting a shockable rhythm soon after collapse. These findings underscore the importance of early rhythm detection through prompt AED use and suggest that extending AED access to home settings warrants further investigation.

articles.title: Experiences and coping strategies of bystanders involved in out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a qualitative study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Participating in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can have a substantial emotional and psychological impact on bystanders. Understanding their experiences and coping strategies may inform supportive interventions that could mitigate the impact on future bystanders.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The study used a qualitative research design grounded in an experiential orientation. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with people who had been involved in CPR during an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in Scotland outside of a professional role. Participants were recruited via social media advertisements. We transcribed and analysed interviews using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eleven interviews were conducted between November 2024 and April 2025. Most bystanders knew the person (n = 9, 81%) as a family member, team member or neighbour. Most were female (n = 9, 82%) and were non-healthcare professionals (n = 7, 64%). Seven of those who experienced OHCA survived, three died, and one outcome was unknown. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four interconnected themes: Emotional impact; Managing multiple roles and responsibilities; Compelled to help but unprepared; and Talking to the right person.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Findings from the interviews with bystanders suggest that OHCA can have a substantial emotional impact, particularly when the person dies or is known to the bystander. Several ways to reduce this impact were identified, including greater emotional preparation in CPR training, involvement in activities that prepare themselves or others for OHCA/CPR, and opportunities to speak with an independent person knowledgeable about OHCA/CPR. Future research should investigate the effectiveness of incorporating these strategies into support interventions for OHCA bystanders.

articles.title: Prehospital Detection of Acute Pulmonary Embolism and Its Association with Clinical Outcomes: A Retrospective Cohort Study.

abstract.text: Background: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially life-threatening condition requiring timely diagnosis and treatment. However, data on prehospital correct PE detection by emergency medical services (EMS) are scarce. Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study at the BG University Hospital Bergmannsheil Bochum, Germany, including all patients with in-hospital confirmed PE (ICD-10: I26.0/I26.9) and admitted by EMS between January 2019 and December 2024. Prehospital PE detection was defined as documentation of PE as the working diagnosis in the EMS protocol. Time to definitive diagnosis was calculated from EMS alarm to computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) acquisition. Multivariable Cox regression and logistic and linear regression models were used to identify predictors of time to diagnosis and clinical outcomes. Main Results: Of 171 patients included, prehospital PE was correctly suspected in only nine cases (5.3%, 95% CI 2.8-9.7%). Time to definitive diagnosis was significantly shorter in patients with correct prehospital PE recognition than in those without (median 2.1 vs. 4.0 h, log-rank p < 0.001). In an exploratory analysis, detection occurred only in physician-staffed EMS encounters (10.8% vs. 0%, p = 0.003). Prehospital intravenous heparin, administered predominantly for suspected myocardial infarction, was also associated with a higher rate of CTPA acquisition, 2.42 (95% CI 1.40-4.19), likely reflecting confounding by indication. Overall, 56 patients (33.1%) were not diagnosed within 6 h of emergency department presentation; 38 (22.5%) were diagnosed only after more than 24 h. Conclusions: Correct detection of PE by EMS is critically low, yet correct detection is associated with earlier imaging. These findings highlight the urgent need for EMS-specific diagnostic strategies and prospective trials to improve prehospital PE detection.

articles.title: Surface Temperature Control After Cardiac Arrest in the Emergency Department Without Feedback-Controlled Devices: An Observational Single-Centre Cohort Study of Routine Care.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Guidelines recommend active fever prevention after cardiac arrest, yet many emergency departments (EDs) lack feedback-controlled temperature-management devices. We describe what simple surface methods achieved in one ED. Methods: Observational cohort of 123 comatose adults with return of spontaneous circulation treated with routine care in a university ED (2017-2020; records to March 2019 analysed retrospectively, later documentation collected prospectively). Technique and length of the management period (12 h or 24 h) were chosen by the treating physician without a written protocol: ice packs (n = 51), ice packs plus a forced-air blanket at its lowest heated setting (32 °C; n = 45), a thin sheet only (n = 21), forced air alone (n = 4) or a circulating-water device (n = 2). Trajectories were compared in a mixed-effects model; the primary endpoint, revised post hoc from the original target of ≤36.0 °C, was fever (≥37.7 °C) after cessation. Results: Ice packs plus forced air gave lower temperatures than ice packs alone from 4 h (adjusted difference -0.68 °C, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.41) to 24 h (-0.44 °C), but overshot below 35.0 °C more often (34/45 vs. 9/51). Fever after cessation was more frequent after physician-selected 12 h than 24 h periods (23/33 vs. 6/90) and in the thin-sheet group (20/21). All 21 thin-sheet patients died; baseline differences suggest allocation by prognosis, and mortality was not analysed causally. Conclusions: Ice packs with or without forced air kept most patients below the fever threshold for up to 36 h; the combination cooled more, which did not mean better control. Safety could not be assessed, and randomised evaluation is needed.

articles.title: Semi-Supervised 2D Pose Estimation for Underwater Divers via Limb-Heatmap-Guided Bidirectional Cross-Representation Consistency Learning.

abstract.text: Underwater image degradation and occlusion make diver keypoints less visually discernible, leading to substantial localization errors in the keypoint pseudo-labels generated by existing semi-supervised methods. These errors can then accumulate and propagate during consistency learning. Moreover, these methods do not fully exploit the human structural information available in unlabeled images. To address these limitations, a limb-heatmap-guided bidirectional cross-representation consistency method is proposed for semi-supervised learning. A keypoint network and a limb network are employed to learn point-level keypoint responses and region-level limb-structure responses, respectively. For labeled data, limb labels are generated automatically from keypoint annotations and a predefined skeletal topology, without additional annotations. For unlabeled data, intra-representation consistency learning is performed for both networks between the easy-augmentation and hard-augmentation views, and bidirectional cross-representation supervision is applied between the two networks. In the keypoint-to-limb path, keypoint predictions are converted into limb pseudo-labels to supervise the limb network; in the limb-to-keypoint path, limb heatmaps reconstructed from keypoint predictions are compared with the predictions of the limb network to constrain the keypoint configuration. During model inference, only the keypoint network is retained, with no additional inference cost. On the independent test set of a single underwater diver dataset constructed for this study, the proposed method achieves a mean PCKh@0.5 of 80.07% using all labeled training data and outperforms the comparison methods at labeled-data proportions of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. These results demonstrate that region-level limb structure provides effective complementary supervision for point-level keypoint localization within the evaluated setting. Broader applicability requires further validation.

articles.title: Prehospital Facial Recognition Technology: Randomized Controlled Simulation Study.
articles.journal_full: The western journal of emergency medicine

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: The risk of medical errors increases for the approximately 689,000 unidentified, noncommunicative patients who present to emergency departments annually. The concomitant rise in hospital admissions, lengths of stay, and mortality will likely persist unless approaches to identifying noncommunicative patients are developed and adopted. Facial recognition technology could provide a solution where scanning the face reliably provides access to identification and medical history of patients who self-enroll in the application database. Our objective was to compare paramedics' ability to identify noncommunicative patients and make related clinical decisions using a cloud-based facial-recognition application vs standard practice.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a double-blind, randomized controlled study with 90 participating firefighterparamedics in a simulated patient encounter. Our primary outcome was patient identification. Secondary outcomes included identification of key medical information, appropriateness of treatment decisions, and transport to the patient's preferred hospital.
